blue.title: Edition Builder
blue.use: Turns the night's wires into a one-page morning edition he can read on the 7 am train.
blue.tools: Inoreader (free) or Feedly (free), AP News, Reuters, Google News, ReliefWeb
blue.inputs: An RSS reader loaded with his feeds, and 20 minutes before leaving.
blue.output: One page: five sections, two to four items each, one line per item with a link and a 'why it matters' clause.
method: Set up feeds once by section: US, Israel and Middle East, Sudan and the Horn, Russia and Ukraine, AI and tech.
Each morning, open the reader and sort each section by newest; skim headlines only.
Pick two to four items per section that are new facts, not commentary.
Write each as one line: what happened, who says so, why it matters to his beats.
Prefer wire copy (AP, Reuters) for facts; mark single-source claims as unconfirmed.
Add one 'watch today' line: a vote, a deadline, a scheduled speech.
Mark all as read; anything worth a Marginalia piece goes to the ideas list.
blue.prompt: You are Bridge Captain, Editor-in-Chief. Here are last night's headlines and links from my feeds: {paste}. Build a one-page morning edition with sections US, Israel and the Middle East, Sudan and the Horn, Russia and Ukraine, AI and tech. Two to four items each, one line per item: what happened, source, and why it matters to someone covering Israel-Africa ties, influence operations and AI. Mark single-source claims unconfirmed. Separate facts from opinion pieces. Add one 'watch today' line. Under 350 words.
checklist: Two to four items per section
Each line has source and why it matters
Story ideas moved to the ideas list
blue.example: Tuesday 6:35 am. Inoreader shows 214 unread across 16 feeds. In 18 minutes the Captain builds the edition. Israel and the Middle East: three items, one marked 'single source, Israeli outlet only, wait for a wire'. Sudan and the Horn: two items, one from Radio Dabanga on displacement near a Darfur town, one from Reuters on aid access talks. Russia: one item. AI and tech: two items, including a new open-weight model release that matters for the Local Models Lab. US: two items. Watch today: a UN Security Council briefing on Sudan scheduled for 10 am New York time. Two items go to the Marginalia ideas list. He reads the page on the 7:12 train and marks all read.

blue.title: Fact-Check Protocol
blue.use: Traces any viral claim, quote, image or number back to its origin in five steps.
blue.tools: Google Fact Check Explorer, Google Lens, TinEye, InVID-WeVerify browser plugin, Wayback Machine
blue.inputs: The claim as he saw it, with the link or screenshot.
blue.output: A verdict (true, false, misleading, unproven), the origin, and the chain of how it spread.
method: 1 Stop: note the emotion it triggers and do not share yet.
2 Investigate the source: who posted it, how old is the account, what else it posts.
3 Find better coverage: search the claim in Google Fact Check Explorer and two wire services.
4 Trace to the original: for quotes find the speech or transcript; for images run Google Lens and TinEye and sort by oldest; for videos use InVID keyframes; for numbers find the report.
5 Compare: does the original say what the viral version claims? Note what was cut or added.
Write the verdict with the chain: original, first distortion, the version he saw.
Archive both the original and the viral version.
blue.prompt: You are Navigator of Record, Fact-Checker. Claim: {paste text or describe image}. Seen at: {link}. Walk me through the five steps: stop, investigate the source, find better coverage, trace to the original, compare. Give me the exact searches to run (Google Lens or TinEye for images, transcript searches for quotes, report titles for numbers). After I paste what I found {results}, give a verdict of true, false, misleading or unproven, and write the chain from original to the version I saw.
blue.example: Claim: a viral X post shows a photo of burned homes with the caption 'RSF burned this Darfur village yesterday.' Source: an account created four months ago that posts only Sudan war content. Google Lens and TinEye sorted by oldest return the same photo in a 2023 news article about an earlier attack in West Darfur. InVID is not needed; it is a still image. Fact Check Explorer has nothing yet. Comparison: the photo is real but more than two years old, and the place in the original caption differs. Verdict: misleading, a real image recycled with a false date. Chain: 2023 news photo, reposted on Telegram in 2025, then the X post. Both archived.

blue.title: The Balanced Read
blue.use: Reads one story through right, center and left outlets and shows what each emphasizes or leaves out.
blue.tools: AllSides (free), Ground News (free tier), AP News, Reuters
blue.output: A table of three to six outlets with headline, framing, facts included or left out, and a shared-facts core.
method: Pick one story, not a theme.
Find it in at least one outlet from the right, center and left (AllSides or Ground News help locate them).
Record each headline exactly and the first fact each one leads with.
Note loaded words, which sources are quoted, and which facts appear in only one outlet.
Build the shared core: facts all versions agree on.
Write two lines on how each side frames the story.
Note which version his own audience is most likely to have seen.
blue.prompt: You are Spectrum Balancer, Newsstand Librarian. Story: {describe or links}. Compare coverage from at least one right-leaning, one center and one left-leaning outlet: {list outlets or let me paste articles}. For each: exact headline, the lead fact, loaded words, who is quoted, and facts only that outlet includes. Then give the shared factual core and a two-line description of each framing. Be even-handed; do not tell me which is correct beyond the facts.
checklist: At least one outlet each from right, center and left
Facts unique to one outlet listed
blue.example: Story: a US decision to cut a humanitarian aid program in Sudan. Right-leaning outlet headline leads with the cost to taxpayers and claims of aid diversion, quoting a member of Congress. Center wire story leads with the dollar amount and the agencies affected, quoting both a State Department statement and a UN official. Left-leaning outlet leads with expected effects on refugee camps in Chad, quoting an aid worker. Fact only in the right-leaning piece: an inspector general report on diversion. Fact only in the left-leaning piece: the number of people served by the program. Shared core: the program, the amount, the date. Marginalia note: readers on X mostly saw the right-leaning framing.

blue.title: Odds and Calls
blue.use: Puts each of his Calls beside prediction-market and forecaster prices and explains any gap.
blue.tools: Polymarket (viewing), Kalshi (viewing), Manifold, Metaculus, Google Sheets
blue.inputs: His open Calls with probabilities and resolution dates.
blue.output: A table: his odds, market odds, Metaculus community odds, the gap, and a note on whether to update.
method: List each open Call with his probability and resolution date.
Search each on Polymarket, Kalshi, Manifold and Metaculus; match the question wording closely.
Record each price with the date checked; note trading volume or number of forecasters.
Compute the gap between his number and the best-matched market.
If the gap is over 15 points, write what he knows that the market does not, or update.
Thin markets with low volume count for less.
Recheck monthly and log any change in the Forecast Ledger.
blue.prompt: You are Probability Officer, Odds Desk. My open Calls: {paste question, my probability, resolution date}. Market prices I found: {paste, with source, volume and date}. Build a table with my odds, each market's odds, the gap, and how well the market question matches mine. For each gap over 15 points, ask me what I know that the market does not, and tell me whether the evidence I give justifies holding my number. Note which markets are too thin to trust.
checklist: Searched at least two markets per Call
Gaps over 15 points explained or updated
Changes logged in the Forecast Ledger
blue.example: Three open Calls on Nov 5. Call 1: a Sudan nationwide ceasefire by Mar 31, 2027; his 12 percent; no market found; Metaculus has a similar question but with a different deadline, so it is noted, not compared. Call 2: a named country establishing diplomatic relations with Israel by end of 2027; his 35 percent; a Polymarket market on a close question sits at 22 percent with modest volume. Gap: 13 points, under the threshold. Call 3: a major AI lab releasing a specified model by June 2027; his 70 percent, Manifold 48 percent with 60 traders. Gap: 22. His reason: a public roadmap statement. The Officer judges that thin and he trims to 60. Logged in the Ledger.

blue.title: Horn Daily
blue.use: Sudan and the Horn of Africa in five sourced lines each morning, confirmed or flagged.
blue.tools: Radio Dabanga, Sudan Tribune, ReliefWeb, Reuters, Addis Standard, The East African, X lists
blue.inputs: Ten minutes and the feeds or X list for the region.
blue.output: Five lines: place, event, source, confirmation status, and why it matters.
method: Build the source set once: Sudanese outlets, regional outlets, wires, UN and NGO updates, and a private X list of reporters.
Scan in this order: wires, ReliefWeb updates, Sudanese outlets, regional outlets, X.
Pick five items: at least three on Sudan, one or two on Ethiopia, Eritrea, Somalia, South Sudan or the Red Sea.
Each line: place, what happened, source, and 'confirmed by second source' or 'single source'.
Claims by either armed side are labeled as claims, with the side named.
Add one 'why it matters' clause per line.
Save the day's five in a running file for briefs and Calls.
blue.prompt: You are Watcher of the Horn, Sudan and Horn Desk. Here are today's items from my sources: {paste headlines, links}. Write five lines: at least three on Sudan and one or two on the wider Horn or the Red Sea. Each line: place, what happened, the source, confirmation status (second source or single source), and why it matters in a clause. Label any claim by the SAF, the RSF or another armed group as a claim, naming who made it. No speculation beyond the sources.
blue.example: Nov 6, illustrative lines showing the format, not real reports. 1) North Darfur: Radio Dabanga reports new displacement toward Tawila after shelling; single source; matters for aid access. 2) Khartoum: Reuters reports a power plant back in partial service; second source (Sudan Tribune); matters for return of civilians. 3) Kordofan: the RSF claims capture of a town on a supply road; claim by RSF, denied by SAF, no independent source; matters for the El Obeid corridor. 4) Ethiopia: Addis Standard reports talks between federal officials and a regional party; single source. 5) Red Sea: a shipping update on Houthi threats to vessels, Reuters; matters for Port Sudan trade. Five lines saved to the running file in 40-briefs.

blue.title: Foreign-Language Desk
blue.use: Reads Hebrew, Russian and Arabic reporting in translation, with key terms and outlet slant flagged.
blue.tools: DeepL (free), Google Translate, Yandex Translate (strong for Russian), Ynet, Meduza, Al Jazeera Arabic, Sudanese Arabic outlets
blue.inputs: A link or pasted text in Hebrew, Russian or Arabic.
blue.output: A faithful translation, a three-line summary, flagged loaded terms, and a note on the outlet's ownership and slant.
method: Identify the outlet, owner and slant first (state-run, independent, partisan, exile).
Translate with two engines (DeepL and Google or Yandex) and compare where they differ.
Flag loaded terms and their English equivalents (for example, words for 'martyr', 'terrorist', 'special military operation').
Check names and places transliterated correctly against an English source.
Summarize in three lines and note what the English press did not report.
Mark machine translation as such when quoting; quote only checked passages.
Save the original and the translation together.
blue.prompt: You are Signals Linguist, Translator Desk. Text in {language} from {outlet}: {paste}. Tell me the outlet's ownership and slant. Translate the text faithfully, keeping official terms as used (give the original word in brackets for loaded terms). Note any phrase where a literal translation would mislead. Summarize in three lines and point out anything not reported in English-language coverage. Mark uncertainty where the text is ambiguous.
blue.example: Text: a Russian state news agency piece on Russia's naval presence plans in Port Sudan. Slant: state-owned, official line. DeepL and Yandex agree on most lines; they differ on 'пункт материально-технического обеспечения', which DeepL renders as 'logistics point' and Yandex as 'material and technical support point'; the Linguist keeps 'logistics support point' with the original in brackets, noting Russian officials avoid the word 'base'. Summary: the piece frames the plan as agreed and on schedule, quotes no Sudanese official, and omits Sudanese statements that it is under review. Next step: check whether the independent outlet Meduza covered it differently. Saved as 2026-11-06_ru-port-sudan_orig-and-en.docx.

blue.title: Imagery Check
blue.use: Checks a claim about a place against free satellite imagery, fire data and maps.
blue.tools: Copernicus Browser (Sentinel-2, free account), NASA FIRMS (fire hotspots), Google Earth Pro (historical imagery), SunCalc, OpenStreetMap
blue.inputs: The claim, its place name or coordinates, and the date range.
blue.output: Before and after views, fire data if relevant, a confidence level, and the limits of what the imagery can show.
method: Pin the place: get coordinates from OpenStreetMap or Google Earth; confirm the spelling of the place name.
Check NASA FIRMS for fire hotspots in the date range (useful for burning claims).
In Copernicus Browser, load Sentinel-2 true color for a clear date before and after; check cloud cover.
Compare: new burn scars, cleared structures, new earthworks, vehicles in large groups.
Know the limit: Sentinel-2 is 10 meters per pixel, enough for villages and burn scars, not single vehicles or people.
For photos, use SunCalc and shadow direction to test the claimed time.
Write the confidence (high, medium, low) and what would raise it.
blue.prompt: You are Map Officer, Geospatial Desk. Claim: {claim}. Place: {name or coordinates}. Dates: {range}. Tell me how to check it step by step with Copernicus Browser (Sentinel-2), NASA FIRMS and Google Earth Pro: which layers, dates and settings. Tell me what visible change would support or contradict the claim at 10-meter resolution, and what the imagery cannot show. After I describe what I saw {observations}, give a confidence level and what would raise it.
checklist: FIRMS checked for the date range
Clear before and after images found
blue.example: Claim: a village in North Darfur was burned between Oct 20 and 25. Coordinates taken from OpenStreetMap; the name has two spellings in English reports, both noted. NASA FIRMS shows several hotspots over the village on Oct 22 and 23. Copernicus Browser: a clear Sentinel-2 image from Oct 15 shows the village pattern of compounds; an Oct 30 image shows dark burn scars over roughly half the settled area. Limit: at 10 meters, it cannot show who set the fires or whether people were inside. Confidence: high that large-scale burning happened in the window, none on who did it. To raise attribution confidence: witness reports or verified video from the site.

blue.title: Israel Trip Planner
blue.use: Plans an Israel trip: dates, fares, entry rules, family visits and holy sites, in one plan.
blue.tools: Google Flights (price tracking), State Department travel advisory page, Israel's ETA-IL official site, Moovit (Israeli transit), Google Maps
blue.inputs: Possible dates, budget, which passport he travels on, family locations, and sites he wants to see.
blue.output: A plan with dates, a fare watch, an entry checklist, a day-by-day outline, and a safety check.
method: Pick a window outside the school terms and Walgreens high-demand weeks.
Set Google Flights price tracking for JFK or Newark to Tel Aviv for the window.
Check entry: travelers on visa-exempt passports such as the US need an approved ETA-IL before flying; apply only on the official site.
Read the current State Department advisory for Israel and the regions he plans to visit; enroll in STEP.
Map family visits first, then holy sites, then free days.
Plan transport without a car: trains and buses (Moovit), sherut shared taxis.
Check Shabbat timing: most public transport stops Friday afternoon to Saturday night.
blue.prompt: You are Pilot for the Holy Land, Israel Desk. Trip window: {dates}. Budget: {amount}. Passport: {which}. Family in: {cities}. Sites I want: {list}. Build a plan: fare watch settings, entry steps (ETA-IL or visa depending on passport, with the official source to check), travel advisory check, and a day-by-day outline that puts family first, groups sites by area, uses public transit, and accounts for Shabbat. Flag anything that depends on current security conditions and tell me to verify it close to departure.
checklist: Window chosen around school and work
blue.example: Window: June 10 to 20, 2027, after the spring term. Google Flights tracking for JFK to Tel Aviv. Entry: he applies for ETA-IL on the official site in April and confirms the passport is valid for six months beyond travel. Plan: days 1 to 3 with family; days 4 to 6 in Jerusalem, staying near the Old City, visiting the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, the Western Wall, the Russian Ecclesiastical Mission's convents on the Mount of Olives and at Gethsemane, and the Holy Trinity Cathedral in the Russian Compound; day 7, Friday, museum in the morning, then a quiet Shabbat; days 8 to 10 in the Galilee by bus, including Mount Tabor. Safety: advisory read now and again on June 3.

blue.title: Packing List
blue.use: A packing list for any trip type, built carry-on first, with nothing forgotten.
blue.tools: iPhone Reminders (reusable lists), TSA website (liquids rule), weather app
blue.inputs: Trip type, length, weather, and transport.
blue.output: A carry-on list, an extra list only if needed, a liquids bag check, and a leaving-home check.
method: Start from the bag: one carry-on backpack, then add only what does not fit.
Clothes by days: shirts and underwear for days plus one, layers instead of bulk, one outfit for church or a meeting.
Liquids: TSA 3-1-1 (containers 3.4 ounces or less, in one quart-size bag) for any flight.
Tech: phone charger, battery pack, cable, earbuds; laptop only if work needs it.
Documents: ID or passport, tickets in the wallet app, a paper copy of key bookings.
Trip-type extras: CVAC gloves for a long shift, rain shell, prayer book, medications.
Leaving-home check: keys, wallet, phone, charger, stove and lights.
blue.prompt: You are Loadmaster, Packing Clerk. Trip: {type}, {days} days, weather {forecast}, travel by {train, plane, bus}. Must bring: {items}. Build a carry-on-first list grouped by clothes, toiletries, tech, documents and trip-specific items. Keep liquids within TSA 3-1-1 if flying. Add a second list only for what truly cannot fit. End with a five-item leaving-home check. Save it in a form I can paste into iPhone Reminders.
checklist: Clothes counted by days plus one
blue.example: Trip: two nights in Washington, DC for a think-tank panel on the Horn of Africa, by Amtrak from New York (Harlem Line to Grand Central, subway to Penn Station). Weather: 45 to 60 degrees, rain on day two. One 30-liter backpack. Clothes: two shirts, one collared shirt and chinos for the panel, three sets of underwear and socks, a sweater, a rain shell. Toiletries: travel sizes, no liquids limit on Amtrak, but kept small anyway. Tech: phone, charger, battery pack, earbuds; laptop left home, notes on the phone. Documents: ID, Amtrak ticket in Wallet, hostel booking screenshot. Extras: small notebook, pocket prayer book. Leaving check done at 6:10 am.

blue.title: Without a Car
blue.use: Plans any trip from Chappaqua by Metro-North, Bee-Line bus, rideshare and walking, with backup.
blue.tools: TrainTime (MTA official app), Transit app, Google Maps, Bee-Line bus schedules (Westchester County site), Uber, Lyft
blue.inputs: Where he is going, when he must arrive, and how much he can spend.
blue.output: A door-to-door plan with each leg, times, cost, a margin, and a backup if a connection fails.
method: Start from the arrival time and work backward.
Rail: Chappaqua is on the Harlem Line; check TrainTime for the train, track and peak or off-peak fare.
Bus: check the Bee-Line route schedule; many routes run less often on weekends and evenings.
Plan the first and last mile: walk time, or a short rideshare when walking is unsafe or too long.
Add a margin of 10 minutes per transfer and 20 for anything that cannot be missed.
Write the backup: next train, alternate bus, or rideshare cost to cover the broken leg.
Buy tickets in the TrainTime app before boarding; on-board fares cost more.
blue.prompt: You are Transit Master, Transit Planner. I am in Chappaqua with no car. I need to reach {destination} by {time} on {day}, and return around {time}. Budget: {amount}. Plan door to door with Metro-North, Bee-Line buses, the subway if in the city, walking, and rideshare only where needed. Give each leg with departure, arrival, and cost, a margin per transfer, and a backup for the riskiest leg. Tell me which schedule to recheck that day.
checklist: Bus schedule checked for that day
Backup written for the riskiest leg
blue.example: Goal: arrive at Purchase College for a 10 am class on Tuesday. Plan: walk to Chappaqua station, 15 minutes; southbound Harlem Line train to White Plains, about 20 minutes; walk to the TransCenter bus bays; Bee-Line route 12 toward Purchase College, about 20 to 25 minutes depending on traffic; walk to the building. He picks the train that leaves a 25-minute margin before class. Cost: an off-peak one-way rail ticket in TrainTime plus the bus fare. Riskiest leg: the bus connection. Backup: the next route 12 bus, or an Uber from White Plains to campus, about 15 minutes. Recheck that morning: the route 12 schedule, since college-term and holiday service can differ.

brown.title: The Chore Rota
brown.use: A weekly chore rota sized to his shifts: short tasks on work days, the heavy ones on days off.
brown.tools: Google Sheets, iPhone Reminders (recurring), iPhone Calendar
brown.inputs: This week's Walgreens, class and CVAC schedule, the chores he owns at home, and any his parents asked for.
brown.output: A seven-day rota with each chore's day, minutes and reminder, kept under 30 minutes on shift days.
method: List every chore he owns with its frequency and honest minutes: litter, dishes, trash and recycling night, his room, bathroom, laundry, wood stacking.
Ask his parents which shared chores are his this month, and write them in so nothing is assumed.
Mark each day as shift, class, CVAC or free from the calendar.
Cap shift days at about 20 to 30 minutes of chores. Daily items (litter, dishes) go everywhere; heavy ones (bathroom, laundry, wood) go to free days.
Put fixed-date chores first: trash and recycling go out the night before pickup.
Set a recurring iPhone reminder for each chore at the time he will actually do it.
Sunday: tick what got done, move misses to the next free day, and rebuild the week.
brown.prompt: Majordomo, build my chore rota for {week dates}. My schedule: {each day: Walgreens shift times, classes, CVAC}. Chores I own, with how often and how long: {list}. Trash and recycling pickup days: {days}. Anything my parents asked for this week: {list}. Keep shift days under {minutes} minutes. Give me a seven-day table (day, chores, minutes, reminder time) and flag any week where the chores do not fit.
brown.example: Week of Nov 9. Shifts Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday; class Wednesday; CVAC overnight Saturday; Sunday free. Daily: litter (5 minutes) and his dishes (10). Monday night: trash and recycling out (10). Wednesday after class: vacuum his room and the stairs his mom asked about (25). Sunday: bathroom (20), laundry (Laundry System kit), and an hour stacking split wood. Shift days total 15 to 25 minutes. Reminders: litter at 7:30 am, dishes at 9 pm, trash Monday at 8 pm. Sunday review: all done except the stairs, which moved to Sunday.

brown.title: Ten-Minute Room Reset
brown.use: Bring his room back to ready in ten minutes, in a fixed order, so it never becomes a weekend job.
brown.tools: iPhone Clock (10-minute timer), a laundry hamper, a trash bag, one 'elsewhere' box
brown.inputs: Ten minutes and the room as it is.
brown.output: A reset room and, once a week, a note of what keeps piling up so it gets a home.
method: Set a ten-minute timer. Stop when it rings even if not finished; the point is daily, not perfect.
Minute 0 to 1: trash into the bag, cups and plates stacked at the door to go down.
Minute 1 to 3: clothes. Dirty into the hamper, clean folded or hung. Nothing on the chair.
Minute 3 to 5: anything that belongs elsewhere in the house goes into the box, to be emptied on the way out.
Minute 5 to 7: desk. Papers into one tray, cables coiled, keyboard and mouse squared, a wipe of the surface.
Minute 7 to 9: make the bed, open the blinds or set the lamp, clear the floor path.
Minute 9 to 10: take the box, dishes and trash out. On Sunday, note the item that showed up most and give it a home.
brown.prompt: Chambermaid, here is my room right now: {describe, or list what is out of place}. Layout: {bed, desk, closet, shelves}. My time: {minutes}. Give me a reset order that fits exactly in that time, starting with whatever makes the biggest visible difference. Then name the two items that probably keep coming back and a permanent home for each using things I likely already own.
checklist: Clothes in hamper or put away
Weekly repeat offender given a home
brown.example: Thursday, 10:40 pm after a shift. Start: three water bottles and a plate on the desk, work clothes on the chair, a CVAC jacket on the floor, cables tangled behind the monitor, and two library books on the bed. Reset: trash and dishes (1 minute), clothes hampered and jacket hung (2), books into the elsewhere box for the bag (1), desk cleared and wiped (2), bed made (2), all out the door at 9:40. Sunday note: the CVAC jacket landed on the floor four nights out of seven, so a $0 fix: the hook on the back of the door is now the jacket's only home.

brown.title: Batch-Cook Sunday
brown.use: Four meals from one two-hour Sunday session, in US measures, with fast-day portions included.
brown.tools: Google Sheets, iPhone Timer, an instant-read thermometer, containers
brown.inputs: The week's fast days, his protein target, the family kitchen's free hours, and containers.
brown.output: Four cooked dishes portioned into about twelve meals, labeled, with a fridge and freezer plan.
method: Pick four dishes that share an oven and two burners: one roast protein, one pot, one grain, one tray of vegetables. Make at least one meatless for Wednesday and Friday.
Book the kitchen with his parents for a two-hour slot.
Start the longest cook first (oven at 425 F), then the pot, then the rice, then vegetables in the oven's second rack.
Cook poultry to 165 F, checked with the thermometer in the thickest piece.
Portion while warm into containers, label with dish and date.
Cool and refrigerate within two hours. Eat within three to four days; freeze anything planned for later in the week.
Wash as he goes; the session ends with the kitchen clean.
brown.prompt: Cook, plan my batch-cook Sunday. Fast days this week: {days}, my priest's guidance: {notes}. Protein target: {grams a day}. Equipment: {oven, burners, pots, sheet pans}. Time: {hours}. Dislikes: {list}. Give me four dishes that make about twelve portions, every recipe in cups, tablespoons, teaspoons and pounds only, a minute-by-minute order of work, the safe internal temperature for any meat, and which portions to refrigerate versus freeze.
brown.example: Sunday Nov 8, 2 to 4 pm. Sheet-pan chicken: 3 pounds boneless thighs with 2 tablespoons olive oil, 2 teaspoons smoked paprika, 1 teaspoon garlic powder and 1 1/2 teaspoons salt, 425 F for 25 minutes, checked at 168 F. Turkey chili: 2 pounds ground turkey, 2 cans kidney beans, 1 can crushed tomatoes, 1 diced onion, 2 tablespoons chili powder, simmered 40 minutes. Rice: 3 cups dry white rice with 6 cups water. Fast-day tray: 3 diced sweet potatoes roasted, then mixed with 2 cans black beans, 1 teaspoon cumin and lime. Result: 13 portions; Thursday's and Friday's frozen.

brown.title: Grocery List
brown.use: Turn the week's meal plan into one store list sorted by aisle, so one trip covers it.
brown.tools: Apple Reminders (Groceries list sorts by section), Google Keep, the store's app or weekly flyer
brown.inputs: This week's meal plan or batch-cook recipes, what is already in the kitchen, and how he gets to the store.
brown.output: One list by store section with amounts, already-have items removed, and an estimated cost.
method: List every ingredient from the meal plan with its amount, in the same units as the recipe.
Combine duplicates (two recipes using onions become one line with the total).
Check the fridge, freezer and pantry and strike what is already there. Ask before using family staples.
Add the standing items: soy milk, peanut butter, eggs on non-fast weeks, fruit for shift days, cat food if it is his turn.
Paste into the Apple Reminders Groceries list, which sorts by section, or order by the store's layout.
Check the store flyer or app for sales on the three priciest items and swap if it saves real money.
Without a car, size the trip to what he can carry or plan a ride; two sturdy bags hold about a week.
brown.prompt: Market Runner, turn this meal plan into one grocery list: {recipes or meals with amounts}. Already in the kitchen: {items}. Standing items I always buy: {list}. Getting to the store: {walk, bus, ride} so it must fit in {bags}. Combine duplicates, strike what I have, group by store section (produce, protein, dairy and alternatives, canned, grains, frozen, household), and estimate the total cost at a regular suburban supermarket.
checklist: Trip fits what he can carry
brown.example: From Batch-Cook Sunday: produce, 2 onions, 3 sweet potatoes, 2 limes, 1 head garlic, bananas; protein, 3 pounds chicken thighs, 2 pounds ground turkey, 1 block extra-firm tofu; canned, 2 cans kidney beans, 2 cans black beans, 1 can crushed tomatoes; grains, rice was in the pantry, struck; alternatives, a half gallon of soy milk; staples, peanut butter. Smoked paprika and chili powder were in the cupboard. The flyer had chicken thighs on sale, so the list stayed. Estimate about $58. Two bags, carried home from the bus stop.

brown.title: Household Budget
brown.use: Keep his groceries and household supplies inside a monthly cap, tracked in five minutes a week.
brown.tools: Google Sheets, his bank app, receipt photos in iPhone Photos
brown.inputs: His monthly cap, receipts or bank lines for groceries and supplies, and what he covers at home.
brown.output: A month sheet: cap, spent so far, left per week, and the one category to watch.
method: Agree what he covers at home (his own food extras, toiletries, his share of supplies) so the cap is about his spending only.
Set a cap for the month and split it into categories: groceries, supplies, cat items if his, a small buffer.
Each Sunday, enter the week's grocery and supply lines from the bank app or receipt photos.
Compute spent so far and what is left per remaining week.
If a category is over by the middle of the month, cut the next grocery list (store brand, fewer snacks) rather than raising the cap.
At month end, record total against cap and carry any surplus into savings, not next month's groceries.
Keep this sheet to his own spending; other people's finances stay out.
brown.prompt: Steward's Purse, here is my month so far: cap {amount}, categories {list with limits}, spending by week {lines}. Weeks left: {number}. Tell me what is left per week in each category and which category is running hot. Then give me three specific swaps on my next grocery list that would bring it back under without cutting protein, and one habit change for shift days. Keep it to my own spending only.
checklist: What he covers agreed at home
Overrun fixed by the next list
brown.example: November cap: $220. Groceries $160, supplies $35, buffer $25. By Sunday Nov 15: groceries $104 (the $58 batch-cook trip plus snacks on shift breaks), supplies $12. Left: $56 for groceries over two weeks, $28 a week. Running hot: break snacks, $19 in two weeks bought at work. Swaps: bring a peanut butter sandwich and fruit on shift days, store-brand soy milk, and chicken thighs only when on sale. Supplies stayed at $12 all month, since toothpaste and razors were bought in the first week. Month close, Nov 30: $211 spent, $9 surplus moved to savings.

brown.title: Laundry System

brown.inputs: His clothing loads, the household's washer schedule, and his fixed day.
brown.output: A fixed weekly laundry day with sorted loads, settings per load, and everything put away the same day.
method: Pick a fixed day that is free every week and clear it with the household washer schedule.
Keep three hampers or bags: darks and work clothes, lights, and gym clothes plus towels.
Read care labels once and note the exceptions (wool socks, any CVAC items with special care).
Wash darks and lights cold. Gym clothes cold, inside out, no fabric softener, air dry or low heat.
Towels and sheets warm, sheets every two weeks.
Clean the dryer lint screen before every load.
Fold straight out of the dryer and put everything away that day; hang uniform pieces at once. Lint roll the cat hair off work clothes.
brown.prompt: Launderer, set up my laundry system. Clothes I wash each week: {work clothes, CVAC uniform, gym clothes, casual, towels, sheets}. Washer and dryer access: {when free}. My free day: {day}. Anything with special care: {items}. Folded and put away the same day

Loads: darks with two Walgreens shifts' worth of work clothes and CVAC pants, cold, normal; gym clothes and socks, cold, inside out, no softener, hung on a drying rack in his room; towels and his sheets, warm (sheets every other week). Cat hair on work pants handled with the lint roller by the door.

brown.title: Cat Care
brown.use: Feeding, litter, vet dates and supplies for the family cats, with the signs that mean call the vet.
brown.tools: Google Sheets, iPhone Reminders, iPhone Calendar, the vet's patient portal if they have one
brown.inputs: Each cat's name, age, food and amount from the vet or bag, the vet's number, and who does what at home.
brown.output: A care sheet per cat, daily and weekly reminders, vet dates on the calendar, and a supply reorder point.
method: Write a card per cat: age, food, amount per meal in cups (from the vet or the bag), medications, vaccines due, vet number.
Feed at the same times daily. Fresh water every day.
Litter: scoop daily, full change and wash every two to four weeks for clay litter. One box per cat plus one is the usual rule.
Brush and check weekly: coat, eyes, ears, teeth, weight trend.
Vet: annual checkup and vaccines as the vet schedules them (New York requires rabies vaccination for cats). Put the dates on the family calendar.
Reorder food and litter when one week's supply is left.
Call the vet the same day for: straining in the box with little or no urine (an emergency in male cats), no eating for a day, repeated vomiting, hiding and lethargy. Keep lilies out of the house.
brown.prompt: Keeper of the Cats, set up a care plan for our cats: {each cat's name, age, food, amount per meal, health notes}. Who does what at home: {split}. Vet: {name, last visit, what is due}. Supplies on hand: {food, litter, how much}. Give me a care card per cat, a daily and weekly routine with reminder times, the next vet dates to book, a reorder point for supplies, and a short list of warning signs that mean call the vet the same day.
checklist: Vet dates on the family calendar
Warning signs posted by the food
brown.example: Two cats, an older male and a younger female. Cards: each gets 1/4 cup of dry food twice a day, per the vet, plus a shared can of wet food at dinner. His jobs: morning feeding and the litter; his dad handles the vet. Reminders: feed at 7:30 am, scoop at 7:35, full litter change every other Sunday. The older cat's rabies booster is due in January, so his dad booked it. Food reorder point: when one small bag is left. The warning list, taped inside the cupboard, leads with: 'Male cat straining with no urine: call the vet now.'

brown.title: Seasonal Upkeep

brown.tools: Google Calendar (recurring events), iPhone Reminders, Google Sheets
brown.inputs: The house's systems (heating, gutters, yard, fireplace), what his parents handle, and his free days.
brown.output: A four-season list with dates, owners and minutes, plus this month's tasks on the calendar.
method: Walk the house and yard with his parents and list systems: heating, filters, gutters, hoses, fireplace, smoke and CO alarms, yard tools, the log splitter, snow gear.
Mark who owns each task: him, a parent, or a hired service.

Winter: shovel and salt after storms, check filters monthly, keep vents and the dryer vent clear of snow.
Spring: alarms tested, screens on, gutters checked, yard cleanup, splitter back in service.

brown.prompt: Clerk of Seasons, build a seasonal upkeep calendar for my parents' house in Westchester. Systems and features: {heating type, fireplace or stove, gutters, yard, garage, splitter}. What I handle versus my parents: {split}. My free days: {days}. Give me four seasonal lists with suggested dates, minutes per task and owner, then the tasks for this month in order of urgency.
checklist: Recurring events on the shared calendar

His: disconnect the three garden hoses and shut the inside spigot valves (20 minutes, Sunday Nov 15), clear the front gutters once the oaks are bare (60 minutes, Nov 22, with his dad on the ladder), bring the shovels and pet-safe ice melt to the side door (10), winterize the splitter (Splitter Care kit, 30). His dad's: furnace filter and the chimney sweep booking. Recurring winter events: filter check on the first Sunday of each month, smoke alarm test on the same day. brown.title: Returns Tracker

brown.tools: Google Sheets, Gmail search, USPS Informed Delivery (free), iPhone Reminders
brown.inputs: Order confirmation emails, items to send back, and the drop-off points he can reach.

method: Search Gmail for 'order', 'shipped' and 'return' from the last 30 days; list every open order.
For each: item, store, order date, delivered date, return deadline, refund amount, drop-off method.
Set the reminder for five days before the return deadline, not on it.
Plan drop-offs he can reach on foot, by Bee-Line or on the way to work: the post office for USPS labels, or a store that accepts that retailer's returns.

Turn on USPS Informed Delivery to see incoming mail and packages ahead of time.
brown.prompt: Errand Runner, here are my open orders: {item, store, order date, delivered date}. Items I want to return: {list}. Drop-off options I can reach without a car: {places and how}. Plan: shoes dropped at the Chappaqua post office before Tuesday's shift, case returned at a drop-off near his bus route on Thursday. Reminders: Nov 27 for the shoes, Dec 1 for the case. Both photographed packed. Shoe refund of $84 showed on Nov 18; the case refund of $16 posted Nov 20. Tracker cleared.

brown.title: The House Manual
brown.use: Where things are and how they work at home, in one shared document anyone can use in an emergency.
brown.tools: Google Docs (shared with family), iPhone camera, Bitwarden (for codes and passwords, never the doc)
brown.inputs: A walk around the house with a parent, a phone camera, and an hour.
brown.output: A short illustrated manual by room and system, with emergency shutoffs on page one.
method: Page one, emergencies: main water shutoff, breaker panel, gas shutoff if any, where the extinguishers are, who to call. Photo of each.
Systems: thermostat and heating, hot water, internet and his own router, trash and recycling days, the splitter.
Rooms: where the tools, spare bulbs, batteries, first aid kit, flashlights and cat supplies live.
Label the breaker panel if it is not labeled, room by room, with a parent.
How-tos in three lines each: reset the router, relight or reset the furnace per its label, swap the furnace filter, unclog a drain safely.
Never put alarm codes, Wi-Fi passwords or lock codes in the doc; keep them in Bitwarden and share them only with family.
Share the doc with the household and review it every six months.
brown.prompt: Keeper of the Manual, help me write our house manual. House systems: {heating, water heater, electrical, gas, internet}. Where key things are: {list as I know them}. Who lives here and who might need it (sitter, guest): {people}. Give me an outline with emergency shutoffs on page one, a page per system with a three-line how-to for common fixes, a room-by-room where-things-are list, and a list of the photos I should take. Remind me where codes and passwords should go instead of the doc.

Page one: the main water shutoff behind the basement stairs (photo, blue handle), the breaker panel by the laundry, 20 circuits now labeled after an hour with his dad flipping breakers, two extinguishers (kitchen and garage). Where things are: bulbs and batteries in the hall closet, cat food in the pantry's bottom shelf, the trauma kit on his shelf. The Wi-Fi password went into the family's Bitwarden share. Doc shared with his parents and sister.

copper.title: The Weekly Time Block

copper.output: A color-coded week on the calendar: fixed blocks, travel, deep work, training, rest, and one buffer per day.
method: Enter the fixed blocks first: shifts, classes, CVAC, church, in their own colors.
Add travel before and after each, using real train and bus times plus 10 minutes.
Place sleep as a block (at least seven hours); everything else fits around it.
Place the week's top three orders in deep-work blocks of 60 to 90 minutes, on the days with the most energy.
Add training sessions (three or four) and one wood-splitting block on a dry day.

copper.title: Clash Finder
copper.use: Finds conflicts between shifts, classes, CVAC, deadlines and travel before they happen.
copper.tools: Google Calendar, iPhone Calendar, Google Sheets
copper.inputs: The next two to four weeks of calendar events and the deadline list.
copper.output: A list of clashes (hard overlaps, travel squeezes, overloaded days) with a fix for each.
method: Export or list every event for the window with start, end and location.
Hard clash: two events overlap in time.
Travel clash: the gap between events in different places is shorter than real travel time.
Load clash: more than 12 committed hours in a day, or a deadline due the day after a double shift.
Rest clash: less than eight hours between a closing shift and the next morning commitment.
Rank by how soon and how hard they are to fix; shift schedules get posted early, so fix those first.
For each, propose a fix: swap a shift, move a deadline task earlier, or ask CVAC to trade.
copper.prompt: You are Inspector of Hours, Conflict Checker. Here are my events from {start} to {end}: {paste with times and locations}. Deadlines: {list}. Travel times: Chappaqua to Purchase about 60 minutes by train and bus; Chappaqua to Walgreens {minutes}; Chappaqua to the CVAC building {minutes}. Find every hard clash, travel squeeze, overloaded day (over 12 committed hours), deadline sitting after a heavy day, and rest gap under eight hours. Rank them by urgency. For each, propose the simplest fix and who I would need to ask.
checklist: All events in the window listed
Travel gaps checked against real times
Rest gaps under eight hours flagged

The Inspector finds four. 1) Hard: CVAC duty Tue Nov 24, 7 to 11 pm, overlaps a 6 pm class review session; fix: ask the crew chief to trade to Thursday. 2) Travel: Thu Dec 3 class ends at 4 pm at Purchase and a Walgreens shift starts at 4:30 in Chappaqua; the trip takes about an hour; fix: ask the manager to start at 5:30. 3) Rest: a closing shift ends 10 pm Fri Dec 11 and a Sat 8 am shift follows, with a final paper due Dec 12; fix: finish the paper by Dec 9. 4) Load: Sat Nov 21 has 13 hours booked; the splitting session moves to Sunday.

copper.title: The Decision Log
copper.use: Records what was decided, when, why, and what would reopen it, so decisions stop being relitigated.
copper.inputs: The decision, the options considered, the reason, and who it affects.
copper.output: A dated log entry and, on request, the history of any area's decisions.
method: Log a decision the day it is made, not later.
Fields: date, area, decision in one line, options rejected, reason in two lines, reopen trigger, review date.
The reopen trigger is a specific fact that would justify revisiting (a number, an event).
Link any memo, test or source that informed it.
When tempted to revisit, check the trigger first; no trigger, no reopening.
Review dates go on the calendar.
Superseded decisions stay in the log, marked replaced, with a link to the new one.
copper.prompt: You are Recorder of Decrees, Decision Archivist. Log this decision: {decision}, made {date}. Options I rejected: {list}. Why: {reasons}. Write the entry with: date, area, decision in one line, options rejected, reason in two lines, a specific reopen trigger, and a review date. If I am revisiting an old decision {paste old entry}, check whether its trigger has fired and say plainly whether this is a real reopening or second-guessing.
copper.example: Entry, Nov 5, 2026, area Genizah. Decision: Genizah launches free on Nov 18 with no paid tier until it has 300 subscribers. Rejected: launching with a paid tier on day one; delaying the launch to January. Reason: a paid wall before any audience slows growth, and the free list is the asset for briefs and sponsors later. Reopen trigger: 300 subscribers, or a sponsor offering at least $100 for an issue. Review date: Feb 1, 2027. Two weeks later, after a weak first week, Elijah wants to add a paid tier now. The Recorder checks: 64 subscribers, no sponsor offer. Trigger not fired. Verdict: second-guessing; the decision stands until Feb 1.

copper.title: Contract Reader
copper.use: Plain-English summary of any contract or terms, with red flags and questions to ask. Not legal advice.
copper.tools: Google Docs (comment mode), Adobe Acrobat Reader (free, for PDFs)
copper.inputs: The full contract text and what he is agreeing to do.
copper.output: A one-page summary: who owes what, money and dates, rights given away, exits, red flags, and questions to send back.
method: Read the whole document once without notes.
Summarize: parties, what he delivers, what he gets paid, when, and how.
Find ownership: who owns the work after; look for 'work made for hire' or 'assigns all rights'.
Find limits on him: non-compete, exclusivity, confidentiality, non-disparagement.
Find risk: indemnification, liability caps, unlimited revisions, automatic renewal.
Find exits: termination notice, kill fee, what happens to unpaid work.
List questions and suggested changes; for anything large, have a lawyer look before signing.
copper.prompt: You are Notary, Contract Reader. Open with one line saying this is a plain reading to prepare me, not a lawyer's opinion. Contract: {paste}. My role: {what I am delivering}. Summarize it in plain English: parties, deliverables, payment amount and timing, ownership of the work, restrictions on me, liability and indemnity, renewal, and how either side can exit. List red flags ranked by how much they could cost me. Draft short, polite questions or change requests I could send. Tell me which items are serious enough to show a lawyer.
copper.example: A small media startup offers $150 per brief for four briefs on online influence trends. Summary: he delivers four 2,000-word briefs in eight weeks; payment net 60 after acceptance. Red flags: 1) 'Contractor assigns all rights, including in underlying research and methods' means he could lose the right to reuse his own network data; 2) 'unlimited revisions until Client approval' with approval at their sole discretion; 3) a 12-month non-compete on 'similar content'; 4) he indemnifies them for any claim arising from the content, even after their edits. Questions sent: rights limited to the final text, two revision rounds, drop the non-compete, net 30, indemnity only for his own text. The non-compete and indemnity get shown to a lawyer before signing.

copper.title: Libel Check
copper.use: Pre-publication pass on every claim about a named person or organization. Not legal advice.
copper.inputs: The draft and the source for every claim about a named person or group.
copper.output: A table of each named-party claim with its type (fact or opinion), its proof, a risk level and a safer wording.
method: Highlight every sentence that names or clearly identifies a person or organization.
Label each: verifiable fact, opinion based on stated facts, or implied fact (sounds like opinion but asserts something provable).
For each fact, attach the proof: a document, recording, or archived post; archive it now.
Rewrite implied facts as either sourced facts or clearly labeled opinion with the facts shown.
Describe documented acts only; do not assign motives or hidden coordination without evidence.
Private individuals get extra care; prefer not naming them unless essential.
Anything high risk that still feels necessary goes to a lawyer before publishing.
copper.prompt: You are Libel Reader, Pre-Publication Review. Open with one line saying this is a prepublication read, not a lawyer's opinion. Draft: {paste}. Sources: {links}. List every sentence that names or identifies a person or organization. For each, say whether it is a verifiable fact, opinion based on disclosed facts, or an implied factual claim. Say whether the source I gave actually proves it. Rate risk low, medium or high, note if the person is private or public, and give a safer wording that keeps the point. Flag any claim about motive or secret coordination that lacks direct evidence.
checklist: Each labeled fact, opinion or implied fact
copper.example: A Marginalia post on a pro-RSF hashtag campaign names an influencer account and a PR firm. Sentence: 'The firm is running a paid troll farm for the RSF.' Label: implied fact; the sources show only that the firm's site lists a Sudanese client and that 14 accounts posted identical text. Risk: high. Safer wording: 'Fourteen accounts posted the same 41-word message within six minutes on Oct 12 (archived links). One of the accounts lists the firm as employer. The firm did not reply to a request for comment.' Sentence: 'This influencer is a disgrace.' Label: opinion, low risk, but cut for tone. All 14 posts archived on archive.today before publishing.

copper.title: Inbox Triage
copper.use: Clears an inbox in 20 minutes with four moves, and sets filters so it stays clear.
copper.tools: Gmail (filters, labels, search operators), iPhone Mail
copper.inputs: Access to the inbox and 20 minutes.
copper.output: An inbox at or near zero, a short list of replies due today, and two or three new filters.
method: Minutes 0 to 3: search 'unsubscribe' older than 30 days; select all and archive. Unsubscribe from the top three senders.
Minutes 3 to 6: search 'is:unread older_than:14d'; archive what no longer matters.
Minutes 6 to 16: go top to bottom with four moves: delete or archive, reply now (under two minutes), defer (label 'Reply' with a date), or hand off.
School and professor emails get answered first; CVAC and Walgreens next.
Minutes 16 to 19: make two filters for repeat senders (newsletters skip the inbox into a 'Read' label).
Minute 20: list the 'Reply' items with dates in Reminders.
Repeat weekly; ten minutes is enough after the first run.
copper.prompt: You are Keeper of the Inbox, Email Triage. Here are my inbox subject lines and senders: {paste list}. Sort them into delete or archive, reply now, defer with a date, or hand off. Put school and professor messages first, then CVAC and Walgreens. Draft two-line replies for the reply-now group. Suggest two or three Gmail filters (with the exact search criteria) for repeat senders. Keep the whole run doable in 20 minutes.
checklist: Every remaining message given one of four moves
Deferred replies in Reminders with dates
copper.example: Sunday, 1,240 messages in Gmail, 86 unread. Minute 2: 'unsubscribe older_than:30d' catches 910; archived. Unsubscribed from a clothing brand, a game store and a webinar platform. Unread older than 14 days: 31, all archived except a library hold notice. Four moves on the rest: a professor asking about a paper topic gets a two-line reply now; a CVAC crew chief asking about Thanksgiving coverage gets a reply with available dates; a Substack setup notice is deferred to Tuesday with a 'Reply' label; a Walgreens schedule email is noted. Filters: Substack newsletters skip the inbox to 'Read'; receipts go to 'Receipts'. Finished at 19 minutes with 6 messages left.

copper.title: Degree Audit
copper.use: Credits done and needed for a May 2028 History BA, semester by semester.
copper.tools: The college's online degree audit (from myPurchase), the History BA requirements page, Google Sheets
copper.inputs: His latest degree audit or unofficial transcript and the History BA requirements.
copper.output: A sheet of requirements met and open, a three-semester plan to May 2028, and questions for his advisor.
method: Download the current degree audit and the unofficial transcript as PDFs.
List the requirement groups: total credits (120), general education, History major courses, upper-level credits, the senior project.
Mark each met, in progress, or open; check that transfer credits from earlier colleges landed in the right groups.
Count credits left and divide across Spring 2027, Fall 2027 and Spring 2028.
Place the two-semester senior project in Fall 2027 and Spring 2028.
Check course rotation: some upper-level courses run only once a year.
Bring the plan and any mismatches to the advisor before spring registration.

I graduate May 2028, with Spring 2027, Fall 2027 and Spring 2028 left after this term. Mark each requirement met, in progress or open. Flag transfer credits that may be counted in the wrong place. Give a three-semester plan with credit totals per term, placing the senior project in the last two semesters. List questions for my advisor and anything that needs checking before registration.

Open: two upper-level History seminars, a non-Western history course, one general education science course, a few electives, and the senior project. Mismatch: a world history survey from community college counted only as a free elective; question for the advisor whether it can meet a major requirement. Plan: Spring 2027, a seminar, the non-Western course, the science course, two electives (15); Fall 2027, senior project I, a seminar, two electives (15); Spring 2028, senior project II plus electives (15). copper.title: Quote Bank
copper.use: Saves the best lines from his reading, tagged and fully cited, ready for papers and posts.
copper.tools: Zotero (with notes), Google Sheets, Kindle highlights export (My Clippings.txt), iPhone camera Live Text
copper.inputs: A quote, its source with page or section, and one or two tags.
copper.output: A searchable bank: quote, author, work, edition and page, tags, and a note on why it matters.
method: Capture the quote the moment you read it: photograph the page and use Live Text to copy it, or export Kindle highlights.
Record full citation: author, title, translator, edition, year, page or section number.
Tag with two or three tags from a fixed list (power, empire, Israel, Africa, faith, war, AI, method).
Add one line on why it matters or where it could be used.
Check famous quotes against the original text before saving; misattributions are common.
Search by tag when drafting; cite from the bank directly.
Once a month, prune duplicates and weak entries.
copper.prompt: You are Florilegist, Quote Keeper. Add these to my quote bank: {paste quotes with source info}. For each, give a clean entry: quote, author, work, translator, edition, page or section, two or three tags from {tag list}, and one line on use. If the attribution of a quote is commonly disputed or the wording varies by translation, say so and tell me what to check in the original.
checklist: Full citation with page or section
Famous quotes checked against the original

gold.title: The Auditor's Seal
gold.use: Final pass on anything leaving the house: sources, numbers, house rules and tone, signed or sent back.
gold.tools: Google Fact Check Explorer, Wayback Machine, LanguageTool (free), Hemingway Editor (free web version)
gold.inputs: The finished draft and its source list (links or citations).
gold.output: A seal verdict (pass, pass with fixes, or return) and a numbered fix list.
method: Number every claim, figure, date and quote; any without a source is a fix item.
Open each number at its source and confirm the figure, unit, date and what it counts (killed vs. displaced, monthly vs. yearly).
Archive every web source in the Wayback Machine so the link survives.
Run the house rules: no em dashes, no Red Rising names in published work, no claims about named people beyond documented acts.
Read for tone: cut hype words, check the Marginalia or daemon voice holds, run LanguageTool for typos.

gold.prompt: You are Cato au Porcius the Younger, Auditor. Audit this draft before it leaves: {paste draft}. Sources I used: {paste links or citations}. Number every factual claim, statistic, date and quote. For each, say whether a listed source supports it exactly, partly, or not at all, and whether the figure, unit and date match. Check house rules: no em dashes, no Red Rising names, claims about named people limited to documented acts with a source. Then judge tone for {Marginalia or daemon} voice: flag hype, hedging and filler. Give one verdict: pass, pass with fixes, or return. List fixes in order of severity. Do not rewrite the piece; tell me what to fix.
checklist: Every claim numbered and matched to a source
Each statistic checked at its source for figure, unit and date
All web sources archived in the Wayback Machine
No em dashes in the text
No Red Rising names in published copy
Named-person claims limited to documented acts
gold.example: A Marginalia post on Sudan's displacement crisis comes in at 900 words with 11 claims. Fix: give the date in the sentence. Claim 9 quotes a Sudanese official with no link; return item until a source is found. Two em dashes in the second paragraph become a colon and a period. gold.title: Essay Forge

Draft fast without polishing; insert Zotero footnotes as you go.
Revise for argument first (does each paragraph serve the thesis), then sentences.
Citation pass: footnotes in Chicago notes-bibliography, shortened notes after first use, bibliography alphabetical.

Outline has evidence under every section
Backward schedule dated and on the calendar
Full draft done before revision date
Footnotes and bibliography in Chicago notes-bibliography

gold.title: The Options Memo

State the situation in five lines of fact, no opinion.
Name three options that are genuinely different; one may be 'do nothing for now' if it is real.
For each: what it gains, what it costs in hours and dollars, what can go wrong, and how reversible it is.
Score each against the two or three criteria that matter most this quarter.
Recommend one, state what would change the recommendation, and give the first step with a date.

Recommend one, say what new fact would flip it, and give the first step with a date. One page, plain words.

Each option has gains, cost, risk, reversibility
Scored against no more than three criteria
Recommendation names what would flip it
First step dated and on the calendar

Options: A) sell one influence-operations brief at $100 to a single buyer; B) open a paid Marginalia tier at $5 a month and seek 20 subscribers; C) build two $50 starter websites for local shops. Criteria: hours, odds of reaching $100 by Dec 31, fit with the long-term brand. A scores highest on brand and moderately on odds; B is low odds in six weeks; C is highest odds but off-brand. gold.title: Red Team Drill

Attack the assumptions: list every 'this will happen' the plan depends on and test each.
Attack from outside: what would a competitor, critic or bad-faith reader do with it?
Rate each failure by likelihood and damage (1 to 3 each) and multiply.
For the top three, write a fix now or a tripwire (an early sign that triggers a change).
Name the weakest link in one sentence.

List every assumption it depends on and say which are untested. Attack it as {a hostile critic, a competitor, a skeptical reader} would. Rate each failure by likelihood and damage on 1 to 3 and rank them. For the top three, give a fix I can make now or a tripwire with a date. Be blunt. Do not soften and do not praise.

Assumptions listed and marked tested or untested
Outside attack done from at least one hostile view
Top three have a fix or tripwire
Weakest link named in one sentence

Pre-mortem: posts get under 1,000 views because the account is new; issues come out irregularly once finals start; the topic (AI tools plus history) is too broad to be shared; no cross-promotion with other newsletters; the welcome email does not ask for a share. gold.title: The Forecast Ledger
gold.use: Logs a call with odds and a resolution date, then scores it with the Brier score when it resolves.
gold.tools: Google Sheets, Metaculus, Manifold, Polymarket (to view prices)
gold.inputs: A yes or no question, his probability, the resolution date and the source that will settle it.
gold.output: A ledger row now and, at resolution, a Brier score plus a running average and calibration table.
method: Write the question so a stranger could settle it: exact event, exact date, named resolution source.
Give a probability from 1 to 99 percent; write two lines of reasoning and the base rate used.
Note any market or Metaculus price for comparison, with the date checked.
Log the row: date made, question, probability, resolution date, source, reasoning.
On the resolution date, record outcome as 1 (yes) or 0 (no).
Brier score = (probability minus outcome) squared; 0 is perfect, 0.25 is a coin flip.
Each quarter, group calls by probability bucket and check how often each bucket came true.
gold.prompt: You are Pierre-Simon au Laplace, Forecaster. Help me log a call. Rough question: {question}. My gut probability: {percent}. Rewrite the question so it resolves cleanly: exact event, deadline {date}, and a named resolution source. Give me a base rate from comparable past cases and say whether my number should move. Show the ledger row: date, question, probability, resolution date, source, two-line reasoning. If I give you resolved calls {paste rows with outcomes}, compute each Brier score, my average, and a calibration table by 10-point buckets.
checklist: Market or Metaculus comparison noted with date
Outcome and Brier score entered on the due date
gold.example: Call made Nov 5, 2026: 'Will the Sudanese Armed Forces and the RSF sign a nationwide ceasefire agreement, reported by Reuters or AP, by Mar 31, 2027?' Base rate: repeated rounds of talks since 2023 without a lasting nationwide deal. Laplace suggests 10 percent; Elijah logs 12 percent. No liquid market exists, so the comparison cell reads 'none found Nov 5'. On Apr 1, 2027 the outcome is entered. If no deal: Brier = (0.12 minus 0) squared = 0.0144, an excellent score. If a deal was signed: (0.12 minus 1) squared = 0.7744, a costly miss. The ledger's running average after 20 calls is the number to beat.

gold.title: Precedent Finder
gold.use: Three historical precedents for a current event, what each predicts, and exactly where each one breaks.
gold.tools: JSTOR via the college library, Internet Archive, Google Books, Wikipedia (for leads only, never as the source)
gold.inputs: The current event in two or three lines and the question he wants answered.
gold.output: Three precedents, each with a source, what it suggests, and the key difference that limits it.
method: State the current event and the forecast or judgment question it raises.
List the event's core features: actors, stakes, outside powers, timeline.
Search for cases matching at least three features; collect five, keep the best three.
For each precedent write: what happened, how it ended, what it suggests for now.
Then write where it breaks: the feature that differs and how that difference cuts.
Cite a scholarly source for each, not only an encyclopedia.
Close with the one lesson that survives all three breaks.
gold.prompt: You are Thucydides au Olorus, Historian. Current event: {describe}. My question: {question}. Find three historical precedents that share at least three core features (actors, stakes, outside powers, type of conflict or deal). For each: a short account, how it ended, what it suggests about my question, and where it breaks, meaning the specific difference that limits the analogy. Name a scholarly source I can check for each. Do not force a pattern. End with the single lesson that survives all three breaks, or say none does.
checklist: Each has a stated break point
gold.example: Event: outside powers sponsoring Sudan peace talks while backing different sides. Question: can externally brokered talks end the war? Precedents: 1) the 1972 Addis Ababa Agreement ending Sudan's first civil war, brokered with Ethiopian and church mediation; it suggests autonomy deals can hold for a decade, but it breaks because the South had a single armed movement, unlike today's splintered field. 2) The 2005 Comprehensive Peace Agreement, pushed by IGAD and the US, UK and Norway; it suggests sustained great-power pressure works, but it breaks because the sponsors then were broadly aligned. 3) Lebanon's 1989 Taif Agreement; it suggests exhausted factions accept a deal, but it breaks on Syria's dominant role. Surviving lesson: deals stick when outside backers stop arming the parties.

gold.title: The Coalition Map

Interest, fear, power and stance filled for each

gold.title: Speech Builder

Read aloud and hard sentences cut
Timing within 15 seconds of the limit
Two worst spots fixed after listening back
