green.title: The Prompt Library
green.use: A versioned library of tested prompts for recurring jobs, with test cases so changes can be checked.
green.tools: GitHub (free private repo), VS Code, promptfoo (open source, optional for tests)
green.inputs: A recurring job, the current prompt, and two or three real inputs to test on.
green.output: One file per prompt with version, purpose, the prompt, test inputs, expected qualities and a change log.
method: Make a private GitHub repo 'prompts' with one folder per house.
One markdown file per prompt: title, version (v1.0), purpose, the prompt with {blanks}, test inputs, what a good output must contain.
Test each prompt on two or three real inputs and save the outputs next to it.
Grade outputs with a short rubric: correct, complete, follows house rules, right length.
When changing a prompt, bump the version, rerun the same tests, and keep it only if scores do not drop.
Optional: use promptfoo to run tests automatically with simple checks such as 'no em dash' and 'contains five lines'.
Log each change in one line at the bottom of the file.
green.prompt: You are Code Mentor, CS Tutor. Here is a prompt I use for {job}: {paste prompt}. Here are two real inputs and outputs: {paste}. Write a library file for it with title, version, purpose, the prompt with blanks, test inputs, and a four-point rubric. Suggest one improvement, explain why, and write it as the next version. Then tell me how to test both versions on the same inputs and decide which to keep. If useful, show a minimal promptfoo config with checks for my house rules.
checklist: Changes tested against the same inputs
green.example: File: blue/horn-daily.md, v1.2. Purpose: five sourced lines on Sudan and the Horn. Test inputs: three saved mornings of headlines from late October. Rubric: five lines, each with a source, confirmation status marked, no em dashes. v1.2 outputs scored 3 of 4 on two mornings because armed-group claims were not labeled. v1.3 adds 'Label any claim by an armed group as a claim and name the group.' Rerun on the same three mornings: 4 of 4 on all. A promptfoo config with two checks (no U+2014 character; output contains 'claim by' when the input does) runs in under a minute. v1.3 kept; change log line: '2026-11-05, v1.3, label armed-group claims.'

green.title: Local Models Lab
green.use: Runs open models locally on the RTX 5070 with Ollama and compares them on his real jobs.
green.tools: Ollama (Windows), Open WebUI (optional), LM Studio (optional), Windows Task Manager (GPU memory)
green.inputs: The PC, about 30 GB of free disk space, and two or three real tasks to test.
green.output: Two or three local models installed, a speed and quality table on his tasks, and a choice of default local model.
method: Install Ollama for Windows from ollama.com; open a terminal and run 'ollama --version'.
The RTX 5070 has 12 GB of video memory: 7 to 8 billion parameter models fit easily; about 12 billion fits at the default 4-bit quantization.
Pull candidates: 'ollama pull qwen3:8b', 'ollama pull llama3.1:8b', 'ollama pull gemma3:12b'.
Run each with 'ollama run <model> --verbose' to see tokens per second; check 'ollama ps' shows 100% GPU.
Test each on the same three tasks (summarize an article, draft a Horn Daily line, explain a code snippet).
Score quality 1 to 5 and record speed in a table.
Pick a default; remove the rest with 'ollama rm' to free disk; the local API runs at localhost:11434 for later scripts.
green.prompt: You are Lamp-Keeper, Local AI. My PC: Windows 11, RTX 5070 with 12 GB VRAM, {RAM} RAM. Tasks I want local models for: {list}. Recommend two or three open models available in Ollama that fit in VRAM, with the exact pull commands and expected download sizes. Give me a short test plan with the same three prompts for each, and a table to fill in for speed and quality. After I paste results {table}, recommend a default and say when I should still use Claude instead.
checklist: Same three tasks run on each
green.example: Sunday afternoon. Ollama installed; three models pulled in about 25 minutes. 'ollama ps' shows each at 100% GPU. Task 1, summarize a Radio Dabanga article in five lines: qwen3:8b scores 4, llama3.1:8b scores 3 (missed the location), gemma3:12b scores 4. Task 2, a Horn Daily line in house format: qwen3:8b 4, llama3.1:8b 3, gemma3:12b 5. Task 3, explain a Python requests snippet: all score 4. Speed from --verbose: the 8B models run fast enough to feel instant; gemma3:12b is noticeably slower but fine for drafts. Default: gemma3:12b for writing, qwen3:8b for quick jobs. llama3.1:8b removed. Rule kept: sensitive drafts stay local; hard reasoning still goes to Claude.

green.title: The OSINT Scraper
green.use: The anchor project: a polite Python collector of public data, built in stages (APIs first, robots.txt, rate limits).
green.tools: Python 3, VS Code, requests, BeautifulSoup, feedparser, SQLite, urllib.robotparser, ReliefWeb API (free, approved appname required)
green.inputs: A research question, the public sources to collect from, and about three hours a week.
green.output: A working collector that saves items to SQLite, a README with its rules, and a weekly CSV export for briefs.
method: Stage 1, question and sources: write the question; prefer official APIs and RSS feeds over scraping HTML.
Stage 2, rules in code: check robots.txt with urllib.robotparser before any fetch; set a User-Agent naming the project and a contact email; wait at least 5 seconds between requests to the same site.
Stage 3, RSS: use feedparser on news feeds (title, link, date, summary) into SQLite with the link as a unique key.
Stage 4, API: pull ReliefWeb reports on Sudan with an approved appname, paging slowly.
Stage 5, HTML only where allowed: requests plus BeautifulSoup on pages robots.txt permits; never log in, never bypass paywalls or blocks.
Stage 6, schedule: run daily with Windows Task Scheduler; log errors to a file.
Stage 7, output: weekly CSV export and a count by source for the Horn Daily and briefs.
green.prompt: You are Tracker, OSINT Analyst. I am at stage {number} of my OSINT collector. Question: {question}. Sources: {list}. Write the code for this stage in Python with comments for a learner. It must check robots.txt before fetching, send a User-Agent naming the project, wait at least 5 seconds between requests per site, store results in SQLite with de-duplication, and never log in or bypass blocks. Prefer an API or RSS feed if the source offers one. Tell me how to test it on a small run first.
checklist: Delay of 5 seconds or more per site
green.example: Stage 3 on a Thursday night. Question: what do Sudanese and international outlets publish about Darfur each week? Sources: four news RSS feeds and, later, ReliefWeb's API. Tracker writes collector.py: feedparser reads each feed, a robots.txt check runs once per domain, a 5-second pause separates requests, and each item is saved to golem_osint.db with the link as a unique key. Test run: 4 feeds, 112 items, 0 duplicates on a second run, 18 seconds total. Stage 4 next week: he requests a ReliefWeb appname and pulls reports tagged Sudan, 50 per page. README lists the rules: public data only, no logins, respect robots.txt and rate limits.

green.title: Security Basics
green.use: A simple threat model and a hardening pass on the PC, iPhone and key accounts, with habits to keep.
green.tools: EFF Surveillance Self-Defense guides, Bitwarden (free), an authenticator app (Ente Auth or Google Authenticator), Have I Been Pwned, Windows Security
green.inputs: His devices, his main accounts, and what he most needs to protect (faceless brand, email, money, GOLEM keys).
green.output: A one-page threat model, a completed hardening checklist, and three weekly habits.
method: Threat model: what to protect, from whom (random criminals, doxxers, hostile accounts), how bad a loss would be, and what he will do about it.
Passwords: install Bitwarden, generate unique passwords, and move the main email, bank and Substack logins first.
Two-factor: passkeys where offered, otherwise an authenticator app; never SMS when there is a choice. Save recovery codes in Bitwarden.
PC: Windows Update on, Windows Security on, device encryption or BitLocker on, a standard (non-admin) daily account.
iPhone: latest iOS, a six-digit or longer passcode, Find My on, Stolen Device Protection on.
Check Have I Been Pwned for his emails and change any breached passwords.
Keep API keys in environment variables or Bitwarden, never in chats, screenshots or code pushed to GitHub.
green.prompt: You are Ice-Builder, Security Engineer. My devices: {list}. Main accounts: {list}. What I most need to protect: {list}. Likely threats: {list}. Write a one-page threat model in plain words, then a hardening checklist in order of impact for my exact devices and accounts, with where each setting is. Include password manager setup, two-factor choices, encryption, updates, and how to store API keys. Finish with three weekly habits that take under five minutes.
checklist: Bitwarden set up with top accounts moved
Two-factor on email, bank, Substack, Claude
API keys out of chats and code
green.example: Threat model: protect the Gmail behind Substack and Genizah, the faceless Marginalia accounts, savings, and GOLEM's API keys. Main threats: password reuse from old breaches, phishing, and someone hostile trying to link the faceless brand to his name. Have I Been Pwned shows his old email in three breaches; those passwords were reused on two sites, both changed. Bitwarden holds 46 logins after an evening. Passkeys turned on for Google; authenticator app for Substack and X; recovery codes saved. PC: device encryption confirmed on, daily work moved to a standard account. iPhone: Stolen Device Protection on. A search of his GitHub repos finds one old commit with a test key; the key is revoked and rotated.

green.title: CTF Path
green.use: Beginner capture-the-flag practice in a fixed order, on legal training platforms only.
green.tools: OverTheWire Bandit, picoCTF (picoGym), TryHackMe (free rooms), PortSwigger Web Security Academy, Hack The Box Starting Point
green.inputs: About three hours a week and a notebook (or Obsidian) for writeups.
green.output: Progress through five stages, a writeup for every solved challenge, and a skills list for his CV.
method: Rule: only attack systems built for practice on these platforms; never real sites, accounts or networks.
Stage 1, Linux and the shell: OverTheWire Bandit, levels 0 to 20.
Stage 2, wide basics: picoGym beginner challenges in general skills, cryptography, web and forensics.
Stage 3, guided learning: TryHackMe free rooms on networking, Linux and web fundamentals.
Stage 4, web security: PortSwigger Web Security Academy apprentice labs (SQL injection, XSS, access control).
Stage 5, first machines: Hack The Box Starting Point free tier.
After every solve, write a short writeup: goal, what failed, what worked, the lesson. Hints are fine; copying answers is not.
green.prompt: You are Range Master, CTF Coach. I am on {platform}, challenge {name}. Here is what I have tried: {steps and output}. Do not give me the flag or the full answer. Give me one hint at a time, starting with the smallest nudge, and ask what I see before giving more. After I solve it, help me write a five-line writeup: goal, approach, what failed, what worked, lesson. Only discuss the practice target on this platform.
green.example: Week 2, Bandit level 12: a file that is a hexdump of data compressed several times. Elijah tries 'cat' and gets noise. Range Master's first hint: 'What does the file command tell you about it?' He runs file, sees hexdump output, and after the second hint uses xxd -r to reverse it. Then a loop of file, rename, and decompress with gzip, bzip2 and tar, seven layers, until the password appears. Writeup: goal, read the password; failed, cat and guessing extensions; worked, checking file type at every layer; lesson, never trust the extension, ask the file what it is. Time: 50 minutes. Bandit 13 next, on SSH keys.

green.title: Web Build Starter
green.use: Learns HTML, CSS and JavaScript by building and publishing one real page, in five sessions.
green.tools: VS Code (with Live Server extension), MDN Web Docs, GitHub Pages (free hosting), Firefox or Chrome developer tools
green.inputs: A page to build and five sessions of about 90 minutes.
green.output: A live, mobile-friendly page on GitHub Pages and a repo he understands line by line.
method: Session 1, HTML: write the structure by hand (header, main, sections, footer) using semantic tags; check MDN for each tag.
Session 2, CSS: one stylesheet; system fonts, a readable column (max-width around 680 pixels), spacing, and one accent color.
Session 3, layout and mobile: flexbox or grid, a media query for phones, test in developer tools' device mode.
Session 4, JavaScript: one small feature (filter a list, toggle details), written without libraries.
Session 5, publish: push to a GitHub repo and turn on GitHub Pages; test on the iPhone.
Run Lighthouse in Chrome developer tools and fix the top two issues.
Keep faceless pages on a GitHub account not tied to his real name.
green.prompt: You are Builder, Engineer. I am building {page} and I am in session {number} of five, working on {HTML, CSS, layout, JavaScript or publishing}. Teach me by having me write the code: give the goal for the session, the smallest next step, and what to look up on MDN. Review the code I paste {code} and point out mistakes and better practice without rewriting the whole file. Keep it plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no frameworks.
checklist: Account choice fits the brand's OPSEC
green.example: Page: 'The Calls', a public list of Marginalia forecasts with odds and resolution dates. Session 1: index.html with a header, an intro paragraph and a table of six Calls. Session 2: style.css with a 680-pixel column, serif headings, and the accent color from the Marginalia banner. Session 3: the table becomes cards on screens under 600 pixels. Session 4: a dropdown filters Calls by status (open, resolved, scored) with 20 lines of JavaScript. Session 5: pushed to a repo under the Marginalia GitHub account, GitHub Pages turned on, checked on the iPhone. Lighthouse flags low contrast on dates and missing alt text on the logo; both fixed. Write the title (under 60 characters), subtitle, and the email preview text in the post settings.
Add the header image with alt text; check every link opens the right page.
Add a subscribe button after the opening and a share button at the end.

Test email read on phone and PC

green.title: The Voice Loop
green.use: Speak with Wispr Flow, hear replies via ElevenLabs on the PC; the API key lives in a Windows env var, never in chat.
green.tools: Wispr Flow (free tier with a weekly word limit), ElevenLabs (free tier), Python 3 with the elevenlabs package, VS Code
green.inputs: The PC with a microphone and speakers, a Wispr Flow account, and an ElevenLabs account and API key.
green.output: A working loop: dictate a prompt, get a text reply, and hear it read aloud by a chosen ElevenLabs voice, saved as an MP3.
method: Install Wispr Flow on Windows; test dictation into Notepad and set the push-to-talk shortcut.
Create an ElevenLabs API key in the account settings; do not paste it into any chat, document or code.
Store it as a user environment variable: Windows search 'Edit environment variables for your account', New, name ELEVENLABS_API_KEY, paste the value there only.
Open a new terminal and confirm it is set without showing it: python -c "import os; print(bool(os.environ.get('ELEVENLABS_API_KEY')))".
pip install elevenlabs; write speak.py that reads the key from the environment, sends text to text-to-speech with a chosen voice ID, and saves reply.mp3.
Mind the free tier: limited monthly credits and no commercial license, so Margin Notes voiceovers need a paid plan.
green.prompt: You are Voice-Smith, Voice Loop Engineer. I am on Windows 11 with Python {version}. My ElevenLabs API key is already stored in the user environment variable ELEVENLABS_API_KEY; never ask me to paste it. Write speak.py that reads the key from the environment, takes text from {a file or the clipboard}, calls ElevenLabs text-to-speech with voice ID {voice id}, and saves an MP3 named by date and time. Add clear error messages if the variable is missing or credits run out. Explain how to run it after dictating with Wispr Flow.
checklist: API key created and never pasted in chat
Key stored as a user environment variable
Key presence confirmed without printing it

Wispr Flow installed; holding the shortcut, Elijah dictates 'Summarize the three things I must do before the Genizah launch' into the Claude window, clean on the first try. ElevenLabs key created and pasted only into the Windows environment variable dialog. A new terminal prints True for the check. Voice-Smith writes speak.py: it reads reply.txt, calls text-to-speech with a calm English voice, and saves 2026-11-10_2214_reply.mp3. Error test: renaming the variable makes the script stop with 'ELEVENLABS_API_KEY not set', as intended. First full loop: dictate, copy reply into reply.txt, run, listen, under 30 seconds. Credits used: about 600 of the free monthly allowance.

green.title: Launch Audit
green.use: Fifty checks before any site or app goes public: security, correctness, launch hygiene. Run on Hearth and the Genizah site.
green.tools: Browser devtools, Lighthouse, a staging URL
green.inputs: The repo or the live staging URL, the stack (Next.js, Supabase, static), who can sign up and who can pay.
green.output: A pass or fail table of fifty items with a fix for each fail, ordered by severity.
method: Security first: no API keys in the frontend, row-level security on, login checked on the server, no open /admin, rate limiting on, nobody can delete another user's data, signup off if it should be, no emails or PII in API responses, security headers set, email confirmation on, .env not in git, the AI has no production database access.

Correctness: no packages that do not exist, framework current, no empty catch blocks, no bare 'something went wrong', no useEffect for everything, no key=index, no duplicate functions, dead code removed, at least smoke tests, commit messages that say what changed, the owner can explain every file.

Launch hygiene: privacy policy, terms, one clear call to action, FAQ, robots.txt, sitemap.xml, custom 404, alt text, analytics, meta titles and descriptions, social share image, favicon, canonical URLs, cookie consent if tracking, mobile layout, accessibility pass, every form tested, no broken links, performance under three seconds.
Mark each item pass, fail or not applicable, with the file or URL where a fail lives.
Fix fails in severity order: security, then correctness, then hygiene. Re-run the failed items only.
Keep the table in the repo as LAUNCH_AUDIT.md with the date; re-run before every public release.
green.prompt: You are Builder of the Core. Run the Launch Audit on {repo or staging URL}, a {stack} app where {who can sign up} and {who can pay}. Check all fifty items in three groups (security, correctness, launch hygiene) and return a table: item, pass or fail or n/a, where, the fix. Order fails by severity. Do not pass an item you could not check; say so.
checklist: No secrets in the frontend or in git
green.example: Illustrative: the Genizah site on a staging URL. Security: 11 of 12 pass; signup was still open to anyone (fail, high). Correctness: 10 of 12; three empty catch blocks and a key=index in the shelf list. Hygiene: 16 of 20; no sitemap, no 404, no social image, no cookie banner. Fixes applied in order; the re-run passed 48 of 50 with two not applicable (no payments yet). LAUNCH_AUDIT.md committed.

grey.title: Konetz Drill
grey.use: Practice the kill word: Konetz stops every GOLEM process at once, Emet resumes only what he names.
grey.tools: Claude Code (Esc to interrupt), Windows Task Manager, Task Scheduler, iPhone stopwatch
grey.inputs: Ten minutes, the PC with GOLEM running, and one harmless long task to interrupt.
grey.output: A timed drill log: seconds to full stop, anything that kept running, and the fix.
method: Write the rule where GOLEM reads it: on 'Konetz', stop every running task, write nothing further, report 'Stopped' with a list of what was halted, then wait.
Write the resume rule: 'Emet' resumes nothing by itself. GOLEM asks which task to resume and he names it.
Start a harmless long task, such as a Claude Code session asked to summarize every file in a test folder.
Say or type Konetz and start the stopwatch. In Claude Code, Esc is the manual backstop.
Check what kept running: Task Manager for node or python processes, Task Scheduler for timed GOLEM jobs, and the folder for files written after the stop.
Say Emet, name one task, and confirm only that task resumes.
Log time to stop and any leak. Repeat monthly and after every GOLEM upgrade.
grey.prompt: Lurcher, run a Konetz drill with me. Running right now: {tasks and agents}. Scheduled jobs I know of: {list}. When I say Konetz, stop everything, write nothing further, and reply only with 'Stopped' and a list of what you halted. Then wait. When I say Emet, ask me which task to resume and resume only that one. After the drill, give me a checklist of places on Windows where something of yours could still be running (processes, scheduled tasks, startup items, background terminals) so I can verify the stop myself.
checklist: Konetz rule written where GOLEM reads it
Emet rule requires naming the task
No files written after the stop
grey.example: Drill, Nov 5. Test task: a Claude Code session summarizing 40 notes in a test folder. Konetz at 0:00; Claude Code replied 'Stopped: summary task, 17 of 40 done' at 0:03. Task Manager showed a node process for the GOLEM hub still running; it was the phone hub server, not an agent, so the rule was amended to name it as exempt or to stop it too. Task Scheduler held the 6:30 AM desk job, which Konetz does not cancel, so he added 'Konetz also pauses scheduled desks until Emet'. No files were written after 0:03. Emet, 'resume summary': it resumed at file 18. Next drill Dec 5.

grey.title: Phishing Check
grey.use: Five checks to tell whether an email, text or DM is real before he clicks, pays or logs in.
grey.tools: VirusTotal (URL scan), urlscan.io, Gmail 'Show original', iPhone long-press link preview, Have I Been Pwned
grey.inputs: The suspicious message (screenshot or forwarded text) and what it asks him to do.
grey.output: A verdict (real, fake, unsure), the evidence for it, and what to do next, including how to report it.
method: Check 1, the ask: does it want a login, a payment, a code or a download, and is it urgent? Urgency plus an ask is the classic pattern.
Check 2, the sender: read the actual address or number, not the display name. Lookalike domains (substack-payouts.com, paypa1.com) are fake.
Check 3, the link: long-press on iPhone or hover on PC to see the real address. Paste unknown links into VirusTotal or urlscan.io instead of opening them.
Check 4, out of band: open the service by typing its address or using the app. If the alert is real, it will be there too.
Check 5, the details: does it know things a real sender would know (last four of an account, his username)? Generic greetings lean fake.
If he already clicked or typed a password: change it from the real site, sign out other sessions, and check Have I Been Pwned.
Report it: Gmail 'Report phishing', forward scam texts to 7726, and delete.
grey.prompt: Picket, check this message: {paste text or describe screenshot}. It came by {email, text, DM} from {sender address or number}. The link points to {address shown on long-press or hover}. It asks me to {action}. Run your five checks (the ask, the sender, the link, out of band, the details) and give a verdict of real, fake or unsure with the evidence for each. Tell me what to do next, and if I already clicked or entered anything, give me the cleanup steps in order.
checklist: Verified in the real app or site
grey.example: Email, a week before the Genizah launch: 'Your Substack payout is on hold. Verify your Stripe account within 24 hours.' Display name: Substack Payments. Actual sender: payouts at substack-stripe-verify.net. Link on hover: a login page on a different domain; urlscan.io flagged it as a known phishing kit. The ask is a login, with urgency. Out of band: the Substack dashboard and the Stripe app both showed nothing pending. Details: it greeted him as 'Dear Creator'. Verdict: fake, five of five. Reported with Gmail 'Report phishing', deleted, and a sender filter added.

grey.title: Account Lockdown
grey.use: Passkeys, two-factor and recovery codes on every account that matters, email first.
grey.tools: Bitwarden (free), Google Authenticator or Ente Auth, Have I Been Pwned, Google Security Checkup, Apple Account settings
grey.inputs: A list of his accounts, his phone, and an hour. A printer for the recovery codes.
grey.output: Every key account with a passkey or app-based two-factor, saved recovery codes, and a dated lockdown log.
method: Rank accounts by blast radius: primary Gmail first (it resets everything else), then Apple Account, bank, GitHub, Claude and Anthropic, Substack, X, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube.
Install Bitwarden and move every password into it, making each one unique.
Primary email: run Google Security Checkup, add a passkey, turn on two-step verification with an authenticator app, remove old recovery phones and unknown devices.
Apple Account: confirm two-factor, add a recovery contact, review signed-in devices.
For each other account, prefer a passkey; otherwise an authenticator app over SMS. Save or print recovery codes as they appear.
Search his emails on Have I Been Pwned and change any password from a listed breach.
Store printed codes in a sealed envelope at home, plus a copy in Bitwarden. Log the date and repeat every six months.
grey.prompt: Sentry of Names, lock down my accounts. My accounts: {list}. Current setup: {which have two-factor, which use SMS, which share passwords}. Devices: {phone, PC}. Rank them by blast radius and give me the order to work in. For each one, tell me the strongest option it supports (passkey, authenticator app, SMS), where in its settings to turn it on, and whether it gives recovery codes. Flag any account whose recovery depends on a phone number or email I could lose.
checklist: Authenticator app replaces SMS where possible
grey.example: Lockdown, Nov 5. Gmail: passkey added, Google Authenticator set, an old Cobleskill-era recovery email removed, two stale devices signed out. Apple Account: two-factor on, his sister added as recovery contact. GitHub: passkey plus authenticator, recovery codes printed. X and Instagram moved from SMS to the authenticator app. Have I Been Pwned listed his old email in two breaches; both reused passwords changed. Substack and Claude both sign in through that Gmail, which is why it went first. Envelope of codes filed in his desk; Bitwarden holds copies. Next review May 5, 2027.

grey.title: Faceless OPSEC
grey.use: Keep Marginalia and daemon unlinked from his face, name and location, by habit rather than luck.
grey.tools: Proton Mail (free), separate Chrome profiles, ExifTool, Google Lens, TinEye, Google Voice
grey.inputs: The list of brand accounts and his personal accounts, and the places he posts from.
grey.output: A link map showing every way a brand could tie back to him, each with a fix, and a monthly audit routine.
method: Separate identities: a Proton Mail address per brand, a separate Chrome profile per brand, never logged in beside personal accounts.

Phone numbers: never upload phone contacts to a brand Instagram or TikTok; contact sync suggests the brand to everyone he knows. Use a Google Voice number for brand two-factor if a number is required.
Media: strip location and metadata from every image (ExifTool, or share with Location off on iPhone). Check backgrounds for mail, badges, windows and reflections.
Screen recordings for daemon: his Windows username appears in paths like C:\Users\Elijah. Record from a separate Windows account with a neutral name, or crop.
Writing and timing: no catchphrases shared with his personal posts; schedule brand posts instead of posting live from a shift break.
Money: check that payout pages, receipts and the Substack about page show the brand, not his legal name.
Monthly audit: search the brand name with his name and town, and run the brand avatar through Google Lens and TinEye.
grey.prompt: Shadow Legionnaire, audit my faceless setup. Brand accounts: {list with platforms}. Personal accounts: {list}. Email and phone used for each: {details}. Where I post from: {devices, places, times}. What I publish: {text, images, screen recordings, voice}. Build a link map: every way a stranger or a platform could connect a brand to me, ranked by likelihood, with a fix for each. Include metadata, contacts sync, usernames, writing tics, posting times, payments and screen recordings. End with a ten-minute monthly audit checklist.
checklist: Separate email and browser profile per brand
Contacts never synced to brand apps
Recordings free of username and paths
Monthly search and image audit done
grey.example: Audit before the Genizah launch. Found: the daemon Substack was created with his personal Gmail, so the account email was switched to a new Proton address. A draft screen recording of Claude Code showed C:\Users\Elijah\Jarvis in the terminal title; he made a Windows account named 'studio' for recordings. The Marginalia X account had 'Find contacts' on from setup; turned off and uploaded contacts deleted in settings. Two Marginalia posts and his personal account used the same phrase, 'receipts or it didn't happen'; retired from the personal side. Google Lens on the Marginalia avatar found only the brand's own pages.

grey.title: Ipcha Mistabra Case File
grey.use: The Tenth Man case: argue the opposite of the consensus, climbing the Rungs of Proving only on documented acts.
grey.tools: Google Docs, Wayback Machine, Google Scholar, official records and court filings, the Libel Check kit
grey.inputs: A consensus view to test, the institution or named people involved, and the documents he has so far.
grey.output: A case file: consensus, the Tenth Man argument, evidence on each rung, the highest rung proven, and what would disprove it.
method: State the consensus in one sentence, then the Ipcha Mistabra: the strongest opposite reading.
List only documented acts: dated statements, filings, votes, budgets, orders, reporting from named outlets. Each act gets a link.
Climb the Rungs of Proving from the bottom: forgetting, negligence, indifference, self-interest, coordination, design. Each rung must rule out the one beneath it with evidence.
Stop at the highest rung the documents support. Coordination needs proof of communication between actors; design needs proof of intent in their own words or records.
Name institutions and people only for acts in the record. No group, ethnicity, religion or family is ever treated as an actor or as a hidden hand.
Write what would knock the case down a rung, and what document would settle it.
Before anything is published, run it through the Libel Check kit and the Auditor's Seal.
grey.prompt: Inquisitor of Ipcha, open a Tenth Man case file. Consensus view: {view}. Institution or named people: {who}. Documents I have: {list with links}. Argue the strongest opposite reading. Then test it rung by rung (forgetting, negligence, indifference, self-interest, coordination, design), citing only the documented acts I gave or ones you can point me to with a source. Stop at the highest rung the evidence supports and say why the next rung up fails. List what would disprove the case. Never treat an ethnic, religious or family group as an actor.
checklist: Each rung rules out the one below
Stopped at the highest supported rung
No group or family treated as an actor
grey.example: Consensus: famine data on Sudan was slow because war made counting impossible. Tenth Man: delay also served the government. Acts on file: a famine finding for Zamzam camp by the IPC's review committee in August 2024; reporting that Sudan's government disputed the classification; its announced withdrawal from the IPC in December 2024 (dates to be confirmed against the originals). Forgetting and negligence fail, since the dispute is on record. Indifference fails, since officials engaged actively. Self-interest is supported by the government's own statements on sovereignty and aid access. Coordination fails: no record of a joint plan with any other actor. Case filed at rung four, self-interest; disproof would be records showing the withdrawal was driven by technical method disputes alone.

grey.title: CVAC Hours
grey.use: Track CVAC hours against 150 by Dec 31, with the weekly pace needed to get there.
grey.tools: Google Sheets, iPhone Calendar, iPhone Reminders
grey.inputs: Hours logged so far (from CVAC's own record), shifts already on the calendar, and Walgreens shifts.
grey.output: A tally sheet, hours remaining, the weekly pace needed, and the shifts to request.
method: Get the official number from CVAC's record, not memory. His sheet follows the corps' count.
Keep one row per shift: date, start, end, hours, type (crew, standby, training, overnight), and whether CVAC has recorded it.
Compute remaining hours and weeks left to Dec 31. Pace = remaining divided by weeks.
Lay the needed shifts over Walgreens and class hours in the calendar. Find the blocks that fit first; finals weeks will be thin.
Front-load: get ahead before Thanksgiving and finals, not behind them.
Each Sunday, update the row count, confirm CVAC recorded last week's shifts, and request next week's.
If the pace climbs over what fits, talk to the scheduler early about overnights or extra standby.
grey.prompt: Medic's Tally, update my CVAC count. Official hours so far: {hours} as of {date}. Shifts booked: {dates and times}. Walgreens shifts: {dates and times}. Classes and finals: {dates}. Goal: 150 hours by Dec 31. Tell me hours remaining, the weekly pace needed, which booked shifts still need CVAC to record them, and which open blocks in the next three weeks I should request, avoiding clashes. Flag any week where the pace becomes unrealistic.
checklist: Every shift logged in its own row
Needed shifts mapped around work and class
grey.example: Nov 8: CVAC's record shows 104 hours. Remaining: 46 over about seven and a half weeks, a pace of about 6.2 hours a week. Booked: a Tuesday evening crew shift and a Saturday overnight, 18 hours in the next two weeks. Walgreens covers most weekday daytimes, and finals run the week of Dec 14, so the plan front-loads: 18 hours booked plus one more evening crew shift the week of Nov 16 puts him at 128 by Thanksgiving, needing 22 in December, which two overnights cover. One booked shift from late October was missing from CVAC's record; flagged to the scheduler.

grey.title: EMT Drills
grey.use: Protocol drills and flashcards for the EMT course, fifteen minutes a day.
grey.tools: Anki (desktop and AnkiWeb free; AnkiDroid free), Quizlet (free tier), his course skill sheets, NYS and regional BLS protocols
grey.inputs: This week's chapters, the course skill sheets, and fifteen minutes a day.
grey.output: A deck of cards for the week, one spoken scenario drill, and a log of weak cards.
method: Build cards from the week's chapters only: one fact per card (a vital sign range, a mnemonic step, a drug's indication).
Add the mnemonics as ordered cards: SAMPLE, OPQRST, AVPU, DCAP-BTLS. Ask for the next letter, not the whole list.
Review daily in Anki (AnkiWeb in Safari on the iPhone is free). Ten minutes of reviews, five of new cards.
Twice a week, run a spoken scenario: GOLEM gives dispatch info, he talks through scene size-up, primary assessment, history, secondary assessment and reassessment out loud, in skill-sheet order.
Score against the skill sheet. Critical fails (no scene safety or PPE, missed bleeding) go on a weak list.
Practice hands-on skills only in class and on CVAC training nights, under an instructor.
His instructor and the NYS and regional protocols override any card. Fix cards that disagree.
grey.prompt: EMT Instructor, run a scenario drill. This week's chapters: {chapters}. Give me dispatch information for a {medical or trauma} call, then answer my assessment questions as the patient and scene would, one at a time. I will talk through scene size-up, primary assessment, history, secondary assessment and reassessment. Do not prompt me. At the end, score me against a standard EMT assessment skill sheet, list any critical fails, and give me five flashcards for what I missed. Note that my course and NYS protocols override you.
checklist: Cards made from this week's chapters
grey.example: Scenario: 'Respond to a 67-year-old male, difficulty breathing, at the Chappaqua train station.' He opened with scene safety and gloves, then general impression, AVPU (alert), airway open, breathing labored at 28, radial pulse 112. He took SAMPLE and OPQRST cleanly but forgot to ask about home oxygen and did not reassess vitals before 'transport'. Score: no critical fails, two misses. New cards: 'COPD patient history: ask about home O2 and inhalers', 'Reassess an unstable patient every 5 minutes', and three on respiratory rate ranges. His weak list now leads with reassessment timing.

grey.title: Trauma Kit Check
grey.use: Check his personal bleeding-control kit: contents, expiry dates and restock, every three months.
grey.tools: Google Sheets, iPhone Reminders, Stop the Bleed (stopthebleed.org) course finder
grey.inputs: His personal kit laid out on a table, and fifteen minutes. CVAC's own equipment follows CVAC's checks, not this one.
grey.output: A contents sheet with quantities and expiry dates, a restock list, and the next check date.
method: Lay everything out. Core contents: tourniquet, hemostatic or compressed gauze, pressure dressing, gloves, trauma shears, marker, chest seals if trained, emergency blanket.
Check each tourniquet for cracks, worn velcro and a working windlass. Buy only from authorized sellers; counterfeit tourniquets fail under load.
Read every expiry date. Hemostatic gauze, chest seal adhesive and gloves degrade; log each date in the sheet.
Replace anything opened, wet, torn or expired.
Keep a separate trainer tourniquet for practice so the real one stays sealed and unworn.
Repack in the order of use, with the tourniquet reachable one-handed.
Set the next check for three months out, and take a Stop the Bleed class if he has not yet.
grey.prompt: Kit Medic, here is my personal trauma kit: {item, quantity, expiry date for each}. Where I carry it: {bag, car, CVAC bag}. My training so far: {course, Stop the Bleed, EMT chapters}. Tell me what is missing for a basic bleeding-control kit, what is expired or close, which items I should not carry until trained, and the order to pack it so the tourniquet comes out first. Keep costs low and name the kind of seller to buy from.
grey.example: Check, Nov 9. Found: one CAT tourniquet (sound), a QuikClot gauze expiring March 2027, one 6-inch pressure dressing, four nitrile gloves (one torn), shears, no marker, and a chest seal pack expired in 2025. Restock: replace the chest seal (he has covered them in his course), add a Sharpie, add two pairs of gloves, and note QuikClot replacement for February. A trainer tourniquet he practices with stays in his room. Repacked with the tourniquet on top, folded and staged. Next check Feb 9. A Stop the Bleed class at a Westchester hospital put on the calendar.

grey.title: Fire Walkthrough
grey.use: A room-by-room home fire-safety walkthrough of his parents' house, done with them.
grey.tools: iPhone camera and Notes, NFPA and Red Cross home fire safety checklists (free), a step stool
grey.inputs: Thirty minutes, his parents' agreement, and a step stool.
grey.output: A room-by-room list of fixes, alarm dates, an escape plan with two ways out of each room, and a meeting place.
method: Smoke alarms: one in each bedroom, outside each sleeping area and on every level. Press test on each. Read the date on the back; replace at 10 years.
Carbon monoxide alarms near sleeping areas and on each level if the house has gas, oil, a fireplace or an attached garage.
Kitchen: extinguisher present with the gauge in the green; nothing stored on the stove; towels away from burners.
Heat sources: space heaters three feet from anything that burns; fireplace or stove ashes in a lidded metal can, set outside away from the house; chimney inspected this year.
Electrical and batteries: no daisy-chained power strips, no warm outlets; lithium devices and power banks never charged on a bed.
Laundry: dryer lint screen cleaned every load, vent duct clear.
Escape plan: two ways out of every room, windows that open, a meeting spot outside, and a drill with everyone.
grey.prompt: Fire Marshal, guide me through a fire-safety walkthrough of my parents' house. Layout: {floors and rooms}. Heat sources: {furnace type, fireplace or wood stove, space heaters}. Garage: {attached or not}. Current alarms: {where, how old}. Walk me room by room with what to check in each, then give me a fix list ranked by risk and a simple escape plan with two ways out of every bedroom and one meeting place. Keep it suitable to do together with my parents in thirty minutes.
checklist: Every smoke alarm tested and dated
Space heaters and ashes handled safely
No overloaded strips or bed charging
Escape plan and meeting place agreed
grey.example: Walkthrough, Sunday Nov 15, with his parents. Five smoke alarms tested: four sounded; the hallway unit was dated 2013 and went on the replace list (New York now sells sealed 10-year battery units). No CO alarm on the bedroom floor despite the fireplace; one added to the list. The kitchen extinguisher gauge read green. Ashes were kept in a paper bag by the hearth, so a lidded metal can was bought. His room had two power strips chained under the desk; one removed. Meeting place: the big oak at the end of the driveway. Drill done that evening in under two minutes.

grey.title: Emergency Comms
grey.use: Who to call, how, and where to meet when phones or power fail, on one wallet card.
grey.tools: NY-Alert (free), FEMA app, iPhone Wi-Fi Calling and Emergency SOS, Ready.gov family plan template
grey.inputs: Household members, an out-of-area contact, and the places the family spends most time.
grey.output: A wallet card and phone note with contacts, two meeting places and backup channels, plus alerts set up.
method: Pick an out-of-area contact everyone texts if local lines jam; long-distance often works when local is overloaded.
Write key numbers on paper: family, the out-of-area contact, CVAC, Walgreens store, a neighbor. Phones die; paper does not.
Choose two meeting places: one just outside the house, one outside the neighborhood such as the Chappaqua Library.
Coverage gaps: with weak Verizon at home, turn on Wi-Fi Calling, and remember it fails when the house Wi-Fi is off overnight. Know where signal is strongest.
Backups: text before calling (texts get through on weak signal), iPhone Emergency SOS via satellite on iPhone 14 or later, a charged power bank.
Sign up for NY-Alert for Westchester and turn on emergency alerts in iPhone settings.
Laminate the card, share the note with family, and review it each spring and fall.
grey.prompt: Signal Warden, build my emergency comms plan. Household: {people}. Out-of-area contact: {person and city}. Places we spend time: {home, Walgreens, SUNY Purchase, CVAC}. Phone and carrier: {model, carrier, home coverage}. Home internet: {details, when it is off}. Give me a wallet card (contacts, two meeting places, what to do if calls fail), a list of phone settings to change, the free alert services for Westchester, and a short script for the first text to send after an emergency.
checklist: Wi-Fi Calling on, overnight gap known
grey.example: Plan, Nov 2026. Out-of-area contact: a relative in Israel, reachable by WhatsApp when US lines jam. Card: parents, sister, CVAC dispatch line, the Walgreens store number, a neighbor two houses down. Meeting places: the end of the driveway, then the Chappaqua Library. Coverage: Verizon is weak indoors and the house Wi-Fi goes off at night, so overnight his best signal is the upstairs window; noted on the card. His phone supports satellite SOS; he ran the demo in settings. NY-Alert set for Westchester weather and emergencies. First text script: 'Safe at {place}. Phone at {percent}. Meeting at {spot} at {time}.'

obsidian.title: Bench 225
obsidian.use: A bench program toward 225 lb at about 150 to 155 lb bodyweight, run in 12-week blocks.
obsidian.tools: Hevy (free tier) or Strong (free tier), Google Sheets, a rack with safety arms or a spotter
obsidian.inputs: A recent heavy set (weight and reps), training days available around shifts, and bodyweight.
obsidian.output: An estimated max, a 12-week block with three bench days a week, and an honest timeline to 225.
method: Estimate the max from a recent hard set of 3 to 5 reps: weight times (1 + reps divided by 30). Set a training max at 90 percent of that.

Bench three days a week, 48 hours apart, around shifts: Heavy (top set of 3 to 5 at 85 to 90 percent of training max, 3 back-off sets of 5), Volume (5x5 at 75 percent), Light (paused or close-grip, 4x6 at 65 percent).
Accessories twice a week: rows, overhead press, dips or push-ups, band pull-aparts.
Add 5 lb to the training max every three weeks if every Heavy top set hit. A miss holds; two misses mean deload.
Eat for it: about 0.8 to 1 g of protein per lb of bodyweight, and a slow gain of about 0.5 lb a week.
Safety arms just below chest height or a spotter, every session. Sharp shoulder or elbow pain: stop and see a clinician.
Retest at Test Day every 12 weeks and reset the training max from the result.
obsidian.prompt: Jarl, build my next 12-week bench block. Recent best set: {weight} lb for {reps} reps on {date}. Bodyweight: {lb}. Days I can lift: {days, around shifts}. Equipment: {rack with safeties or spotter, dumbbells, bands}. Goal: 225 lb. Give me my estimated max and training max, a week-by-week table of Heavy, Volume and Light days with sets, reps and weights rounded to 5 lb, the accessories, the rule for adding weight, and an honest estimate of how many blocks to 225 at my bodyweight.
checklist: Estimated max and training max set
Three bench days placed around shifts
Weights rounded and written in the app
obsidian.example: Recent set: 175 lb for 3 at 151 lb bodyweight. Estimate: 175 times 1.1, about 193 lb; training max 175. Days: Monday, Wednesday, Saturday mornings before shifts. Week 1 Heavy: 155 for a top set of 5, then 3 sets of 5 at 140; Volume: 5 sets of 5 at 130; Light: paused bench 4 sets of 6 at 115. Every third week the training max rises 5 lb if Heavy sets hit. Honest timeline: about 32 lb to go, likely three to four blocks (9 to 12 months) with a slow gain to around 158 lb. The first block's target is a 205 estimate by early February.

obsidian.title: Form by Video
obsidian.use: Film a set, check it against cues frame by frame, and pick one fix for next session.
obsidian.tools: iPhone camera (slo-mo), Kinovea (free, Windows), Hevy notes
obsidian.inputs: A filmed working set from two angles and the lift's cue list.
obsidian.output: Two or three timestamped faults, one cue to fix next session, and a before and after clip pair.
method: Set the phone at hip height on a bag or bench. Side view for bar path and depth; a 45-degree front view for elbows and knees.
Film a working set, not a warm-up. Fatigue shows faults warm-ups hide.
Open the clip in Kinovea on the PC. Step frame by frame and use its tracking tool to draw the bar path.

Check the cues. Bench: shoulder blades pinned, feet planted, bar touches lower chest, elbows tucked about 45 to 70 degrees, wrists stacked over elbows, butt on the bench. Squat: brace, knees track the toes, depth below parallel, even pressure across the foot.
Mark each fault with its timestamp and which rep it began on.
Choose one cue for next session. More than one at a time means none stick.
Film the same lift next session from the same spot and compare side by side. Pain is not a form issue to film through: stop and see a clinician.
obsidian.prompt: Shieldbearer, I filmed {lift} at {weight} lb for {reps} reps from {angles}. What I see frame by frame: {describe bar path, elbows, hips, feet, depth, any rep where it changed}. My cue list for this lift: {cues or 'use standard cues'}. Tell me the two or three most important faults in order of risk, which rep each began on, the one cue I should use next session, and a drill or lighter set to groove it. Do not diagnose pain; tell me to see a clinician if I mention any.
checklist: Phone at hip height, two angles
Repeat clip filmed from the same spot
obsidian.example: Clip: bench, 155 lb for 5, side and 45-degree front. In Kinovea the bar path drifted toward his face on reps 4 and 5, and the front view showed elbows flaring near 80 degrees from rep 3, with his hips lifting off the bench on rep 5. Ranked: hips lifting (it makes the lift a different lift), then elbow flare. Cue for next session: 'drive the floor away, glutes on the bench'. Groove set: 3 sets of 5 at 115 with a two-second pause on the chest. Next clip, same spot: hips stayed down on all five reps; elbow flare is next week's cue.

obsidian.title: Body Metrics Log
obsidian.use: Weight, lifts and measurements once a week, read as trends instead of daily noise.
obsidian.tools: Google Sheets, Apple Health, Hevy, a cloth tape measure, a bathroom scale
obsidian.inputs: Morning weigh-ins on the days he can, a tape measure, and his top sets from the week.
obsidian.output: One weekly row: average weight, waist and two measurements, top lifts, and the trend over four weeks.
method: Weigh in the morning after the bathroom, before food, on the same scale. Log what days he can; the weekly average is the number that counts.
Once a week, measure waist at the navel, chest and relaxed upper arm with the cloth tape, same spot, same time.
Copy the top set for bench, squat and one pull from Hevy.
Compute the four-week trend: average weight change per week, waist change, estimated bench max change.
Read the trend against the goal: for the bench block, weight up about 0.5 lb a week with the waist steady is on track.
Change one thing at a time, by small amounts, after two weeks of trend, never after one weigh-in.
Keep any progress photos local and private, never in a shared or brand folder.
obsidian.prompt: Skald of Scars, here is my week: morning weights {list}, waist {inches}, chest {inches}, arm {inches}, top sets {bench, squat, pull}. Last four weeks: {rows}. Goal: {e.g. slow gain for the bench block}. Give me the weekly average, the four-week trend for each number, whether I am on track, and at most one small change if two or more weeks point the same way. Keep it neutral and factual.
obsidian.example: Week of Nov 2. Weigh-ins: 151.2, 150.6, 151.8, 151.4 (four days; a CVAC overnight and two early shifts skipped). Average 151.3 lb. Waist 30.5 in, chest 37.75 in, arm 12.75 in. Top sets: bench 155 for 5, squat 185 for 5, pull-ups bodyweight for 8. Four-week trend: weight up 0.2 lb a week, waist unchanged, estimated bench max up 5 lb. Read: on track for strength, slower than the 0.5 lb a week planned. One change: add a peanut butter and soy milk shake on Walgreens days, then reread in two weeks.

obsidian.title: Fast-Day Meals
obsidian.use: High-protein meals for Orthodox fast days (no meat, dairy or eggs), in US measures.
obsidian.tools: Google Sheets, Cronometer (free tier) for protein counts, Apple Reminders for the shopping list
obsidian.inputs: Which fast days are coming (Wednesdays, Fridays, the Nativity Fast), what his priest has said about fish and oil, and his protein target.
obsidian.output: A fast-day menu with amounts in cups, tablespoons and teaspoons, protein estimates, and a shopping list.
method: Mark the fast days ahead on the Julian calendar: Wednesdays, Fridays, and the Nativity Fast (Nov 28 to Jan 6 on the civil calendar).
Ask his priest what applies to him for fish, shellfish and oil; practice varies by parish and by day. The kit plans meals; it does not rule.
Build each day on protein anchors: extra-firm tofu, lentils, chickpeas, black beans, textured vegetable protein (TVP), edamame, soy milk, peanut butter, a pea protein powder.
Aim for about 100 to 130 g of protein on a fast day, spread over four meals.
Cook two big batches that cover several days (a lentil pot, a TVP chili) and one quick meal (tofu scramble).
On days without oil, water-sauté onions and season harder with garlic, cumin, smoked paprika and lemon.
Check the labels for hidden dairy and eggs: whey, casein, milk powder, egg white.
obsidian.prompt: Hearth-Keeper, plan my fast-day meals for {dates}. My priest said: {fish, oil, other guidance}. Protein target: {grams} per day. Kitchen time: {minutes per day, batch day}. Foods I dislike: {list}. Give me a menu for each day with four meals, each recipe with amounts in cups, tablespoons, teaspoons or pounds only (no grams or ounces in recipes), protein estimates per meal, and a combined shopping list. Do not add meat, dairy or eggs, and only include fish if my priest's guidance allows it that day.
checklist: Fast days marked on the Julian calendar
Priest's guidance on fish and oil noted
Two batch recipes and one quick meal
Labels checked for dairy and eggs
obsidian.example: Wednesday, Nov 11, priest's guidance: no fish, oil allowed. Breakfast: tofu scramble from 1 block extra-firm tofu (about 1 pound) crumbled with 1/2 teaspoon turmeric, 1/2 teaspoon cumin and 1 cup spinach, half the pan, about 22 g protein. Lunch: red lentil and chickpea stew from 1 cup dry red lentils, 1 1/2 cups cooked chickpeas, 1 can crushed tomatoes, 1 diced onion, 1 tablespoon curry powder and 3 cups water, a third of the pot, about 23 g. Walgreens break: shake of 1 1/2 cups soy milk, 2 tablespoons peanut butter and 1 scoop pea protein, about 38 g. Dinner: TVP chili, 1/2 cup dry TVP per serving with black beans, about 30 g. Total about 113 g.

obsidian.title: Mobility Routine
obsidian.use: Ten minutes a day for hips, shoulders and spine, built around bench and long shifts.
obsidian.tools: iPhone Clock (timer), a resistance band, a pull-up bar or doorway
obsidian.inputs: Ten minutes, a floor, a band, and which spots feel tight lately.
obsidian.output: A fixed ten-minute sequence with timings, a tightness check, and a weekly note.
method: Minute 0 to 1: cat-cow, slow, ten reps, breathing out on each round.
Minute 1 to 3: 90/90 hip switches, ten each side, sitting tall.
Minute 3 to 5: world's greatest stretch (lunge, elbow to instep, rotate the arm up), five each side.
Minute 5 to 6: thoracic open books lying on each side, eight each.
Minute 6 to 8: band pull-aparts, two sets of fifteen, and wall slides, ten, to balance all the pressing.
Minute 8 to 9: couch stretch for the hip flexors, thirty seconds each side, after hours standing at the register.
Minute 9 to 10: dead hang from a bar or doorway frame, two holds of 20 to 30 seconds. Stretch to mild tension only; pain means stop.
obsidian.prompt: Ice-Runner, adjust my ten-minute mobility routine. What feels tight: {spots}. What I did this week: {lifting days, shifts, runs}. Equipment: {band, bar, foam roller}. Keep the total at ten minutes. Swap in moves for my tight spots, give exact reps or seconds, and tell me where in the day to do it (before lifting, on a break, before bed). Nothing painful; tell me to see a clinician if anything I describe sounds like an injury.
checklist: Tight spots noted for the week
obsidian.example: Week of Nov 9. Tight: front of the hips after two 8-hour register shifts, and the right shoulder after Wednesday's bench. Routine kept at ten minutes but swapped thirty seconds of cat-cow for an extra thirty-second couch stretch on the right side, and added a sleeper stretch for the right shoulder in the open-books slot. Placement: right after Walgreens on shift days, as a warm-up before lifting on Monday and Saturday. Six of seven days done (missed the CVAC overnight). Note for Sunday: hips noticeably better by Friday; the shoulder unchanged, so it goes on the Form by Video list for elbow flare.

obsidian.title: Recovery Week
obsidian.use: Know when to deload, and run a recovery week that keeps the habit without the fatigue.
obsidian.tools: Hevy, Google Sheets, iPhone Sleep data (Health app)
obsidian.inputs: The last four to six weeks of training logs, sleep averages, and the calendar for next week.
obsidian.output: A deload yes or no with the reasons, and the full recovery week written out.
method: Deload if two or more are true: top sets stalled or dropped for two weeks, joints achy going into sessions, sleep under about 6.5 hours for a week, motivation flat, five to six hard weeks in a row.
Also deload on purpose in weeks that will be wrecked anyway: finals, a run of CVAC overnights, travel.
Keep the schedule and the movements. Cut the volume in half and the load to about 60 to 70 percent.
No sets to failure, no new maxes, no testing.
Walk daily, keep the mobility routine, and aim for an extra 30 to 60 minutes of sleep.
Eat normally. A recovery week is not a diet week.
Return the next week at the training max where he left off. Joint pain that lasts into the deload goes to a clinician.
obsidian.prompt: Valkyrie, decide whether I should deload next week. Last {weeks} weeks of top sets: {list}. Joints: {notes}. Sleep average: {hours}. Motivation: {1 to 5}. Next week's calendar: {shifts, finals, CVAC, travel}. Tell me yes or no with the reasons, then write my recovery week day by day with sets, reps and loads based on my current program: {program}. Keep me moving; nothing to failure.
checklist: Volume halved, loads at 60 to 70 percent
obsidian.example: Check, Sunday Dec 6. Bench top set stuck at 160 for 4 two weeks running, sleep averaging 6.2 hours (two CVAC overnights), and finals the week of Dec 14. Four signs true, so deload, timed for finals week. Plan: Monday bench 3 sets of 5 at 115, rows 3 sets of 8; Wednesday squat 3 sets of 5 at 125 and push-ups 2 sets of 15; Saturday paused bench 3 sets of 5 at 105. Daily 25-minute walk, which doubles as study time with flashcards. Bed by 11 on non-shift nights. Return Dec 21 with the training max at 175, as before.

obsidian.title: Ruck Plan
obsidian.use: A safe ruck progression in weight, distance and route, starting from where he is.
obsidian.tools: Strava (free tier), Apple Maps, iPhone Health, a sturdy backpack, water jugs or sandbags
obsidian.inputs: His bodyweight, current walking or ruck history, the pack, and days available.
obsidian.output: A week-by-week progression, routes from home, and foot-care and safety notes.
method: Start light: about 15 lb for 2 to 3 miles, at a brisk 15 to 17 minutes per mile. A gallon of water is about 8.3 lb and makes adjustable weight.
Progress one variable a week: add half a mile to a mile, or 5 lb, never both.
Cap the load near a third of bodyweight (about 45 to 50 lb at his size) and the long ruck at about 8 miles for now.
Ruck once or twice a week, not on the day after heavy squats.
Routes: a 2-mile neighborhood loop from home, a 4-mile out-and-back, and the North County Trailway from Millwood for long days. Map each in Apple Maps or Strava.
Feet: broken-in boots or trail shoes, wool socks, and tape on hot spots before they blister.
Visibility: November dark falls before 5 pm, so wear a reflective vest and headlamp on roads and walk facing traffic.
obsidian.prompt: Trailbreaker, build me a ruck progression. Bodyweight: {lb}. Ruck or hiking history: {recent}. Pack and weights: {details}. Days available: {days}. Goal: {e.g. 6 miles at 35 lb by a date}. Give me a week-by-week table (weight, distance, target pace), routes I can walk from {home area} without a car, foot-care steps, and safety notes for roads and early darkness. One variable up per week, and tell me when to repeat a week instead.
checklist: Load capped near a third of bodyweight
Reflective vest and headlamp after dusk
obsidian.example: Start, Nov 8: 151 lb bodyweight, no recent rucks. Week 1: 15 lb (two gallon jugs in a towel inside the pack) for 2 miles. Week 2: 15 lb, 3 miles. Week 3: 20 lb, 3 miles. Week 4: repeat, since Thanksgiving week is busy. Week 5: 20 lb, 4 miles on the out-and-back. Goal: 30 lb for 6 miles on the North County Trailway by late January. Week 1 logged in Strava at 16:20 per mile; a hot spot on the left heel at mile 1.5 was taped at home and pre-taped for week 2. Rucks after 4:30 pm wear the vest and headlamp.

obsidian.title: Test Day
obsidian.use: A quarterly strength and conditioning test in a fixed order, so every quarter compares fairly.
obsidian.tools: Hevy, Strava, Google Sheets, a stopwatch, a measured 1.5-mile route or track
obsidian.inputs: A rested day (no heavy lifting for 48 hours), a spotter or safety arms, and two hours.
obsidian.output: A test card with every result, the change from last quarter, and the targets for the next block.
method: Schedule it at the end of a training block, after an easy day, at the same time of day each quarter.
Warm up the same way every time: 5 minutes easy cardio and the mobility routine.
Order matters, so keep it fixed: bench 3-rep max with safeties or a spotter, max strict pull-ups, max push-ups in 2 minutes, 1.5-mile run, and on a separate day a 4-mile ruck at 25 lb for time.
Bench: work up in jumps, take a 3-rep max you could have done once more. No grinders, no solo failure without safeties.
Log everything on the card, including bodyweight that morning, sleep the night before, and conditions.
Compare with last quarter and set the next block's targets from the results.
Stop any test that causes sharp pain, and see a clinician if it persists.
obsidian.prompt: Keeper of the Kjrdakan, here are my Test Day results for {date}: bodyweight {lb}, sleep {hours}, bench 3RM {weight}, pull-ups {reps}, push-ups in 2 minutes {reps}, 1.5-mile run {time}, 4-mile ruck at 25 lb {time}. Last quarter: {results or 'baseline'}. Build my test card with the changes, tell me which number moved most and least and why that might be, and set realistic targets for each test at the next quarterly test on {date}.
checklist: Same warm-up and time of day
obsidian.example: Baseline, Saturday Nov 14, 9 am. Bodyweight 151.4 lb, 7 hours of sleep. Bench 3RM: 175 lb, solid. Strict pull-ups: 9. Push-ups in 2 minutes: 52. 1.5-mile run on the measured road loop: 12:48. Ruck on Sunday, 4 miles at 25 lb: 1:06:30. With no prior card, these set the bar. Targets for the February test: bench 3RM 190, pull-ups 11, push-ups 60, run under 12:15 (helped by the Run Base kit), ruck under 1:03. Card saved to the Longhouse sheet and the next Test Day set for Saturday, Feb 13.

obsidian.title: Posture Reset
obsidian.use: Desk and phone posture habits plus three daily drills, for a student who also stands at a register.
obsidian.tools: iPhone Screen Time (pickups), iPhone Clock, a wall, a doorway
obsidian.inputs: Where he sits and stands most, how he holds his phone, and five minutes a day.
obsidian.output: Three daily drills with reps, two setup changes, and a two-week check.
method: Phone: raise it toward eye level instead of dropping the head. Check daily pickups in Screen Time; fewer pickups means less time looking down.
Desk: use the Workstation kit settings so the monitor top sits at eye level and he sits back in the chair.
Register: weight on both feet, a soft bend in the knees, and a step or shift every few minutes instead of locking out.
Drill 1, chin tucks: 10 slow reps, holding 3 seconds, head sliding straight back.
Drill 2, wall angels: back, head and arms against a wall, 10 slow slides up and down.
Drill 3, doorway chest stretch: forearms on the frame, step through gently, 30 seconds, twice.
Tie the drills to fixed moments: after brushing teeth, after a shift, after the last study block. Numbness, tingling or lasting pain goes to a clinician.
obsidian.prompt: Posture Smith, here is my day: {hours sitting, standing at the register, on the phone}. Where I feel it: {neck, upper back, low back}. My desk setup: {details}. Give me two setup changes for my desk and phone, three daily drills with exact reps and holds, a moment in my day to anchor each one, and a simple self-check I can do in two weeks to see if it is working.
checklist: Desk set per the Workstation kit
obsidian.example: Day: about 7 hours standing at the register on shift days, 3 to 4 hours at the PC, and 214 phone pickups a day in Screen Time. Feels it in the neck and between the shoulder blades by the end of a shift. Changes: phone held at chest height with the elbow on his other arm when reading, and a Screen Time limit on Instagram at 45 minutes. Drills anchored: chin tucks after brushing teeth, wall angels in the break room on his 15-minute break, doorway stretch after the last study block. Two-week check, Nov 23: back flat against the wall without strain for 30 seconds, and the end-of-shift ache rated 2 of 5, down from 4.

obsidian.title: Run Base
obsidian.use: Build an easy running base week by week, conversational pace, through a Westchester winter.
obsidian.tools: Strava (free tier), None to Run or NHS Couch to 5K (free apps), iPhone Health
obsidian.inputs: Current running ability, three days a week, and decent running shoes.
obsidian.output: A ten-week plan from run-walk to 30 minutes of easy running, with winter safety notes.
method: Start with run-walk at a pace where he can speak in full sentences: week 1 is 8 rounds of 1 minute running and 2 minutes walking.
Run three days a week, never two days in a row, and not the day after heavy squats.
Add a little each week: more running, less walking, total time up by about 10 percent. Every fourth week, hold steady.
If breathing gets too hard to talk, slow down or walk. Easy is the point; speed comes later.
Cold weather: dress as if it is 15 to 20 F warmer than it is, cover hands and ears, and watch for ice on shaded roads.
Dark: reflective vest and headlamp, facing traffic, or run on the track at SUNY Purchase before class.
Log every run in Strava. Shin, knee or foot pain that changes his stride means stop and rest, and see a clinician if it lasts.
obsidian.prompt: Pacer, build my running base. Current ability: {e.g. can run 3 minutes nonstop}. Days available: {days}. Other training: {bench days, rucks}. Where I can run: {roads, track, trail}. Weather: {month}. Goal: 30 minutes of easy running nonstop. Give me a ten-week table of run and walk intervals, where each week sits around my lifting and rucks, how to tell if my pace is easy enough, and cold and dark safety notes for Westchester.
checklist: Three runs a week, not back to back
Dressed for cold, visible in dark
obsidian.example: Start, week of Nov 9: he can run about 3 minutes nonstop. Days: Tuesday, Thursday, Sunday, away from Monday and Saturday bench and the Sunday ruck moved to Friday. Week 1: 8 rounds of 1 minute run, 2 minutes walk. Week 3: 6 rounds of 3 and 1. Week 4: repeat week 3 (Thanksgiving). Week 6: 3 rounds of 8 and 1. Week 10: 30 minutes easy. First run logged in Strava: 24 minutes total, 38 F, average pace while running 10:40 per mile, able to talk the whole time. Thursday runs move to the SUNY Purchase track before class, since it is dark by 5.

orange.title: PC Health Check
orange.use: Monthly twenty-minute check of the Windows PC: temperatures, drives, updates, startup apps.
orange.tools: HWiNFO, CrystalDiskInfo, Windows Update, NVIDIA App, Task Manager, Windows Security, Storage Sense
orange.inputs: Twenty minutes at the PC, admin rights, and last month's log line.
orange.output: One log row: temperatures idle and loaded, drive health, updates applied, startup apps changed, one action.
method: Open HWiNFO (sensors only). Note CPU and GPU temperature at idle, then during ten minutes of a game or a local model run. Watch for high idle temps and for clocks dropping under load, not one hot reading.
Open CrystalDiskInfo. Every drive should read Good. Caution or Bad means back up tonight (3-2-1 Backup kit) and plan a replacement.
Run Windows Update, then check the NVIDIA App for a new Game Ready or Studio driver. Restart once.
Task Manager, Startup apps: disable anything he does not need at boot. Check Task Scheduler too, since some apps start from there.
Run a Windows Security quick scan and confirm real-time protection is on.
Let Storage Sense clear temp files; keep the system drive under 80 percent full.
Every third month, power down, unplug, and blow dust from the intake filters and GPU fans with canned air, holding the fans still.
orange.prompt: Master Maker, here is this month's PC check: idle temps CPU {x} C, GPU {x} C; loaded CPU {x} C, GPU {x} C during {workload}; CrystalDiskInfo says {status per drive}; updates applied: {list}; startup apps enabled: {list}; system drive {percent} full. Compare with last month: {last log row}. Tell me what is normal for a Windows desktop with an RTX 5070 and a Ryzen CPU, what is drifting, which startup items are safe to disable and which to keep, and the one action for this month. Do not suggest paid tools or registry cleaners.
checklist: Startup apps and Task Scheduler reviewed
orange.example: November check. Idle: CPU 41 C, GPU 34 C. Under 15 minutes of an 8B model in Ollama: GPU 66 C, clocks steady. CrystalDiskInfo: NVMe Good, the old 1 TB SATA drive Good at 94 percent health. Windows Update installed the monthly cumulative update; the NVIDIA App had a new Game Ready driver. Startup apps showed Steam, Discord, Epic and a Node script for the GOLEM hub. The GOLEM script also had a Task Scheduler entry set to run at boot, which explained why it started before login; he disabled that entry so it only runs when opened. System drive at 71 percent. Action: none beyond the startup fix. Next dust clean due in January.

orange.title: The Dead MacBook
orange.use: Diagnose a 13-inch Touch Bar MacBook Pro that will not power on, cheapest checks first.
orange.tools: Apple Check Coverage (checkcoverage.apple.com), Apple Support app, Apple Configurator (on a borrowed Mac), iPhone flashlight
orange.inputs: The MacBook, any USB-C charger and cable he owns, and an hour. A friend's Mac helps for the last step.
orange.output: A diagnosis log, the step where it failed, and a repair-or-sell decision with a price ceiling.
method: Safety first: a bulging case, raised trackpad or lid that will not close flat can mean a swollen battery. Stop, do not charge, take it to a shop.
Read the A-number on the bottom (A1706: 2016-17; A1989, A2159, A2251, A2289: T2 chip; A2338: Apple silicon) and confirm the serial at checkcoverage.apple.com.
Charge 30 minutes from a known-good USB-C charger of 30 W or more, trying every port.
Rule out a dead screen: flashlight on the display, Caps Lock light, an external monitor over USB-C. The 2016-17 display cables fail often.

Reset the SMC. T2: hold power 10 seconds; then hold right Shift, left Option, left Control 7 seconds, add power 7 more, release, power on. 2016-17: left Shift, Control, Option plus power for 10 seconds.
T2 or Apple silicon: on a borrowed Mac, revive the firmware with Apple Configurator in DFU mode (revive keeps data, restore erases), following Apple's guide for the right port.
An Activation Lock screen in someone else's name means stop: it cannot be unlocked without the owner.
Still dead: get quotes from the Apple Store at The Westchester (Bee-Line to White Plains) and a board-repair shop. Fix only under 60 percent of resale value.
orange.prompt: Fixer, walk me through diagnosing my dead MacBook one step at a time. A-number: {A-number}. Serial check: {result}. Charger: {wattage and type}. Tried so far: {steps and results}. Signs of life: {none, fan, light, heat, chime}. Ask one question at a time, give the next cheapest test and what each result means, and stop me at once if anything suggests a swollen battery. When home tests run out, give me a repair-or-sell call with a price ceiling.
orange.example: A-number A1989: a 2018 T2 model, serial confirmed, no bulge. Thirty minutes on a 61 W charger in each port: nothing, case cold. No faint image under the flashlight and no Caps Lock light, so not just the screen. Both SMC resets: nothing. On his friend's MacBook Air, Apple Configurator showed the dead Mac in DFU, so the board responds. Revive failed; a restore worked (nothing of his was on it). It booted to setup with no Activation Lock. Logged: failed firmware, fixed at home for $0.

orange.title: Phone Data Recovery
orange.use: Get photos and memes off a broken phone, cloud copies first, hardware last.
orange.tools: iCloud.com, Google Photos, Apple Devices app (Windows), Instagram Accounts Center, scrcpy (Android)
orange.inputs: The broken phone, its passcode, his Apple or Google account login, and the PC.
orange.output: A list of what was already in the cloud, what was pulled off the device, and what is still missing.
method: Check the cloud first: iCloud.com Photos for iPhone, photos.google.com for Android. Note the newest photo's date.
Instagram saved posts and sent DMs live on Instagram's servers. Request them with Download your information in Accounts Center.
If the phone powers on and this PC was trusted before, back it up with the Apple Devices app; no screen tap needed.
Android with a dead screen: if USB debugging was on, scrcpy mirrors and controls it from the PC.
Dead screen and never trusted: a cheap replacement screen fitted just long enough to unlock, tap Trust and back up.
No power at all: a board-level repair shop with a no-data, no-fee quote.
Copy recovered memes into a dated PC folder, then into the 3-2-1 Backup.
orange.prompt: Artificer, help me recover data from a broken {iPhone or Android, model}. What works: {powers on, vibrates, charges, shows on PC, nothing}. Screen: {cracked but visible, black, unresponsive}. Was it ever backed up to iCloud or Google, or trusted on my PC: {answer}. What I want back: {photos, memes, messages}. Give me the order of attempts from free to paid, what each attempt needs, and where each kind of file I want is likely stored (on the device versus on a service's servers). Do not suggest anything that risks wiping the phone before a backup exists.
checklist: Backup attempted if the PC was trusted
Recovered files in a dated folder
orange.example: Phone: an iPhone 12 with a black screen that vibrates when plugged in. iCloud Photos was off, so nothing there newer than 2023. The Instagram export arrived the next day and held 1,140 saved-post links and every meme he had sent in DMs, which covered most of what he wanted. The Apple Devices app on the PC saw the phone but asked for Trust on the dead screen. A $35 aftermarket screen fitted at a mall kiosk lit the phone long enough to enter the passcode and tap Trust; the full local backup took 40 minutes. Camera roll memes went to Pictures, Memes, 2026-11 and onto the external drive.

orange.title: The 3-2-1 Backup
orange.use: Three copies of what matters, on two kinds of media, one of them offsite, with a tested restore.
orange.tools: FreeFileSync, Windows File History, Veeam Agent for Windows Free, Google Drive (15 GB free), Cryptomator, GitHub (private repos)
orange.inputs: A list of folders he cannot lose, an external drive, and a free cloud account.
orange.output: A written backup map (what, where, how often), one scheduled job, and a dated restore test.
method: List the irreplaceable set: GOLEM (C:\Users\Elijah\Jarvis), writing drafts, school papers, photos and memes, CVAC records. Note the size of each.
Copy 1 is the PC. Copy 2: an external USB drive, synced weekly with a FreeFileSync mirror job or Windows File History.
Copy 3 offsite: the most precious folders to Google Drive. Put anything sensitive inside a Cryptomator vault first.
Code goes to private GitHub repos. Keep .env files and API keys out with .gitignore and check before every first push.
Optional: a Veeam Agent Free system image to the external drive monthly, so a dead SSD is an evening, not a week.
Test a restore: delete a copy of one file and bring it back from each copy. A backup that has never restored is a hope.
Write the map on one page and set a monthly reminder to check the last-backup dates.
orange.prompt: Toolroom Keeper, build my 3-2-1 backup plan. Folders I cannot lose, with sizes: {list}. Hardware: {PC drives, external drive size}. Cloud accounts: {Google, iCloud, OneDrive, GitHub}. Anything sensitive: {yes or no, which}. Give me a table of copy 1, 2 and 3 for each folder with the tool and schedule, steps to set up one FreeFileSync job, which folders need a Cryptomator vault, what my .gitignore must exclude, and a five-minute restore test. Free tools only, and say if my data will not fit in the free tiers.
checklist: Sensitive files in an encrypted vault
orange.example: His set came to about 62 GB: GOLEM 3 GB, writing and school 2 GB, photos and memes 54 GB, CVAC and admin 1 GB, plus the game project. Plan: copy 2 is a 1 TB USB drive with a FreeFileSync mirror job every Sunday night; copy 3 puts writing, school, GOLEM and admin (6 GB) on Google Drive's free 15 GB, with admin inside a Cryptomator vault. Photos do not fit free, so the second copy of those sits on an old USB stick kept at a friend's house, refreshed monthly. GOLEM's repo got a .gitignore entry for .env before the first push. Restore test: a deleted essay came back from all three in under four minutes.

orange.title: The Workstation
orange.use: Set up desk, chair, monitor and light so long sessions do not cost his neck, wrists or eyes.
orange.tools: Tape measure, Windows Night light, f.lux, books or a box as a monitor riser
orange.inputs: His desk, chair and monitor as they are, a tape measure, and fifteen minutes.
orange.output: Measured settings for chair, desk, monitor and light, a short shopping list if needed, and a before and after.
method: Sit back in the chair with feet flat. Thighs should be level and knees near 90 degrees. Too high, add a footrest (a box works).
Set keyboard and mouse at elbow height, forearms level, shoulders down. If the desk is too high, raise the chair and use the footrest.
Monitor: an arm's length away, top edge at or slightly below eye level, centered on the keyboard. Stack books under it if needed.
Light: no bright window behind the screen or directly behind him. Add a desk lamp to the side; turn on Windows Night light or f.lux for evenings.
Lower back: a small cushion or rolled towel at belt height if the chair lacks support.
Clear the cable mess under the desk with velcro ties, and keep the power strip off the floor where feet hit it.
Work in a 20-20-20 habit: every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds.
orange.prompt: Desk Architect, here are my measurements: desk height {inches}, chair seat height {range}, my height {feet and inches}, monitor size {inches} and its top edge sits {inches} from the desk, distance to screen {inches}. Window position: {where}. Main uses: {writing, coding, gaming, editing}. Tell me the target number for each, what to change today with what I already own, and a short list of anything worth buying under $30 if the free fixes are not enough.
checklist: Monitor top at or below eye level
orange.example: Before: a 30-inch desk, chair at its lowest, the 27-inch monitor's top edge four inches below eye level, and a window behind the screen glaring in the afternoon. He is 5 feet 9.
