Changes: chair up two inches, a sturdy shoebox as a footrest, the monitor raised on two hardcover history books, the desk turned 90 degrees so the window sits to his left, and Night light set for 8 pm. A rolled bath towel went behind his lower back. One purchase listed: a $20 clamp desk lamp. After a week he noticed the end-of-shift neck ache was gone on writing nights.

orange.title: Battery Care
orange.use: Keep phone, laptop and power-bank batteries healthy longer, and know when one needs replacing.
orange.tools: iPhone Settings (Battery Health and Charging), coconutBattery (Mac), Call2Recycle drop-off locator
orange.inputs: His phone model, any laptops and power banks, and how he charges them now.
orange.output: Settings changed, a habit list, health numbers logged, and a replace or recycle note for any bad battery.
method: iPhone: Settings, Battery, Battery Health. Log the maximum capacity. Turn on Optimized Battery Charging, or the 80 percent limit if the model offers it.
Heat is the main killer. No charging under pillows, in sun or while gaming hot. Remove thick cases when fast-charging.
Keep everyday charge between about 20 and 80 percent; one full cycle now and then is fine.
Mac (once revived): check cycle count and condition in System Settings or coconutBattery.
Power banks for CVAC overnights: charge on a hard surface, store half full if unused, retire any that swell, smell or get hot.
Below 80 percent capacity and the phone dies by evening: book a battery service rather than a new phone.
Never toss lithium cells in the trash. Find a drop-off on the Call2Recycle locator.
orange.prompt: Power Warden, here is my battery situation: phone {model}, Battery Health {percent}, charging habit {when, where, which charger}; other devices {laptops, earbuds, power banks with ages}. My day: {shift lengths, overnights}. Tell me which settings to change, which habits are hurting the battery, whether any device is near replacement, and what a battery service would likely cost compared with a new device. Flag anything unsafe.
checklist: Swollen or old cells set aside for recycling
orange.example: iPhone health read 84 percent after two years. Habit: charging on the bed overnight with a thick case, often after a hot gaming session on the phone. Changes: charger moved to the nightstand, case off for fast charging, Optimized Battery Charging on. His older power bank from 2021 had a slight bulge at one corner, so it went into a metal tin and then to a Call2Recycle drop-off; he used the newer 10,000 mAh bank for the next CVAC overnight. Decision: keep the phone; book a battery service when it drops below 80 percent. Re-check set for February.

orange.title: Secondhand Checklist
orange.use: Test used gear before money changes hands, so no more dead MacBooks.
orange.tools: CTIA Stolen Phone Checker (stolenphonechecker.org), Apple Check Coverage, HWiNFO, a USB stick, phone flashlight
orange.inputs: The listing, the seller's answers to three questions, and time to test in person.
orange.output: A pass or walk-away decision, the agreed price, and photos of the item and serial.
method: Before meeting, ask: why are you selling, any repairs, is it signed out of every account? Vague answers on repairs mean walk away.
Check the serial or IMEI: CTIA Stolen Phone Checker for phones, Apple Check Coverage for Apple devices.
Meet somewhere public in daylight; many police stations have safe exchange spots. Cash or a protected payment only, never a deposit.
Power it on and use it. Phones: every camera, Face ID or fingerprint, speakers, mic, charge port, battery health. Laptops: full boot, every key, every port, trackpad, webcam, battery cycle count.
Account locks: the seller signs out of Find My or Google in front of him. Macs with Activation Lock or a work management profile are a walk away.
PC parts: ask for a demo under load and watch temperatures in HWiNFO.
Haggle with what testing found, photograph the item and serial, and get a text receipt from the seller.
orange.prompt: Salvager, I am looking at a used {item} listed for {price} on {platform}. Listing text: {paste}. Seller answers so far: {answers}. Give me the three questions I still need to ask, the in-person tests for this exact item in order, the red flags that mean walk away, a fair price range based on condition, and how to pay safely. Keep it short enough to read on my phone while I test.
checklist: Item powered on and tested fully
Account locks removed in front of him
Receipt text and serial photo saved
orange.example: Listing: an iPad Air for $180 on Facebook Marketplace, 'works perfect'. Seller said it was her daughter's and never repaired. CTIA checker: clean. They met in the New Castle police station lobby. Testing found it booted fine and Touch ID worked, but battery health was not shown and the charge port only worked at one angle. Settings showed it was still signed in to her daughter's Apple Account; she called her, and they signed out with him watching. He offered $140 citing the port; she took $150. Serial photographed, and a text receipt from the seller saved to the Bureau folder.

orange.title: Loadout Sheet
orange.use: Any kit on one sheet: airsoft day, CVAC overnight or travel, packed and checked the night before.
orange.tools: Google Sheets, iPhone Notes (checklist), iPhone Reminders
orange.inputs: The kind of outing, its length and weather, and any rules from the field, agency or carrier.
orange.output: A one-page loadout: no-go items, standard kit, comfort items and spares, each with where it lives.
method: Name the outing, its length, the weather and the rules that apply (field rules, CVAC policy, airline limits).
List no-go items first: what makes the trip fail if forgotten (ID, eye protection, uniform, ticket, charger).
Add standard kit, then comfort items, then spares. Each item gets a location: bag, pocket or pouch.
Mark anything that needs charging, refilling or checking the night before.
Pack from the sheet the night before and tick each line as it goes in.
After the outing, add one thing he missed and cut one thing he never used.
Save each sheet as a template: airsoft, CVAC overnight, day in the city, travel.
orange.prompt: Armorer, make me a loadout sheet for {outing}, lasting {hours or days}, weather {forecast}. Rules that apply: {field rules, CVAC policy, airline limits}. Getting there by {Metro-North, bus, ride}. Gear I already own: {list}. Give me a table: item, quantity, where it lives, charge or check the night before, category (no-go, standard, comfort, spare). Put no-go items at the top and keep the whole sheet to one phone screen.
checklist: Packed and ticked the night before
orange.example: Outing: a CVAC overnight, 6 pm to 6 am, 34 F and windy. No-go: CVAC ID, uniform shirt and pants per corps policy, boots, phone, charger. Standard: watch with a second hand, penlight, trauma shears, pen and notepad, warm jacket. Comfort: fleece, toothbrush, spare socks, EMT flashcards, a fast-day dinner for Wednesday (lentil soup in a thermos). Spares: power bank, extra shirt. Night-before: charge the power bank and phone, fill the thermos at 5 pm. After-action: he wanted earplugs for the bunk room and never touched the paperback, so earplugs went in and the book came out.

orange.title: Godot Brief
orange.use: Write a BRIEF for one feature of the Godot 4 GOLEM game, in house format, ready for Claude Code.
orange.tools: Godot 4 (portable, in GOLEM-Game\tools), Claude Code, Git, VS Code
orange.inputs: One feature idea, what the player should see, and the scene it lives in. The game is paused; use when it resumes.
orange.output: A one-page BRIEF in house format, small enough for one session, with acceptance tests he can check by playing.
method: Write the goal as one player-visible sentence: 'When I do X, I see Y.'
Fill the house format: ID, Title, Goal, Why now, Scope in, Scope out, Scenes and nodes, Files, Controls, Acceptance tests, Risks, Time box, Rollback.
Name exact paths in the project (res://scenes/..., res://scripts/...) and the node types (Area3D, CanvasLayer, signals).
Write three to five acceptance tests he can check by playing, each with a pass condition.
Put the tempting extras under Scope out.
Set a time box (one session, two hours) and a rollback: commit before, revert if tests fail.
Give the BRIEF to Claude Code in C:\Users\Elijah\Jarvis\GOLEM-Game, play the build, tick the tests, and file what is left as the next BRIEF.
orange.prompt: Engine-Wright, turn this feature idea into a BRIEF in house format for my Godot 4 GOLEM game: {idea}. The player should experience: {what they see and do}. It lives in: {scene}. Existing pieces I know of: {nodes, scripts}. Use the headings ID, Title, Goal, Why now, Scope in, Scope out, Scenes and nodes, Files, Controls, Acceptance tests, Risks, Time box, Rollback. Keep it to one session of work. Acceptance tests must be things I can check by playing, not by reading code. Ask me up to three questions first if anything is unclear.
checklist: Exact paths and node types named
Three to five playable acceptance tests
orange.example: BRIEF G-014, 'The Filing Cabinet'. Goal: when I walk up to the cabinet in the Bureau wing and press E, a panel opens listing that house's files. Scope in: an Area3D on the cabinet, a CanvasLayer panel, reading the file list from a JSON file. Scope out: opening the files themselves, animations, sound. Files: res://scenes/bureau.tscn, res://scripts/cabinet.gd, res://ui/file_panel.tscn. Control: an 'interact' action mapped to E. Tests: the prompt appears within two meters; E opens the panel; Esc closes it; walking away hides the prompt. Time box: two hours. Rollback: commit 'before G-014'. Claude Code finished it in one session; all four tests passed.

orange.title: Splitter Care
orange.use: Run and maintain the hydraulic log splitter safely, from pre-start checks to winter storage.
orange.tools: The splitter's owner's manual (or the maker's site), a dipstick, a flat file, a grease gun, a scrap of cardboard
orange.inputs: The splitter's make and model, and its manual if he can find it.
orange.output: A pre-start checklist, safe operating rules, a maintenance log and a winter storage routine.
method: Gear up: safety glasses, steel-toe boots, close-fitting gloves, hearing protection; no loose sleeves or cords.
Pre-start, engine cold, on level ground with wheels chocked: check engine oil and hydraulic fluid on the dipsticks, look over the hoses, check tire pressure.
Find leaks with cardboard, never a hand. A pinhole hydraulic leak can inject fluid under the skin; that is an emergency room visit even if it looks small.
One operator at the controls. Nobody holds the log while the ram moves. Hands off the wedge and the log ends.
Split one round at a time, cut ends square, with the grain. Large rounds go in vertical mode if the splitter has it.
Stuck log: stop, retract the ram, shut the engine off before clearing it.
After each session, file burrs off the wedge and lubricate the beam as the manual says. Log hours, then change oil on the manual's schedule.
Winter storage: fresh fuel with stabilizer, run it two minutes, cover it, store it out of the snow.
orange.prompt: Mechanic, my log splitter is a {make and model, gas or electric, tons}. Hours used so far: {hours}. Last oil change: {date or unknown}. What I have noticed: {sounds, leaks, slow ram}. Give me a pre-start checklist I can read on my phone, the maintenance due now based on typical schedules (tell me to confirm against the manual), the warning signs that mean stop using it, and how to store it for winter. Safety first, and plain steps.
checklist: Engine oil and hydraulic fluid checked
Hoses checked with cardboard, not hands
orange.example: Splitter: a 25-ton gas model, about 40 hours on it, oil change date unknown. Pre-start: engine oil low and dark, so it was topped and an oil change scheduled for the weekend; hydraulic fluid at the mark. Cardboard under the hose fittings showed a damp spot at the pump coupling, so he tightened the fitting with the engine off and rechecked it the next session: dry. During the session a knotty oak round jammed; he retracted, shut the engine off, rotated the round and split it from the other end. After: wedge filed, beam lubricated, 3.5 hours logged. Woodyard Tally updated.

pink.title: Date Night
pink.use: Three date ideas each week, near home or in the city, reachable without a car and kept off work talk.
pink.tools: MTA TrainTime app, Google Maps, Eventbrite, Bee-Line bus schedules
pink.inputs: His and Andy's free evenings this week, a budget, the weather, and what they did last time.
pink.output: Three ideas (one near home, one in the city, one at home) with times, train or bus plan and cost.
method: Find the shared free evening or two from both calendars before planning anything.
Idea one, near home: something reachable on foot or one Metro-North stop, like a film at the Jacob Burns Film Center in Pleasantville or a walk and dinner in town.

Idea two, in the city: Harlem Line to Grand Central, then something walkable. Free or cheap options: the High Line, Bryant Park's winter rink (free entry), the Met (pay what you wish for New York residents with ID).
Idea three, at home: cook something new together, a film night with a theme, a board game.
For each, check the last train back in TrainTime and buy off-peak tickets in the app.
Agree one rule: no Marginalia, Genizah or channel planning on date night. Work talk gets its own slot.
After, note what they loved in the Keepsake Journal so future picks get better.
pink.prompt: Revel-Planner, give me three date ideas for this week. Free evenings: {days and times}. Budget: {amount}. Weather: {forecast}. Last few dates: {list}. What Andy is into lately: {interests}. One idea near Chappaqua (walking or one train stop), one in Manhattan by Metro-North from Chappaqua, one at home. For each: what, when, how to get there and back including the last train, rough cost for two, and one small touch that makes it feel planned.
checklist: One near home, one city, one at home
No work talk on the night
Highlights noted in the Keepsake Journal
pink.example: Week of Nov 16, free nights Wednesday and Saturday, budget $70. Near: Wednesday, the 7 pm film at the Jacob Burns in Pleasantville, one stop south, then pizza on Wheeler Avenue, about $45. City: Saturday afternoon, the 1:05 train to Grand Central, walk Bryant Park's winter village and the rink (free entry, rentals extra), then the New York Public Library's main reading room before dinner, last convenient train home at 9:50. Home: Sunday, cook the batch-cook chili together and watch a film he has never seen. They picked the city; the note afterward said the library was the best part.

pink.title: Gift Finder
pink.use: The right gift from what he knows about the person, inside a budget, ordered in time.
pink.tools: Google Sheets (person notes), Google Shopping, the Returns Tracker kit, iPhone Calendar
pink.inputs: Who the gift is for, the occasion and date, the budget, and what he knows about them.
pink.output: Three gift options ranked, with where to buy, the order-by date, and a card line.
method: Open the person's note (or start one): interests, recent mentions ('I need a new...'), what they already have, any rules (kosher, allergies, no clutter).
Pick the category that fits the relationship: something they use, something they experience, something meaningful, or something consumable.
Generate three options within budget, each tied to one specific thing he knows about them.
Check any rules: food gifts for observant Jewish friends need a reliable kosher certification on the package.
Find the order-by date for the occasion, with shipping, and set a reminder a week earlier.
Write a one-line card note that names why he chose it.
Log the gift in the person's note so he never repeats it, and add the order to the Returns Tracker.
pink.prompt: Gift-Finder, help me pick a gift for {person and relationship} for {occasion} on {date}. Budget: {amount}. What I know: {interests, recent mentions, what they own}. Rules: {kosher, allergies, no clutter, other}. Give me three options ranked, each tied to something specific I told you, with where to buy it, the latest order date for on-time delivery, and a one-line card note in my voice.
checklist: Order-by date set with a buffer
pink.example: For: the Chabad rabbi who studies with him, for Hanukkah, which begins the evening of Dec 4. Budget: $40. Known: he mentioned enjoying Rabbi Jonathan Sacks' essays, and the family hosts many guests. Options: 1) a hardcover volume of Sacks' Covenant and Conversation on the weekly portion, $32; 2) a box of chocolates with a reliable kosher certification, $25, for the household; 3) a donation in his name to the Chabad house's holiday fund. Chose the book plus a small certified box for the children, $38. Order-by Nov 26 with a buffer. Card: 'For the conversations, with thanks for every one of them.'

pink.title: Hard Conversation Prep
pink.use: Prepare a hard conversation: what he wants, how to open, what to listen for, and how to close.
pink.tools: Google Docs or iPhone Notes, a quiet five minutes beforehand
pink.inputs: Who it is with, what happened, what he wants to come out of it, and what he fears they will say.
pink.output: A one-page prep: his goal, their likely view, an opening line, the one ask, listening cues and a closing line.
method: Write his goal in one sentence: what should be different after the talk? Not 'win', a concrete change.
Write their side as fairly as he can: what they want, what pressure they are under.
Draft a soft opening: start with the shared interest, then the issue in one sentence, using 'I' and specifics, not 'you always'.
Make one clear ask and one fallback he could accept.
List what to listen for: their actual constraint, any offer hidden in a complaint. Plan to repeat back what he heard before answering.
Pick time and place: private, not rushed, not at the end of a draining shift.
Write a closing line that names the agreement and the next step. Afterward, note what was decided in the Decision Log.
pink.prompt: Shadow Dancer, help me prepare a conversation with {person, role} about {issue}. Background: {what happened}. What I want to change: {goal}. What I fear they will say: {fears}. What I know about their position: {constraints}. Give me a fair summary of their side, a soft opening of two sentences, my one ask and an acceptable fallback, three things to listen for, two likely pushbacks with calm replies, and a closing line that confirms the agreement.
pink.example: With: the Walgreens store manager, about his availability. Background: he asked for Wednesday nights off from Nov 1 for class and CVAC, but a Wednesday shift still appeared on the schedule. Goal: Wednesday nights off on the system, from the next schedule on. Their side: the store is short-staffed for the holiday season. Opening: 'I want to keep being reliable through the holidays. To do that I need my Wednesday nights fixed as unavailable.' Ask: update it in the system today. Fallback: one Wednesday a month through December, then fully off. Listen for: whether the problem is the system or staffing. Close: 'So Wednesdays come off starting with the schedule posted next week. Thank you.'

pink.title: Keepsake Journal
pink.use: Moments worth keeping, dated, in two minutes a night, so the good days are not lost in the busy ones.
pink.tools: Apple Journal (free on iPhone), Day One (free tier), iPhone Photos
pink.inputs: Two minutes before bed and, when there is one, a photo from the day.
pink.output: A dated entry with the moment, who was there, one detail and an optional photo; a monthly look-back.
method: Set a bedtime reminder. Two minutes, not a diary; one moment is enough.
Write the date, the moment in one or two sentences, who was there, and one sensory detail (what was said, the light, the weather).
Attach a photo if there is one. Apple Journal suggests moments from the day's photos and places.
Tag entries by person (Andy, family, friends, CVAC, parish visits) so he can find them later.
Keep private things private: the journal is not for posting and never feeds a brand account.
On the first Sunday of each month, read the last month's entries and star the best three.
Use the stars for anniversaries, letters and gifts: the Gift Finder and Letters and Thanks kits read from here.
pink.prompt: Keeper of Keepsakes, help me write tonight's entry. What happened today that I want to keep: {moment}. Who was there: {people}. Any detail I remember: {words said, place, weather}. Turn it into a short dated entry of three or four sentences in my plain voice, suggest two tags, and ask me one question that might bring back a detail I forgot.
checklist: Photo attached if there is one
pink.example: Entry, Saturday Nov 21: 'Andy and I took the 1:05 into Grand Central. In the library's reading room he whispered that the ceiling looked like a painted sky over a train station, which is exactly backward and exactly right. It was cold enough to see our breath on the walk back to the train.' Tags: Andy, city. Photo: the reading room lamps. Question back: 'What did you eat after?' He added: 'Dumplings, standing up, near the 42nd Street entrance.' On Dec 6, the monthly look-back starred this entry, his first overnight at CVAC, and his sister's call from campus.

pink.title: Follow-up Tracker
pink.use: Who he owes a reply to and since when, cleared in fifteen minutes before it becomes awkward.
pink.tools: Gmail (stars and snooze), iPhone Messages (pin and mark unread), Google Sheets, iPhone Reminders
pink.inputs: His inbox, texts and DMs, and fifteen minutes twice a week.
pink.output: A short owed-replies list sorted by age, with a drafted reply or holding line for each.
method: Twice a week, scan Gmail, Messages, Instagram and X DMs, LinkedIn and Substack replies for anything waiting on him.
Log each in the sheet: person, channel, what they asked, date received, days waiting.
Rule of 48 hours: anything older gets at least a holding line ('Got this, I will answer properly by Friday').
Sort by days waiting and by stakes: professors, CVAC, work and mentors first, friends close behind.
Draft replies in a batch, send, and mark them done with the date.
For anything he is waiting on from others, log it too with a nudge date seven days out.
Never let a message from a mentor or a new contact pass a week without a reply.
pink.prompt: Remembrancer, here are the messages I owe replies to: {person, channel, what they asked, date received}. Today is {date}. Sort them by how long they have waited and how much is at stake, then draft a reply for each in my voice: short, warm, specific. Where I cannot answer fully yet, write a holding line with a date I will commit to. Also list anything I am waiting on from others and the date to nudge.
checklist: Each owed reply logged with its date
pink.example: Monday Nov 9 scan. Owed: his advisor's email about spring sections, 6 days; the CVAC scheduler's text about a Saturday overnight, 2 days; a Substack reader asking for a source on the Jebel Amer short, 4 days; a Chabad friend's text inviting him to a class, 1 day. Order: advisor (holding line: 'I will send my section choices by Thursday'), scheduler (yes to the overnight), the reader (link to the Global Witness report), the friend. Waiting on: Walgreens to confirm Wednesday availability, nudge Nov 16. All four sent in 14 minutes.

pink.title: Warm Introductions
pink.use: Make or request an introduction both sides welcome, using double opt-in and a forwardable note.
pink.inputs: Who wants to meet whom, why it helps both, and his relationship with each side.
pink.output: A double opt-in ask, a short forwardable blurb, and the intro email once both say yes.
method: Write why the meeting helps both sides, one line each. If it only helps one, it is a favor, not an introduction; ask accordingly.
When asking someone to introduce him, write the forwardable blurb for them: who he is, what he has done, what he asks, in under 100 words.
Double opt-in: ask each side privately first, and give them an easy way to say no.
When both agree, send one short email to both: why each should know the other, then step back.
The person introduced replies within a day and moves the introducer to bcc.
Thank the introducer after the meeting happens, with one line about how it went.
Log every introduction (who, when, outcome) in the contacts sheet.
pink.prompt: Matchmaker of Houses, help me with an introduction. I want to {make or request} an introduction between {person A, who they are} and {person B, who they are}. My relationship with each: {details}. Why it helps each side: {reasons}. Write the private opt-in message to each side, a forwardable blurb under 100 words, and the final introduction email to send once both agree. Keep each one short enough to read on a phone.
pink.example: Request: he wants to meet a researcher at a think tank who works on Sudan's war economy. His history professor knows her from a conference. Benefit to her: a student who has already mapped RSF gold routes from public sources and can share the dataset. Blurb for the professor to forward: 'Elijah is a History junior at SUNY Purchase who writes on Sudan and online influence operations. He has built a public-source map of gold trade routes out of Darfur and would value 20 minutes of your view on its gaps. Happy to share the data either way.' She said yes in two days. He replied within the hour, moved the professor to bcc, and booked a call.

pink.title: Letters and Thanks
pink.use: Thank-you notes and short letters in his own voice, written and sent within 48 hours.
pink.tools: Google Docs, iPhone Notes, plain cards and USPS stamps
pink.inputs: Who it is for, what they did, one specific detail, and whether it is handwritten, email or text.
pink.output: A note of four to six sentences in his voice, ready to copy by hand or send.
method: Write within 48 hours. A late note is still better than none, but specific memories fade.
Open with the person and the thing, not 'I just wanted to say'.
Name one specific detail: what they said, did or taught, and what it changed for him.
Say what he will do with it, if anything (use the advice, come back next week).
Close warmly and simply. No apologies for writing, no flourish he would not say aloud.
Handwrite for elders, clergy, mentors and hosts; email or text for peers and quick favors.
Log the note in the person's contact entry with the date.
pink.prompt: Letter-Writer, draft a thank-you note to {person, relationship} for {what they did}. The specific detail I remember: {detail}. What it changed or what I will do with it: {effect}. Format: {handwritten card, email, text}. My voice is plain, warm and a little dry, no gushing. Four to six sentences. Give me one version and one shorter version for a small card.
checklist: Opens with the person and the thing
pink.example: For: the CVAC crew chief on his first overnight, who walked him through restocking the rig at 3 am and talked him through his first call. Detail: she said 'slow is smooth, and smooth is fast' when he fumbled the stretcher straps. Draft: 'Thank you for Saturday night. You turned a 3 am restock into a lesson, and on the call your "slow is smooth" stayed in my head the whole time. I strapped the next patient in without a fumble. I am glad to be on your crew, and I will be back next Saturday. Elijah.' Handwritten on a plain card, left in her cubby on Sunday, logged.

pink.title: Event Finder
pink.use: Talks, salons and public events in Westchester and New York City that fit his interests and his train times.
pink.tools: Eventbrite, Meetup, Luma, NYPL events calendar, Columbia Harriman Institute events, Chappaqua Library events, MTA TrainTime
pink.inputs: His free evenings for the next two weeks, topics he wants, and a budget.
pink.output: Up to five events with date, cost, registration link, travel plan and why each is worth it.
method: List his free slots for the next two weeks around shifts, class and CVAC.
Search by topic, not by venue: Sudan and the Horn, Israel, Russia and Orthodoxy, AI and security, history, writing and media.

Check the regular free sources: NYPL events, Columbia's Harriman Institute (Russia and Eurasia), the Center for Jewish History, the Chappaqua Library, SUNY Purchase's own calendar, Luma for tech meetups.
Keep events where he can learn and meet one or two people. Skip ones that are just a crowd watching a panel he could stream.
Check the last train home in TrainTime before registering.
Register, put it on the calendar with travel time, and write one question to ask.
Afterward, log anyone he met in the contacts sheet and send a follow-up within two days.
pink.prompt: Salon-Finder, find events for me in Westchester and Manhattan between {dates}. Free evenings: {slots}. Topics: {list}. Budget: {amount}. I travel by Metro-North Harlem Line from Chappaqua, so events must end in time for a train home. Give me up to five, each with date, time, venue, cost, how to register, why it is worth it for my work, and one question I could ask. Mark which ones are good for meeting people versus only listening.
pink.example: Search for Nov 16 to 29, free nights Wednesday and one weekend afternoon, budget $20. Kept: a Harriman Institute evening panel on Russia's influence operations in Africa (free with registration, ends 8 pm, the 9:12 train home), a Luma-listed AI security meetup in Midtown (free, good for meeting people), and a Chappaqua Library author talk on Cold War history (walkable). Skipped: a $60 gala. Question for the panel: 'Which Russian networks in Sudan have outlasted Wagner's rebranding?' He met a graduate student there and followed up the next morning with his Jebel Amer short.

pink.title: Mentor Outreach
pink.use: Find a fitting mentor and write a first message short and specific enough to get a yes.
pink.tools: LinkedIn (free), Google Scholar, Substack and X search, Gmail
pink.inputs: What he wants to learn, the work he can show, and two or three possible mentors.
pink.output: A ranked shortlist with reasons, and a first message of under 120 words for the top pick.
method: Define the gap in one line: what he wants to be able to do in a year that he cannot now.
Find people one or two steps ahead, not the most famous name: authors of recent work on the exact topic, practitioners who post about method.
Read two recent pieces by each. The message must show he did.
Pick one piece of his own work to show: a brief, a dataset, a Marginalia essay.
Write under 120 words: who he is in one line, the specific piece of theirs that helped, his work in one line with a link, one small ask (a 15-minute call or one question by email).
Send on a weekday morning. One polite follow-up after ten days, then let it go.
If they say yes, arrive with three questions and send a thank-you the same day.
pink.prompt: Seeker of Mentors, help me approach a mentor. What I want to learn: {gap}. Candidates: {names, roles, links to their recent work}. My work to show: {link and one-line description}. Rank the candidates by fit and reachability, then write a first message to the top pick under 120 words: one line about me, the specific piece of theirs that helped and why, my work with a link, and one small ask. No flattery, no long life story.
checklist: Candidates one or two steps ahead
Two recent pieces read per candidate
One piece of his work chosen
pink.example: Gap: produce a paid brief on online influence operations to a professional standard. Candidates: an analyst at the Atlantic Council's DFRLab who writes on African information operations, a Clemson Media Forensics Hub researcher, and a Substack writer who left a trust and safety team. Ranked: the DFRLab analyst first (closest topic, active on LinkedIn). Message: 'I am a History student at SUNY Purchase writing on influence operations in Sudan. Your piece on coordinated Telegram networks changed how I collect data: I now log channel creation dates first. Here is a public-source draft brief on RSF messaging: {link}. Could I ask you one question about attribution standards by email?' 83 words. She replied in four days.

pink.title: The Horn Contacts
pink.use: Map his Israel-Africa contacts by sector with warmth and one next step each, reviewed monthly.
pink.tools: Google Sheets or HubSpot (free CRM), LinkedIn (free), Gmail
pink.inputs: Everyone he knows or has met in the Israel-Africa and Horn space, and the people he wants to reach.
pink.output: A contact map by sector with warmth scores, one dated next step per person, and a monthly short list.
method: List every contact with: name, role, organization, sector (government and development agencies such as MASHAV, NGOs such as IsraAID, academia, journalism, diaspora community, business), how he knows them.
Score warmth from 0 to 3: 0 never met, 1 one exchange, 2 real conversation, 3 would take his call.
Write one next step per person with a date: share a piece, ask one question, congratulate, introduce.
Mark the gaps: sectors with no warm contacts. Those set next month's outreach.
Use the Warm Introductions kit to reach the cold names through the warm ones.
Give before asking: send useful reporting, datasets or translations before any request.
Review on the first Sunday of each month: update warmth, finish or redate next steps, pick five to contact.
pink.prompt: Envoy to the Horn, here are my contacts in the Israel-Africa and Horn space: {name, role, organization, how I know them, last contact}. People I want to reach: {list}. Build a map: sector, warmth score 0 to 3, one next step with a date for each, and a gap list of sectors where I have no warm contacts. Then pick the five I should contact this month and draft a first line for each that gives something before asking.
checklist: Cold names routed through warm ones
pink.example: Map, Nov 2026: 14 contacts. Academia 5 (his professor at 3, two researchers at 1), NGOs 3 (an IsraAID program officer met at a webinar, warmth 1), journalism 2, diaspora 2 (a Sudanese community organizer in Tel Aviv reached through family, warmth 2), government 1 (a former MASHAV staffer, 1), business 1. Gaps: no warm government or business contacts. This month's five: send the IsraAID officer his translated summary of Arabic-language reporting on aid access in Darfur; ask the community organizer one question about returnees; congratulate a researcher on a new paper; and two Warm Introductions requests through his professor. Review set for Dec 6.

red.title: The Labors Card
red.use: Today's three Labors on one card: one Duty, one Build, one Keep, each with a clear 'done when'.
red.tools: iPhone Notes (pinned note or widget), an index card, iPhone Calendar
red.inputs: Today's schedule (shift, class, CVAC), the open orders, and five minutes in the morning.
red.output: One card with three Labors, a time for each, and a 'done when' line, ticked by night.
method: Read today's fixed blocks first: Walgreens shift, class, CVAC. The Labors fit around them.
Labor 1, Duty: one piece of the Duty triad (wood, CVAC, school). Example: 'Read chapter 9 and draft the response paper intro.'
Labor 2, Build: one piece of income work toward the first $100 (Genizah, Marginalia, a brief).
Labor 3, Keep: body, faith or home (the bench session, the evening rule of prayer, the room reset).
Write 'done when' for each: a visible finish line, not a duration. 'Draft sent to Andy', not 'work on script'.
Give each a time slot. On a full shift day, shrink the Labors; never add a fourth.
At night tick or move each one. A moved Labor goes on tomorrow's card first.
red.prompt: Foreman, build today's Labors card. Today: {date}. Fixed blocks: {shift, class, CVAC times}. Open orders and deadlines: {list}. Energy today: {1 to 5}. Give me exactly three Labors: one Duty (wood, CVAC or school), one Build (income work toward my first $100 online), one Keep (body, faith or home). For each: a one-line task, a 'done when' finish line, and a time slot that fits my blocks. If the day is too full, shrink the Labors rather than dropping one.
checklist: Each Labor has a time slot
red.example: Thursday, Nov 12. Blocks: Walgreens 1 to 9:30 pm. Card: Duty, 8:30 to 9:30 am, 'US foreign policy reading, chapter 9 done when the three-sentence summary is in the notes doc.' Build, 10 to 11:15 am, 'Genizah issue 1 draft done when the full draft is in Substack as a draft and the headline list is attached.' Keep, 11:30 am, 'Bench Volume day done when 5 sets of 5 at 130 are logged in Hevy.' Night: Duty and Keep ticked; Build reached the draft but not the headlines, so 'Headline Forge for issue 1' went first on Friday's card.

red.title: Focus Guard
red.use: One protected deep-work block a day: one task, phone gone, distractions blocked and caught on paper.
red.tools: iPhone Focus modes, Windows Focus sessions (Clock app), Cold Turkey Blocker (free version), LeechBlock NG (browser extension)
red.inputs: The task for the block, its finish line, and 60 to 90 minutes with no shift or class.
red.output: A guarded block, a distraction list, and a one-line log of what got finished.
method: Name one task and its output for the block, such as 'first draft of the methods section'. One task only.
Schedule it in his best hours (see the Energy Map) and put it on the calendar as busy.
Phone into a Focus mode that silences everything except his parents, Andy and CVAC, then put it in another room.
On the PC, start a Windows Focus session and block feeds with Cold Turkey or LeechBlock: X, Instagram, YouTube, news sites.
Keep paper beside the keyboard. Any urge or idea gets written down, not acted on.
Work until the timer ends. A stuck moment is a reason to write a rough version, not to check something.
Log one line: task, minutes, what got done, how many distractions were written down.
red.prompt: Canary, set up my focus block. Task: {task}. Output that counts as done: {output}. Time: {start and length}. My usual distractions: {apps, sites, habits}. People who must be able to reach me: {list}. Give me the exact iPhone Focus settings, which sites to block on the PC, a two-minute start ritual, what to do when I get stuck mid-block, and a one-line log template.
checklist: One task and its output named
Phone in Focus and out of the room
red.example: Sunday, Nov 15, 8 to 9:30 am. Task: Genizah issue 1, final edit. Output: the issue scheduled in Substack for Nov 18. Phone in a Focus mode called Forge that lets through only his parents, Andy and the CVAC scheduler, left in the kitchen. Cold Turkey blocked X, Instagram, YouTube and two news sites; a Windows Focus session ran for 90 minutes. Paper list by the end: 'check Calls market price', 'reply to the reader', 'is the Ollama version current'. Log: 'Issue 1 edited and scheduled, 90 minutes, 7 distractions written down, none followed.'

red.title: Time Audit
red.use: Where a week actually went, hour by hour, against where he meant it to go.
red.tools: Toggl Track (free tier), iPhone Screen Time, Google Sheets
red.inputs: One ordinary week of honest logging, and Screen Time numbers for the same week.
red.output: A 168-hour table by category, planned versus actual, and the two hours to reclaim next week.
method: Pick an ordinary week, not a holiday or finals week.

Log in Toggl Track as he goes, or fill a sheet with one row per hour each night. Categories: sleep, Walgreens and commute, class and study, CVAC, income work, training, faith, home and chores, Andy and people, phone and feeds, other.
Pull Screen Time for the week and set phone hours against the log; they usually hide inside other categories.
Total each category. The total must reach 168; any gap is 'unaccounted' and counts as a finding.
Put the plan beside it: the hours he meant to spend on income work, study and training.
Find the two biggest gaps between plan and actual, and their likely cause.
Choose two specific hours to move next week, such as 'Sunday 7 to 8 pm from feeds to income work'.
red.prompt: Tally Man, here is my week of {dates}: {hours by category}. Screen Time: {daily average and top apps}. My plan for the week was: {planned hours by category}. Build a 168-hour table of planned versus actual, flag unaccounted time, name the two biggest gaps and their likely causes, and pick two specific hours I should move next week with what they should become. Be blunt but fair.
red.example: Week of Nov 2 to 8. Sleep 48, Walgreens and commute 44, class and study 13, CVAC 12, income work 4 (planned 10), training 5, faith 3, home and chores 6, Andy and people 9, phone and feeds 19, other 3, unaccounted 2: 168. Screen Time showed 2.7 hours a day, mostly Instagram and X, spread across late nights after shifts. Gaps: income work 6 hours short; feeds took most of it, between 10 pm and midnight. Moves: Sunday and Wednesday 9 to 10 pm become Genizah work in a Focus block, with Instagram limited to 45 minutes a day in Screen Time.

red.title: Energy Map
red.use: Find his best hours from a week of ratings and match the hardest work to them.
red.tools: Google Sheets, iPhone Reminders (rating pings), iPhone Health (sleep)
red.inputs: Seven to ten days of quick energy ratings and his usual schedule.
red.output: An energy map by hour and day type, and a work-to-hours match for shift days and free days.
method: Set reminders every two hours while awake: rate focus energy 1 to 5 and note one word (what he was doing).
Log sleep from the Health app beside each day.
Separate day types: Walgreens shift days, class days, CVAC days, free days. Energy patterns differ by type.
Average the ratings by hour for each day type and color the sheet: 4 and 5 green, 3 yellow, 1 and 2 red.
Sort his work by difficulty: hard (writing, coding, studying new material), medium (editing, flashcards, outreach), light (email, chores, admin).
Put hard work in green hours, medium in yellow, light in red. Protect the best green block with the Focus Guard kit.
Re-run the map after any schedule change, such as new Walgreens hours or a new semester.
red.prompt: Lamp-Keeper, here are my energy ratings for {dates}: {time, rating 1 to 5, one word, day type}. Sleep each night: {hours}. Build my energy map by day type with average ratings by hour, then match my work to it: hard tasks {list}, medium {list}, light {list}. Tell me my single best block for deep work on shift days and on free days, and one change to sleep or routine that would likely raise my worst hours.
red.example: Nine days logged. Free days: green from 8 to 11:30 am (average 4.4), yellow after lunch, a second green patch from 8 to 9:30 pm. Shift days with a 1 pm start: green 8 to 11 am, then red after the shift, averaging 1.8 from 10 pm. Days after a CVAC overnight: red until early afternoon. Match: writing and coding go to 8 to 11 am on every non-CVAC day; flashcards and editing to yellow afternoons; email and chores after shifts. The 9 to 10 pm Genizah slot from the Time Audit moved to free days only. Change: lights out by 11:30 on nights before free days.

red.title: Restart Protocol
red.use: The morning after a missed day: one honest line, one small win, then today's plan, no catch-up spiral.
red.tools: iPhone Notes, the Labors Card kit, the Laurel log
red.inputs: What was missed, why (if he knows), and today's fixed blocks.
red.output: A logged miss, a two-minute starter done, today's three Labors re-picked, and anyone affected told.
method: Write one neutral line in the log: date, what was missed, likely cause (sleep, shift, mood, chaos). No essays, no verdicts.
Do a two-minute starter at once: make the bed, open the draft and write one sentence, or ten Anki cards.
Do not double up. Yesterday's work does not stack onto today; pick today's three Labors fresh with the Labors Card.
Move only the one missed item that has a real deadline; the rest wait for Sunday.
Tell anyone it affects (a teammate, Andy, CVAC, a professor) in one short message.
If the cause was sleep or a shift, fix that tonight, not tomorrow.
Three misses in a row trigger a Pivot Check instead of more willpower.
red.prompt: Second Wind, I missed {what} on {date}. Likely cause: {cause}. Today's fixed blocks: {blocks}. Real deadlines coming: {list}. Write my one-line log entry, pick a two-minute starter I can do right now, re-pick today's three Labors without stacking yesterday's onto them, tell me which single missed item to move and where, and draft any message I owe someone. Keep the tone level, not guilty.
red.example: Miss: Tuesday, Nov 10, all three Labors after a CVAC overnight and an afternoon shift. Log line: 'Nov 10: no Labors. Cause: four hours of sleep after the overnight.' Starter at 8:05 am Wednesday: opened the response paper and wrote its first sentence. Today's card: Duty, finish the paper intro (due Friday); Build, 45 minutes on the Genizah draft; Keep, mobility routine only, with the bench moved to Thursday. Moved: the paper intro, since it has a deadline. Message to Andy: 'Lost yesterday to the overnight, script notes by tonight.' Fix: no afternoon shifts after CVAC overnights, raised with Walgreens.

red.title: The Shift Pack
red.use: What to study and do on Walgreens breaks, packed so a 15-minute break produces something.
red.tools: AnkiWeb (in Safari), iPhone Voice Memos, iPhone Notes, printed readings
red.inputs: His break lengths for the shift, this week's study load, and what fits in a pocket.
red.output: A break plan for each break with a ready task, and a log of what the breaks produced.
method: Breaks only: no study on the clock, and follow the store's phone policy.
Load the pack the night before: today's Anki decks open, one printed reading folded in a pocket, one draft open in Notes.
15-minute break: 10 minutes of Anki (EMT or Slavonic), then 3 minutes of stretching or the posture drills.
Meal break: eat first, then 15 minutes of reading or a draft paragraph. Margin Notes ideas go into a voice memo.
Keep one reply from the Follow-up Tracker for the end of a break if there are two minutes left.
Rest counts. On a heavy shift, a break with no task is allowed and logged as rest.
At day's end, tick what the breaks produced and move ideas from voice memos into the right kit.
red.prompt: Shift Steward, plan my breaks for today's shift. Shift: {start to end}. Breaks: {lengths and rough times}. This week's study: {courses, EMT chapters, Slavonic}. Drafts in progress: {list}. Energy: {1 to 5}. Give me a task for each break that fits its length and can be started in ten seconds, what to load the night before, and a rest option if the shift is heavy.
red.example: Shift: Friday, 1 to 9:30 pm, a 15-minute break around 4 and a 30-minute meal at 6:30. Night before: EMT chapter 14 deck and the Slavonic deck open on AnkiWeb, a printed eight-page article on Sudan's 2019 revolution in his pocket. 4 pm: 32 EMT cards, then chin tucks and a doorway stretch. 6:30 pm: ate the batch-cook chili, read five pages, recorded a 40-second voice memo: 'Hook idea, the revolution that was organized on WhatsApp.' End of day: the memo went to the Hook Lab kit; 32 cards and five pages logged.

red.title: Laurel Entry
red.use: The week's Laurel entry, numbers first, drafted Saturday night and ready for the Sunday review.
red.tools: Google Sheets (the Laurel log), the Ledger, Hevy, the CVAC Hours and Woodyard Tally sheets
red.inputs: The week's numbers from each tracker, the Labors cards, and ten minutes.
red.output: One entry: the scoreboard, three wins, one miss and its cause, one lesson, next week's three priorities.
method: Pull the scoreboard: online income to date against the first $100, CVAC hours against 150, cords split, school (assignments done, grades back), Labors ticked out of 21, posts published.
Write three wins as facts with numbers, not feelings.
Write one miss and its cause in one line, without excuses.
Write one lesson that changes next week's plan.
Pick next week's three priorities, one from each part of the Duty triad or the Build if the triad is on track.
Check the entry against the trackers; every number must trace to a sheet.
Save it Saturday night so the Sunday review starts from it, not from memory.
red.prompt: Keeper of the Laurel, draft my Laurel entry for {week dates}. Numbers: online income to date {amount}, CVAC hours {total}, cords split {total}, school {assignments and grades}, Labors ticked {x of 21}, posts {count}. What happened: {notes}. Write the scoreboard as a short table, three wins with numbers, one miss with its cause, one lesson, and next week's three priorities. Keep it under 150 words and plain.
checklist: Every number traced to a sheet
red.example: Week of Nov 2 to 8. Scoreboard: online income $0 of $100; CVAC 104 of 150 hours; 2.25 cords split; school, two readings and one quiz done, quiz back at 9 of 10; Labors 15 of 21; posts, 4 Shorts, 9 X posts, 1 Substack. Wins: 18 CVAC hours booked through Nov 21; the Jebel Amer short hit 74 percent viewed; 0.75 cord split in one session. Miss: Wednesday's Genizah block, lost to scrolling after class. Lesson: the 10 pm to midnight window is where the week leaks (19 hours of feeds), so it gets a Focus block. Next week: Genizah issue 1 scheduled for Nov 18, the response paper submitted, one more CVAC shift booked.

red.title: Pivot Check
red.use: Decide whether a plan should continue, adjust, pivot or stop, from evidence and tripwires set in advance.
red.tools: Google Sheets, the Weekly Analytics Read and Laurel logs, the Kill or Keep kit (Silver) for products
red.inputs: The plan, the tripwire he set when he started (or one set now), and the last three to four weeks of numbers.
red.output: A verdict (persevere, adjust, pivot or stop) with the evidence, the cost of switching, and the next test.
method: State the plan and its goal in one line each, and the tripwire: the number that would mean change (set it now if it was never set).
Gather three to four weeks of numbers. One bad week is weather; a month is climate.
Separate signal from noise: is the trend clear, or within the normal swing?
Ask four questions: is the goal still right? Is the method working at all? What would a small change test? What does switching cost in hours already sunk and momentum lost?
Pick one: persevere (on track), adjust (same goal, change one variable), pivot (same goal, new method), stop (goal no longer worth it).
Set the next test with a date and a tripwire, so the next check is quick.
Record the verdict in the Decision Log. Products go through Kill or Keep instead.
red.prompt: Tunnel-Turner, run a pivot check. Plan: {plan}. Goal: {goal}. Tripwire I set: {number and date, or none}. Last four weeks of numbers: {data}. Hours spent so far: {hours}. Answer the four questions (goal still right, method working, small change to test, cost of switching), then give me one verdict: persevere, adjust, pivot or stop, with the evidence. Set the next test with a date and a tripwire.
checklist: Three to four weeks of numbers
red.example: Plan: post a daily X thread for Marginalia to drive Substack subscribers. Goal: 100 Substack subscribers by Dec 31. Tripwire set Oct 12: fewer than 20 clicks to Substack a week by mid-November. Numbers, four weeks: X clicks 11, 9, 16, 14 a week; Shorts drove 7, 12, 15, 18 Substack visits. Goal: still right. Method: X works weakly; Shorts are growing. Small change: three X threads a week, and the saved hours go to a fourth Short. Cost: low; nothing is deleted. Verdict: adjust. Next test, Dec 13: X clicks steady at three threads a week and Shorts above 25 visits.

red.title: Woodyard Tally
red.use: Count cords split against the Duty triad target by Dec 31, measured, not guessed.
red.tools: Tape measure, Google Sheets, iPhone Calendar, the Splitter Care kit
red.inputs: The stacks as they stand, a tape measure, and the remaining pile.
red.output: Cords split to date, cords remaining, the weekly pace, and splitting sessions placed on the calendar.
method: Measure each finished stack: length times height times depth in feet. A full cord is 128 cubic feet (4 by 4 by 8 feet stacked).
Record depth honestly: a single row of 16-inch pieces is 1.33 feet deep. A face cord (4 by 8 feet of 16-inch pieces) is about a third of a full cord.
Add the stacks for cords split so far.
Estimate the remaining unsplit pile the same way, or count rounds against what one cord of split wood took last time.
Pace: remaining cords divided by the weeks to Dec 31. Use his measured rate per session to set the number of sessions.
Book the sessions on free daylight afternoons. Never split alone in the dark or tired after a shift.
Update the tally after every session and copy it into the Laurel entry.
red.prompt: Helldiver, update my woodyard tally. Finished stacks: {length, height, depth in feet for each}. Remaining pile estimate: {dimensions or rounds}. Last session: {hours} for {cords}. Weeks to Dec 31: {number}. Free daylight afternoons: {days}. Compute cords split, cords remaining, pace per week, sessions needed at my rate, and propose dates. Flag if the target is not realistic and say what to change.
red.example: Nov 8. Stacks: 16 ft long, 4 ft high, 1.33 ft deep (85 cubic feet, 0.67 cord); 24 by 4 by 1.33 (128, 1.0 cord); 12 by 3.5 by 1.33 (56, 0.44 cord). Split to date: 2.1 cords, rounded to 2.25 after the half-row on the porch. Remaining: about 1.75 cords of rounds. Last session: 0.75 cord in 3.5 hours. At that rate, about three sessions; seven weeks left. Booked: Sundays Nov 15 and 22, 1 to 4:30 pm, and Saturday Dec 5. Buffer: one more Sunday in December if rain cancels one. Target realistic.

red.title: The Why Card
red.use: One private card of his own reasons, written once, read when it gets hard.
red.tools: iPhone Notes (pinned) or Lock Screen widget, an index card for the wallet
red.inputs: Twenty quiet minutes, his honest answers to five questions, and one line of scripture or text he trusts.
red.output: A five-line card in his own words, pinned on the phone and carried on paper, reviewed each season.
method: Answer five questions in a sentence each: Who am I becoming? What is the work for? Who is it for? What does quitting cost? What do I owe today?
Use his own words. No borrowed slogans; it must sound like him talking to himself.
Add one line of scripture or text he trusts, with its reference.
Cut it to fit one phone screen and one index card.
Pin it in Notes and put the card in his wallet. It stays private: not for posting, and story names stay out of anything published.
Read it when a Restart Protocol starts, on the worst shift of the week, and before a Pivot Check.
Rewrite it each season or after a big decision; date every version.
red.prompt: Eo's Song, help me write my Why Card. My answers, rough: who I am becoming {answer}; what the work is for {answer}; who it is for {answer}; what quitting would cost {answer}; what I owe today {answer}. The line I trust: {verse or text}. Tighten each answer to one sentence in my own voice, cut nothing true, add nothing I did not say, and make the whole card fit one phone screen.
checklist: Fits one screen and one card
red.example: Card, Nov 5, 2026: 'I am becoming a man who builds, with work that stands on its own, not a shift schedule. The work is for freedom from the register, and for a voice worth hearing on Israel, Africa and the truth about how influence is bought. It is for Andy, for my parents' faith in me, and for the neighbors in the back of the ambulance. Quitting costs the version of me who already did the hard part. Today I owe three Labors and one honest line in the log. Unless the Lord builds the house, they labor in vain who build it (Psalm 127:1).' Pinned in Notes; the paper copy is behind his CVAC ID.

silver.title: The Monthly Close
silver.use: Reconciles the month's accounts and categorizes every transaction into a one-page month.
silver.tools: Bank and card CSV exports, Google Sheets
silver.inputs: CSV exports for checking, savings and any card for the month; Walgreens pay stubs; online income payouts.
silver.output: One page: income by source, spending by category, savings moved, net for the month, three notes.
method: On the 1st, download last month's CSVs from each account.
Paste into one sheet with columns: date, description, amount, account, category.
Categorize with a fixed list: pay, online income, transit, food, phone and internet, subscriptions, school, gear, giving, savings, other.
Reconcile: each account's starting balance plus transactions must equal its ending balance; find any gap.
Check each Walgreens deposit against its pay stub hours.
Build the one-page summary with a pivot table and compare with last month.
Write three notes: one win, one leak, one change for next month.
silver.prompt: You are Quicksilver, Treasurer. Close the month of {month}. Here are my transactions: {paste CSV rows}. Starting and ending balances: {balances}. Categorize every row using: pay, online income, transit, food, phone and internet, subscriptions, school, gear, giving, savings, other. Show any row you could not categorize. Reconcile each account and report any gap to the cent. Then give a one-page summary: income by source, spending by category, net, savings rate, change versus {last month figures}, and three notes (a win, a leak, one change).
checklist: Each account reconciled to the cent
silver.example: October close, run Nov 1. Income: four Walgreens deposits totaling about $2,560 take-home; online income $0. Spending: food $212, transit $96 (Metro-North tickets and one Uber), subscriptions $58, gear $74 (gym gloves, a lift belt), phone $40, school $35 for a used book. Savings moved: $1,200. Reconciliation finds a $12.99 gap in checking: a charge listed as pending in the bank app on Oct 31 that posted Nov 1. Notes: win, savings rate 47 percent; leak, three separate coffee-and-snack runs on shift adding to $41; change, pack food on double shifts. The page goes in Finance/2026-10 as 2026-10_monthly-close.pdf.

silver.title: Subscription Purge
silver.use: Finds every recurring charge and ranks what to cut, keep or downgrade.
silver.tools: iPhone Settings (Apple ID, Subscriptions), bank app search, Google Sheets
silver.inputs: Three months of bank and card statements; the iPhone subscriptions list.
silver.output: A ranked list of recurring charges with monthly cost, last real use, and a cut, keep or downgrade verdict.
method: Open iPhone Settings, tap your name, then Subscriptions; list each active one.
Search three months of statements for repeating amounts and merchant names (Google, Spotify, OpenAI, Anthropic, Adobe, Amazon).
For each, note monthly cost (yearly divided by 12), renewal date and the last time it did real work.
Score value: does it earn money, save time, or serve the plan? 0 to 2 each.
Cut anything scoring 0 or 1 or unused for 30 days; look for a free tier before cutting a useful one.
Cancel at the source and screenshot the confirmation.
Put the next renewal date of every kept subscription on the calendar three days early.
silver.prompt: You are Cutter of Tributes, Subscription Hunter. Here are three months of my transactions: {paste}. Here is my iPhone subscriptions list: {paste}. Find every recurring charge, including yearly ones and free trials that converted. For each give: name, monthly cost, renewal date if known, and what it does for me. Ask me the last time I used any you cannot judge. Score each 0 to 2 on earning money, saving time, and serving my current plan. Rank them, give a cut, keep or downgrade verdict with any free alternative, and total the monthly savings.
checklist: Each scored and given a verdict
silver.example: Found nine recurring charges totaling $87 a month. Ranked: Claude Pro $20 (keep, runs GOLEM and study); iCloud+ 200 GB $2.99 (keep, phone backup); Spotify $11.99 (keep, used daily); ElevenLabs Starter $5 (downgrade to free tier until the Voice Loop is built); a second cloud storage plan $9.99 (cut, files moved to Google Drive's free 15 GB); a VPN trial that converted at $12.99 (cut, unused since August); a fitness app $14.99 (cut, workouts are logged in a sheet); a news site $4 (keep for Sudan coverage); a game pass $5 (cut until finals end). Savings: $48 a month, $576 a year, moved to the runway fund.

silver.title: Pricing Lab
silver.use: Sets anchors and tiers for a product, tested against real comparables before launch.
silver.tools: Google Sheets, Substack (pricing pages of comparable writers), Gumroad (free to list)
silver.inputs: The product, who buys it, what it costs him in hours, and five comparable offers.
silver.output: A price table with three tiers, the anchor, the reasoning, and a test plan.
method: Define the buyer and the job the product does for them.
Collect five to eight comparables: price, what is included, delivery time.
Price the hours: estimate hours per unit and set a floor that pays at least double his Walgreens rate.
Build three tiers (good, better, best); the top tier is the anchor that makes the middle look reasonable.
Write what each tier includes in one line; the difference between tiers must be obvious.
Test: show the table to three likely buyers or post it, and log responses for two weeks.
Adjust once, then hold the price for at least 30 days.
silver.prompt: You are Price-Setter, Pricing Analyst. Product: {product}. Buyer: {who and why they buy}. My hours per unit: {hours}. Comparables: {list with prices and what is included}. Set a floor price that pays at least {hourly target} per hour. Propose three tiers with names, prices and one-line inclusions, and name the anchor. Explain each price against the comparables. Flag if I am underpricing. Give a two-week test plan: who sees it, what I count as a yes, and when to adjust.
checklist: Price held 30 days after one adjustment
silver.example: Product: a short brief on one online influence operation. Hours per brief: 8. Floor at $36 per hour is $288, so a $50 brief only makes sense as a sample. Comparables: freelance OSINT reports on Upwork range widely, and newsletter analysts sell single reports from $25 to $150. Tiers: Snapshot, $49, a five-page brief on a named narrative from published sources; Standard, $149, full brief with network map and 90-day trajectory; Custom, $450, a brief on a topic the buyer names with a 30-minute call. Custom is the anchor. Test: the table goes to three possible buyers and in a Marginalia footnote for two weeks; one asks about Standard, nobody asks about Snapshot, so Snapshot becomes a free sample.

silver.title: Kill or Keep
silver.use: The 30-day test for any venture or channel: keep, fix or kill, decided by numbers set in advance.
silver.tools: Google Sheets, native analytics (Substack, YouTube Studio, X Analytics)
silver.inputs: The venture, the date it started, hours spent per week, and the numbers it has produced.
silver.output: A verdict (keep, fix or kill) with the numbers behind it and the next 30-day target or the shutdown steps.
method: On day 0, write the success line: one or two numbers that must be met by day 30.
Log weekly hours spent and the numbers each week.
On day 30, compare results with the line.
Keep if it met the line; fix if it hit at least half and one clear cause can be changed; kill if under half.
For fix: change one thing only and set a new 30-day line.
For kill: archive the work, note what was learned, and free the hours on the calendar.
Record the verdict in the Decision Log.
silver.prompt: You are Liquidator, Kill Judge. Venture: {name}. Started {date}. Success line set on day 0: {numbers}. Weekly hours: {hours}. Results by week: {numbers}. Apply the rule: keep if the line was met, fix if at least half was reached and one cause can be changed, kill if under half. Give the verdict, the arithmetic, and the cost in hours per result. If fix, name the single change and a new 30-day line. If kill, give the shutdown steps and where the freed hours should go. Do not let sunk effort change the verdict.
checklist: For fix: one change and a new line
For kill: work archived and hours freed
silver.example: Venture: Margin Notes shorts on YouTube. Started Oct 6. Day-0 line: 10 shorts posted and 2,000 total views by Nov 5. Hours: about 4 a week with Andy cutting. Result: 9 shorts, 1,140 views, best one 410 views on a Byzantine map piece. 57 percent of the line, so fix, not kill. One cause stands out: the first two seconds are a title card in every short. Single change: open on the map or object itself, no title card. New line by Dec 5: 8 shorts, 2,000 views. Cost so far: 16 hours for 1,140 views, about 71 views per hour. Logged in the Decision Log on Nov 5.

silver.title: Launch Checklist
silver.use: Everything due in the seven days before a launch, by day, with an owner for each item.
silver.inputs: Launch date, what is launching, who helps (Andy), and channels to announce on.
silver.output: A day-by-day list from launch minus seven to launch day, plus a day-after review.
method: Write launch date and the single goal (for example, 50 subscribers in the first week).
Day minus 7: product finished; first issue drafted.
Day minus 6 to 5: about page, welcome email, subscribe button, header image, custom URL checked.
Day minus 4: teaser posts drafted; list of 20 people to tell personally.
Day minus 3 to 2: test emails sent to yourself on phone and PC; links clicked; spelling pass.
Day minus 1: schedule the issue; queue posts; rest.
Launch day: send, post, message the 20 people, answer every reply. Day after: count and note.
silver.prompt: You are Herald of Markets, Launch Planner. I am launching {product} on {date}. Goal for week one: {goal}. Help: {who}. Channels: {list}. Build a day-by-day checklist from seven days out to launch day with an owner for each item. Include: product finished, landing or about page, welcome email, test sends on phone and PC, link checks, teaser posts, a list of people to tell personally, scheduling, and launch-day replies. Add a day-after review. Flag anything that must happen early because it depends on someone else.
checklist: About page and welcome email live
Test emails checked on phone and PC
silver.example: Genizah launches free on Wednesday Nov 18. Goal: 50 subscribers in week one. Nov 11: issue one drafted. Nov 12 to 13: about page in the daemon voice, welcome email, header made in Canva by Andy, URL checked. Nov 14 (Saturday, after the morning splitting session): three X teasers and a Substack Note drafted; list of 20 people. Nov 15 to 16: test sends; a broken footnote link and a missing image alt text fixed. Nov 17: issue scheduled for 8 am; teasers queued for 8:15, 12:30 and 7 pm. Nov 18: send, personal messages before his shift, replies on breaks. Nov 19: 31 subscribers, 58 percent open rate; second push planned for Nov 25.

silver.title: The Runway Model
silver.use: Models how many months until online income replaces Walgreens take-home, under three scenarios.
silver.inputs: Monthly Walgreens take-home, current online income by source, growth assumptions, and savings.
silver.output: A sheet with low, base and high scenarios, the crossover month for each, and the leading numbers to watch.
method: Set the target: average monthly Walgreens take-home from the last three stubs, plus a 10 percent buffer for self-employment tax.
List each online source: Substack paid, briefs, websites, sponsorships, with this month's income.
For each source set a monthly growth assumption in three scenarios (low, base, high).
Project 24 months with compounding: next month equals this month times (1 plus growth), plus new sources on their start month.
Find the crossover month: first month online income meets the target, held for three months.
Add savings as runway: months of expenses covered if he quit at crossover.
Update monthly with real numbers and note which assumption was most wrong.
silver.prompt: You are Reckoner of Runways, Financial Modeler. My Walgreens take-home is {monthly amount}. Target equals that plus 10 percent. Online sources and current monthly income: {list}. Savings: {amount}; monthly expenses: {amount}. Build a 24-month projection with low, base and high growth per source, and say what each growth rate assumes in plain words (for example, subscribers per month). Give the crossover month for each scenario, held three months. Name the two leading numbers I should watch monthly. Show formulas I can paste into Google Sheets.
checklist: Target set from three recent stubs plus 10 percent
Three growth scenarios defined in plain words
silver.example: Target: about $2,560 take-home plus 10 percent, so $2,816 a month. Today online income is $0, so the model starts sources on assumed dates. Base: briefs start in January at one $149 brief a month, adding one more every two months; Marginalia paid tier opens in March with 10 paying at $5, growing 15 percent a month; Genizah sponsorships start in month 10 at $100. Base crossover: about month 21 (summer 2028, just after graduation). Low never crosses within 24 months; high crosses at month 14. Leading numbers: briefs sold per month and paid subscriber count. Savings of $6,000 against $900 monthly expenses give about six months of runway. Formula sample: =B5*(1+$C$2)+IF(A6>=$D$2,$E$2,0).

silver.title: Grant Finder
silver.use: Finds grants, fellowships and scholarships that fit him, with deadlines and eligibility checked.
silver.tools: SUNY Purchase financial aid and scholarship pages, ProFellow (free database), Scholarships.com, Fastweb, Google Sheets
silver.inputs: His profile (year, major, interests, citizenship), what the money is for, and how many applications he can do.
silver.output: A ranked table of real opportunities with amount, deadline, eligibility match, effort, and a warning date.
method: Write a profile line: History BA junior, graduating May 2028, interests in Israel, Africa, Sudan, AI, Russian.
Search three places: the college's own scholarships and fellowships office, ProFellow, and large free databases.
Add field-specific programs: language study (Boren), Jewish thought and Israel studies programs, history society prizes.
For each, confirm eligibility on the program's own site, not a list site.
Record amount, deadline, requirements (essays, letters, transcript), and hours to apply.
Rank by fit times amount divided by effort; pick the top three.
Set a warning date three weeks before each deadline for letters of recommendation.
silver.prompt: You are Seeker of Patronage, Grants Scout. My profile: {year, major, graduation date, interests, citizenship, GPA if relevant}. I need funding for {purpose}. I can do {number} applications this semester. Suggest opportunities in these groups: my college's own awards, national fellowships for undergraduates in history or international affairs, language study funding, and Israel or Jewish studies programs open to non-Jewish students. For each give amount, typical deadline month, eligibility, and effort. Mark anything you are unsure still exists so I can verify it on the official site. Rank the top five.
checklist: At least one national database searched
Eligibility confirmed on each official site
Warning dates set three weeks early
silver.example: Need: funding for a summer 2027 language or research program. The scout returns eight leads; four survive the official-site check. Boren Scholarship: funds study of less commonly taught languages such as Arabic or Hebrew abroad, carries a federal service requirement, deadline typically late January; fit high, effort high. A Purchase College scholarship for continuing students listed on the financial aid site; fit medium, effort low. A summer program in Jewish thought and Western civilization that accepts non-Jewish undergraduates; fit high, effort medium. A history honor society paper prize; fit medium, effort low with an existing paper. Top three set with warning dates; recommendation requests to two professors go out by Dec 15.

silver.title: Sponsor Pitch
silver.use: A one-page pitch to a sponsor or brief buyer: who reads, what they get, the price, the ask.
silver.tools: Google Docs, Canva (free), Substack and X analytics
silver.inputs: The buyer, audience numbers, what is being offered, the price, and one sample of work.
silver.output: A one-page pitch as PDF plus a short cover email.
method: Research the buyer: what they sell or care about and why your audience matters to them.
Lead with the reader or the finding, not with yourself.
Show numbers honestly: subscribers, open rate, impressions; small numbers framed as niche and engaged.
Offer: what exactly they get (placement, brief, dates, deliverables).
Price with one anchor and one option, from the Pricing Lab.
One proof: a sample excerpt, a past result or a reader quote.
End with a single ask and a date; send with a five-line email.
silver.prompt: You are Promoter, Pitch Builder. Write a one-page pitch to {buyer} for {offer}. About them: {what they do, why my work fits}. My numbers: {subscribers, open rate, impressions, sample}. Price: {from Pricing Lab}. Use this order: one-line hook about their need, who my readers are, the offer and deliverables, price, one proof, one ask with a date. Keep the numbers honest and frame a small audience as specific. Then write a cover email under 100 words. Keep Marginalia faceless: no photo, no personal name unless I say so.
silver.example: Buyer: the research lead at a small nonprofit that tracks online antisemitism. Hook: 'Your team tracks what spreads; this brief maps who spreads it on Sudan-related hashtags where antisemitic narratives are now appearing.' Readers: early Marginalia list, 140 subscribers, 52 percent open rate, mostly analysts and students of the region. Offer: one Standard brief within 14 days, with network map, three case studies and a 90-day outlook. Price: $149, or $450 for a custom topic with a call. Proof: a two-paragraph excerpt from a sample brief. Ask: a 15-minute call the week of Dec 7. Cover email: four sentences, the PDF attached, signed Marginalia.

silver.title: Tax Season Pack
silver.use: Keeps side-income records, sets aside quarterly estimates, and builds the folder to hand a preparer.
silver.tools: Google Sheets, Google Drive, IRS.gov (Form 1040-ES, Schedule C, Schedule SE), IRS Free File, VITA locator
silver.inputs: Online income payouts, business expenses with receipts, W-2 from Walgreens, and any 1099 forms.
silver.output: A running income and expense sheet, a set-aside amount each quarter, and a year-end folder checklist.
method: Open a sheet: date, source, gross, fees, net, and an expense tab with date, item, amount, business purpose, receipt link.
Save every receipt as a PDF in Drive the same day (software, domain, research books).
Set aside 25 to 30 percent of each online payout in savings; self-employment tax alone is 15.3 percent on net earnings.
Self-employment tax applies once net side earnings reach $400 for the year.
Option that avoids quarterly forms: raise Walgreens W-4 withholding to cover the side tax.
If paying estimates, use 1040-ES; due dates are mid April, June, September and January.
In January, build the folder: W-2, 1099s, income sheet, expense sheet, receipts; take it to a preparer or a free VITA site.
silver.prompt: You are Tithe-Reckoner, Tax Clerk. This year my side income so far is {list of payouts with dates and fees}. Expenses: {list with purpose}. My Walgreens W-2 income is about {amount} with {withholding}. Estimate net self-employment earnings, the self-employment tax, and a rough federal and New York income tax on the side income. Tell me whether raising my W-4 withholding would cover it instead of quarterly payments, and by how much per paycheck. List every document a preparer will want. Say clearly where my facts are uncertain and what to confirm with a preparer.
checklist: Income sheet updated with every payout
Receipts saved as PDFs the same day
25 to 30 percent of each payout set aside
Quarterly due dates on the calendar if estimating
silver.example: By Dec 31, 2026 Elijah earns $250 online: two $100 briefs paid through Stripe and $50 from a website job, minus $9 in fees. Expenses: a $12 domain and $20 of research books, so net is $209. That is under the $400 self-employment tax line, so no SE tax this year, but the income still goes on his return (Schedule C). He sets aside $60 anyway. For 2027, with briefs expected monthly, the Reckoner suggests adding $25 per paycheck in extra W-4 withholding rather than quarterly payments, reviewed in June. Folder for January: W-2, any 1099-NEC or 1099-K, both sheets, receipts. The final call on what to file belongs to the preparer at the VITA site.

silver.title: The Walgreens Exit
silver.use: Sets the income threshold for leaving Walgreens, then runs notice and the last-day checklist.
silver.tools: Google Sheets, Google Calendar, Walgreens employee portal
silver.inputs: The Runway Model results, savings, health coverage status, and the planned exit month.
silver.output: A go or wait verdict against the threshold, a notice letter, and a last-week checklist.
method: Set the threshold: online income at or above Walgreens take-home for three straight months, plus six months of expenses saved.
Check health coverage: confirm he stays on a parent's plan (possible until 26 under the ACA) or line up another plan.
Check the date against the Duty triad and the school calendar; avoid leaving during finals.
If go: write a short notice letter, two weeks minimum, delivered to the store manager in person and by email.
Last week: confirm final paycheck date, unused PTO policy, any 401(k) balance and where it goes.
Last day: return badge, vest, keys; collect W-2 address confirmation; ask for a reference contact.
Move the freed 40 hours onto the calendar before the first free week starts.
silver.prompt: You are Exit Engineer, Walgreens Exit. My online income for the last three months: {amounts}. Walgreens take-home: {amount}. Savings: {amount}; monthly expenses: {amount}. Health coverage: {status}. Planned exit: {month}. Check the threshold (three months at or above take-home and six months of expenses saved) and give go or wait with the gap. If go, write a two-week notice letter that is warm and brief, and a last-week checklist covering final pay, PTO, 401(k), W-2 address, items to return, and a reference. If wait, tell me the earliest month the numbers could work.
checklist: Three months at or above take-home
Date clear of finals and Duty triad deadlines
Notice delivered in person and by email
Freed hours put on the calendar
silver.example: Run in a sample month, March 2028: online income for Dec, Jan and Feb was $2,300, $2,650 and $2,900 against a $2,700 take-home. Only one month clears the line, and savings cover four months, not six. Verdict: wait. Earliest go: June 2028, if April and May clear $2,700 and he saves $700 a month, which also puts the exit after May graduation. The Engineer drafts the notice anyway for the file: 'I am writing to give two weeks' notice; my last shift will be June 20. Thank you for the years on this team.' Checklist prepared: confirm final paycheck date, PTO policy, the 401(k) balance, and ask the store manager to serve as a reference.

violet.title: Hook Lab
violet.use: Ten first lines for any video, sorted by hook type, with the best two marked.
violet.tools: CapCut, YouTube Studio, TikTok Studio, Google Docs
violet.inputs: The topic or script, the platform, and the one fact that surprised him most in research.
violet.output: Ten opening lines in five hook types, the top two paired with a first image.
method: Write the video's core claim in one sentence. No sentence, no hooks yet.
Pull the most surprising fact, number or image from the research. Build hooks from that, not from the topic.
Draft two lines in each of five types: contradiction, number, stakes (who pays), cold open (a year and a place), open loop.
