Cut each line to 12 words or fewer. Read aloud and trim anything over two seconds.
Delete any line the video does not pay off; overpromising costs retention and trust.
Pair the top two with a first image (map, document, artifact).
Post one. At 48 hours, log 3-second retention in YouTube Studio or TikTok Studio against that hook type's tally.
violet.prompt: Overture Master, write ten opening lines for a {platform} short about {topic}. Core claim: {one-sentence claim}. Most surprising fact: {fact, with source}. Two lines in each of five types: contradiction, number, stakes, cold open (year and place), open loop. Rules: 12 words or fewer, speakable in two seconds, nothing the script cannot pay off, nothing that reveals who I am (faceless; Marginalia voice is dry, precise, a little wry). Then mark your top two, name the first image for each, and flag any line that overstates the evidence.
checklist: Core claim fits in one sentence
Surprising fact has a named source
Ten lines, two per hook type
Every line under two seconds aloud
No hook promises more than the script delivers
Top two paired with a first image
Retention logged at 48 hours by hook type
violet.example: Topic: how the RSF pays for its war. Core claim: Sudan's war runs on gold as much as on guns. Fact: the RSF took over Darfur's Jebel Amer gold mines in 2017 (Global Witness, 2019). Kept: 'Sudan's war has a payroll. It is paid in gold.' (contradiction), 'One mountain in Darfur bankrolled an army.' (number turned image), 'Darfur, 2017. A mountain changes hands.' (cold open). Cut: 'The secret history of Sudan's gold', since the script has no secret. Top pick: the payroll line over a slow push into a map of Jebel Amer. At 48 hours, 3-second retention was 71 percent against a 58 percent channel average, so contradiction gets a mark.

violet.title: Cut Sheet
violet.use: Turn a long take into a 30-second short, beat by beat, with timecodes and visuals.
violet.tools: DaVinci Resolve, CapCut, Whisper (local on the RTX 5070), Google Sheets, Wikimedia Commons
violet.inputs: The long recording, a transcript if one exists, and the one point the short must land.
violet.output: A six-beat cut sheet: source timecodes, words kept, visual and caption for each beat.
method: Transcribe with Whisper on the PC or CapCut auto captions; paste into a sheet with timecodes.
Highlight the one sentence that is the point. Everything else is a candidate for the cut.
Lay out six beats: hook (0-2 s), setup (2-7), evidence one (7-14), evidence two (14-21), turn (21-27), button (27-30).
Copy in and out timecodes for each beat. Trim breaths and openers like 'so' and 'basically'.
One visual per beat, held four seconds at most: map, document scan, public-domain photo (Wikimedia Commons, Library of Congress) or kinetic text.
Write captions of seven words or fewer per screen.
Edit at 1080x1920, watch once on mute, and fix anything that fails silent. Make the last line lead back into the first.
violet.prompt: Cutter, here is a transcript with timecodes: {paste transcript}. The short must land this point: {one sentence}. Build a 30-second cut sheet as a table: beat, target seconds, source in, source out, exact words kept, visual, caption (seven words max). Six beats: hook, setup, evidence one, evidence two, turn, button. Use only words in the transcript; if a beat needs a line I never said, mark it RECORD and write it. Suggest a public-domain visual per beat and where to find it. End with total runtime and whether the last line loops into the first.
checklist: Six beats with in and out times
Every visual his own or public domain
Last line loops into the first
violet.example: Long take: an 11-minute voice memo from a Walgreens break on the Berlin Conference. Point (4:12): 'Berlin set the rules for claiming Africa; it did not draw the map.' Sheet: hook 4:12 to 4:15 over an engraving of the conference from Commons; setup 0:40 to 0:45, 'Everyone learned about the room with the ruler'; evidence one 6:02 to 6:09 on 'effective occupation' over the General Act from Wikisource; evidence two 7:30 to 7:36, most borders came later in two-power treaties, over an 1890 Anglo-German map; turn 9:10 to 9:15; button marked RECORD: 'So who drew the lines? Mostly men who never met.' Runtime 29.6 seconds, and the button feeds back into 'the room with the ruler'.

violet.title: Thumbnail Test
violet.use: Three faceless thumbnail options for one video and a fair way to pick the winner.
violet.tools: Canva (free plan), Photopea, YouTube Studio Test and Compare (where available), Wikimedia Commons
violet.inputs: The video title, its one promise, and images he owns or has cleared.
violet.output: Three 1280x720 thumbnails that differ in kind, a shrink-test verdict, and a logged winner.
method: Write the promise in three words or fewer. Thumbnail text adds to the title, never repeats it.
Make three concepts that differ in kind: A, object or document close-up; B, map or diagram with one bold mark; C, two to four words over one textured image.
Faceless rules: no face, no identifiable hands, rings or reflections. Own photos or public domain only; check the Commons license line.
Build at 1280x720 in Canva or Photopea: one focal point, high contrast, text kept off the bottom right where the timestamp sits.
Shrink test: view each about 160 pixels wide on the iPhone. Not clear in one second, revise.
Pick fairly: use Test and Compare if YouTube Studio offers it. Otherwise swap after 48 hours and compare click-through from the same traffic source, never under 1,000 impressions.
Log the winner's kind; after ten videos the tally says what his audience clicks.
violet.prompt: Painter of Faces, design three thumbnail concepts for a video titled {title}. Promise: {promise}. Images I can use: {list, with sources}. Faceless brand (Marginalia: archival, ink, maps, muted color with one accent): no faces, hands or reflections. Give A (object or document close-up), B (map or diagram with one bold mark) and C (two to four words over one image). For each: layout, focal point, exact text, accent color, and how it adds to the title. Then say which you expect to fail a 160-pixel shrink test and the fix.
checklist: Promise in three words or fewer
Three concepts that differ in kind
All three pass the shrink test
violet.example: Video: 'Sudan Signed the Abraham Accords. Then What?' Promise: never ratified. A: a declaration page close-up with a red stamp drawn in Photopea. B: a map of Sudan, Khartoum circled, a thin arrow toward Jerusalem. C: 'SIGNED. NEVER RATIFIED.' in cream letters over a dim Commons photo of the Nile at Khartoum (CC BY-SA, credited in the description). Shrink test: B's arrow vanished at phone size, so it was thickened and the circle filled. Test and Compare ran nine days; C took the largest watch-time share. Logged: text-led, one win.

violet.title: Margin Notes Script
violet.use: Turn one Marginalia piece into a 45 to 60 second Margin Notes script with visuals and sources.
violet.tools: Google Docs, Hemingway Editor (web), ElevenLabs (free tier) or his own voice, CapCut
violet.inputs: The finished Marginalia piece and the single idea in it that stands without the rest.
violet.output: A timed script of 120 to 150 words, a visual per line, and a source card for the end screen.
method: Pick one idea, not a summary. Test: could a stranger repeat it in one breath?
Open like a note in a margin: a quoted line, date or document the script then annotates.
Body in four moves: context, complication, the Marginalia take, a closing line pointing to the full piece.
Hold to 120 to 150 words. Run it through Hemingway Editor and break any very hard sentence.
Mark a visual and its source against every line.
Time it aloud or with an ElevenLabs draft read; trim until under 60 seconds.
Add a source card, run lines about living named people through Libel Check, then hand off to Cut Sheet and Captions and Tags.
violet.prompt: Marginator, here is a Marginalia piece: {paste text or link}. Write a {45 or 60}-second Margin Notes script on this one idea: {idea}. Open on a quoted line, date or document, as if writing in the margin. Then context, complication, the Marginalia take, and a closing line pointing to the full piece. 120 to 150 words, short sentences, dry and exact, no biography of me, nothing the piece does not support. Format as a table: spoken line, visual (with a public-domain source). End with a source card listing every source used.
checklist: Opens on a quote, date or document
Visual and source for every line
Source card and Libel Check done
violet.example: Source: a Marginalia essay on Sudan and the Abraham Accords. Idea: the deal was signed but could never be ratified. Opens on '6 January 2021, Khartoum' over the declaration page: 'Sudan signs on to the Abraham Accords. The ink was real. The ratification never came.' Context: ratification needed a transitional legislature that was never formed. Complication: the October 2021 coup, then war in April 2023. Take: 'Normalization with a state that cannot vote on it is a promise held in escrow.' Close: 'The full note is on Marginalia.' 138 words, 54 seconds aloud. Source card: the declaration text and Reuters reporting from January and October 2021.

violet.title: The Calls Register
violet.use: Log every public Call with odds and a resolution date, then grade it with a Brier score.
violet.tools: Google Sheets, Metaculus, Manifold, Polymarket and Kalshi (prices read only), iPhone Reminders
violet.inputs: The Call in plain words, his probability, the resolution date and the source that settles it.
violet.output: A register row, a due-date reminder, a running Brier score and a quarterly calibration note.
method: Rewrite the Call until a stranger could settle it: who, what, by when, which source decides.
Set a probability from 1 to 99 percent with two lines: the main reason, and what would change his mind.
Record any matching price on Metaculus, Manifold, Polymarket or Kalshi that day, for comparison only.
Add the row: number, date made, Call, probability, market price, resolution date, source, published link.
Set the reminder. Never edit a published Call; a changed view is a new Call with a new number.
When due, score Brier: (probability minus outcome) squared, outcome 1 or 0. Lower is better; a flat 50 percent scores 0.25.
Quarterly, check each probability band (do 70 percent Calls hit about 70 percent?) and publish the scorecard, misses included.
violet.prompt: Keeper of the Calls, help me log a new Call. Rough claim: {claim}. Probability: {percent}. Rewrite it so it is unambiguous: subject, event, deadline ({date}) and the single source that resolves it, and point out any word that could be argued either way. Give the register row (number {next number}, date made {today}, Call text, probability, resolution date, resolving source). Tell me what to search on Metaculus, Manifold, Polymarket or Kalshi for a comparable price. Finish with the one-line reason and the one thing that would change my mind, in Marginalia's voice.
checklist: Comparable price recorded if one exists
violet.example: Draft: 'Sudan's war won't end soon.' Rewritten as Call 7: 'Sudan's army and the RSF sign a nationwide ceasefire agreement by June 30, 2027, as reported by Reuters or AP.' Probability 15 percent. Reason: neither side has run short of outside backers. Mind-changer: the mediators announcing a signing date. A close Manifold market sat at 19 percent, recorded beside it. Reminder set for July 1, 2027. No ceasefire scores (0.15 minus 0) squared, 0.0225; a ceasefire scores (0.15 minus 1) squared, 0.7225. The gap is the cost of confidence when it misses.

violet.title: Headline Forge
violet.use: Twelve headlines for any piece, scored against plain rules, cut to the best three.
violet.tools: Substack (post editor, title test where offered), Google Trends, Google Docs
violet.inputs: The draft or its summary, the outlet (Marginalia, Genizah, X, YouTube) and the intended reader.
violet.output: Twelve scored headlines in four families, the best three, and a subtitle for the winner.
method: Write the piece's finding in one plain sentence. Headlines compress the finding, not the topic.
Draft three in each family: plain statement, specific number, question the piece answers, contrast (X, not Y).
Score each 0 to 2 on specific, honest, short (under 70 characters) and voice (Marginalia or daemon, not a content mill).
Drop anything scoring 0 on honest, whatever else it scores.
Check the key phrase in Google Trends and use searchers' words for YouTube titles.
Keep three; write a subtitle for the winner that adds one fact the headline left out.
Run Substack's title test on the top two if offered; otherwise log the open rate at 72 hours against the last three issues.
violet.prompt: Title-Smith, write twelve headlines for this {Marginalia or Genizah} piece. Finding: {finding}. Reader: {who it is for}. Three each in four families: plain statement, specific number, question the piece answers, contrast (X, not Y). Score each 0 to 2 on specific, honest, short (under 70 characters) and voice ({voice notes}) in a table, and remove anything scoring 0 on honest. Give me the best three with a line on why, and a subtitle for the winner that adds one fact the headline leaves out.
violet.example: Piece: a Genizah issue in the daemon voice on running open models at home. Finding: a gaming PC with an RTX 5070 runs a capable 8-billion-parameter model locally and free with Ollama. Drafts include 'Your Gaming PC Is Already an AI Lab' (statement, 7 of 8), 'One GPU, Zero Subscriptions: Local AI in 20 Minutes' (number, 7), 'Do You Need the Cloud for AI?' (question, 5) and 'Run AI at Home, Not on Someone Else's Server' (contrast, 6). 'The AI Secret Big Tech Hides' scored 0 on honest and was cut. Winner's subtitle: 'What an RTX 5070 can and cannot run, tested on a Windows desktop.'

violet.title: Captions and Tags
violet.use: Subtitles, captions and hashtags written per platform for one finished video.
violet.tools: CapCut auto captions, Whisper (local), YouTube Studio, TikTok Studio, Meta Business Suite
violet.inputs: The final video or its transcript, the target platforms, and one search phrase it should be found by.
violet.output: A corrected subtitle file, a caption per platform and a short hashtag set for each.
method: Generate subtitles with CapCut or Whisper, then check every line against the audio. Fix names and dates by hand; auto captions mangle 'Darfur' and Slavonic words.
Upload the .srt in YouTube Studio as well as burning captions in, so subtitles are searchable.
YouTube Shorts: title under 60 characters with the search phrase first, two-line description with one source, up to three hashtags.
TikTok: caption opens with the search phrase in plain words (TikTok search reads captions), then three to five hashtags.
Instagram Reels: a first line that works before the 'more' cut, a source line, three to five hashtags. X: one sentence, one hashtag at most.
Keep a tag bank of tags that brought views. Never use an unrelated trending tag.
violet.prompt: Surtitler, here is the transcript of a finished {length}-second video: {transcript}. It goes to {platforms}. Search phrase: {phrase}. First list every proper noun, date and number so I can check them against the audio. Then write: a YouTube Shorts title under 60 characters, a two-line description and up to three hashtags; a TikTok caption that opens with the search phrase plus three to five hashtags; a Reels caption whose first line works before the 'more' cut plus three to five hashtags; and one sentence for X. Faceless brand: nothing personal, no emoji.
checklist: Every subtitle line checked against audio
Hashtag counts within each platform's set
violet.example: Video: a 30-second Margin Notes on the Berlin Conference. Whisper wrote '1844' for 1884 and 'effective a cupation'; both fixed. YouTube title: 'The Berlin Conference Did Not Draw Africa's Map', description citing the 1885 General Act, tags #history #africa #berlinconference. TikTok: 'Berlin Conference myth: the rules, not the map. Most borders came later, in two-power treaties.' with #history #africanhistory #colonialism #maps. Reels first line: 'Nobody drew Africa's borders in one room.' X: 'Berlin set the rules for claiming Africa. The lines came later.' A week on, the tag bank shows #africanhistory carried most TikTok search views.

violet.title: Weekly Analytics Read
violet.use: One Sunday sheet from the platforms' own dashboards: what moved, why, and one decision.
violet.tools: YouTube Studio, TikTok Studio, Instagram professional dashboard, Substack dashboard, X post analytics, Google Sheets
violet.inputs: Fifteen minutes and access to each native dashboard for the last seven days.
violet.output: One page: six numbers per platform, best and worst post with reasons, one change for next week.
method: Open every dashboard on the same Monday-to-Sunday window. Native numbers only.
Record six per platform: posts, views or impressions, average percent viewed (open rate for Substack), followers gained, shares plus saves, clicks to Substack.
Pick best and worst by percent viewed, not raw views. Views measure the algorithm; retention measures the work.
Write one line on why for each (hook, topic, length, time, thumbnail). Label guesses as guesses.
Compare with last week. Under 20 percent change on fewer than 1,000 views is noise.
Make one decision only and put it at the top of next week's sheet, with the number that would prove it.
Copy the online-income line from the Ledger beside it.
violet.prompt: Reader of the Crowd, here are my numbers for {week dates}: {six numbers per platform}. Best post by percent viewed: {post and stats}. Worst: {post and stats}. Last week's decision: {decision}, result: {result}. Build my one-page read: a table of the six numbers per platform with change from last week, noise marked (under 20 percent change on fewer than 1,000 views), a likely reason for the best and worst post, and exactly one decision for next week with the number that would show it worked.
checklist: Best and worst by percent viewed
One decision with a target number
Income line copied from the Ledger
violet.example: Week of Nov 2 to 8. YouTube Shorts: 4 posts, 3,900 views, 62 percent viewed, 11 subscribers. TikTok: 4 posts, 2,100 views, 48 percent. Substack: 1 post, 41 percent open rate on 64 subscribers, 3 new. X: 9 posts, 6,800 impressions, 14 link clicks. Best: the Jebel Amer gold short at 74 percent (contradiction hook, map visual). Worst: a 58-second Fashoda piece at 31 percent (cold open took four seconds). TikTok's drop from 2,600 views is noise. Decision: no short over 40 seconds; success is TikTok above 60 percent viewed. Ledger: $0 of the first $100.

violet.title: The eli Grid
violet.use: Plan the faceless eli Instagram grid three posts ahead so every new row looks deliberate.
violet.tools: Instagram (drafts, grid preview), Canva (free plan), Meta Business Suite (free scheduling), iPhone Photos
violet.inputs: The last nine posts, a folder of candidate photos, and what is coming in the next two weeks.
violet.output: The next row of three: image, crop, caption, alt text and scheduled time for each.
method: Screenshot the grid and name its pattern: palette, subject rhythm (object, place, text card), light.
Choose the next three to alternate subject types inside one palette. Newest sits on the left.
Faceless rules: no face, reflections, house numbers, plates, school ID or Walgreens badge. Share from iPhone Photos with Location turned off under Options.
Crop for the 4:5 feed and check the 3:4 grid thumbnail still shows the subject.
Captions: one line of observation, one of context or quote, nothing personal. Add alt text.
Mock the row in Canva beside the last six posts and adjust.
Schedule in Meta Business Suite, and plan the following row before the last one goes live.
violet.prompt: Mask of eli, plan the next row of three for my faceless Instagram grid. Last nine posts, left to right by row: {descriptions}. Candidates: {list}. Coming up: {events or themes}. Keep the palette {palette} and alternate subject types. For each post: image, crop note for 4:5 and 3:4, a two-line caption with no personal or location details, alt text, and a day and time. Flag any candidate that could identify me or where I live, and say what gives it away.
violet.example: Last row: an icon corner in candlelight, a Metro-North window at dusk, a Church Slavonic text card. Plan: split oak rounds in frost (object, warm brown against a cool row); a close crop of a 1913 Nile map from the Library of Congress with one pencil line (place); a text card, 'Every empire keeps its receipts.' Flagged: the woodpile shot showed a neighbor's mailbox number, so it was recropped. Captions include 'November work. The fire is paid for in October.' and 'Khartoum, as London saw it in 1913.' Scheduled Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday at 7:30 pm in Meta Business Suite.

violet.title: Humor Profile
violet.use: Sort his saved and sent memes by topic and format, then write a humor profile GOLEM can learn.
violet.tools: Instagram Accounts Center (Download your information), Google Sheets, VS Code or Notepad++ for JSON
violet.inputs: His Instagram data export (saved posts and messages) or a folder of meme screenshots.
violet.output: A tagged sheet, counts by topic, format and mechanism, a short humor profile and a do-not-post list.
method: Request the export: Accounts Center, Your information and permissions, Download your information. JSON, all time, saved posts and messages. It can take a day.
List saved-post links in a sheet; add memes he sent in DMs.

Tag each with one topic (history, Orthodoxy, Judaism study, politics, tech and AI, retail work, gym, absurd), one format (macro, screenshot, video, map joke) and one mechanism (irony, exaggeration, niche reference, deadpan, callback).
Tag 100 first; the counts settle fast.
Pivot the tags and note the top three of each, plus what he never saves.
Write the profile in eight lines or fewer: what lands, which formats, what he shares versus only saves.
Build a do-not-post list: anything punching at an ethnic or religious group, showing a real private person, or tying a brand to him.
violet.prompt: Archivist of Jests, here are {number} memes I saved or sent, one per line with a short description: {list}. Tag each with one topic, one format and one mechanism (irony, exaggeration, niche reference, deadpan, callback). Return a table, then counts per tag, then a humor profile in eight lines or fewer: what lands for me, favored formats, what I share versus only save, what I never save. Finally list any meme that should never be posted from my brands, and why (targets a group, shows a real private person, or identifies me).
checklist: Profile in eight lines or fewer
Profile saved where GOLEM can read it
violet.example: First 100 from the November export. Topics: history 31, tech and AI 17, Orthodoxy 14, politics 12, retail work 9, absurd 9, gym 8. Formats: screenshot 38, macro 33, video 22, map joke 7. Mechanisms: niche reference 41, deadpan 27, irony 19. Profile lines: 'Lands hardest when the joke needs a footnote.' 'Shares map and Byzantine jokes; only saves gym memes.' 'Deadpan over loud.' 'Never saves reaction-face videos.' Do-not-post: four items (two punch at a religious group, one shows a coworker's real screenshot, one shows his old username). Saved to the Atelier folder for the Hook Lab and eli Grid kits.

white.title: Rule of Prayer Builder
white.use: Drafts a short morning and evening prayer rule in Slavonic and English to bring to his priest.
white.tools: azbyka.ru (Slavonic and Russian prayer texts), the Jordanville Prayer Book (Holy Trinity Monastery), iPhone Notes
white.inputs: Minutes available morning and evening, which prayers he already knows, and any rule a priest has already given.
white.output: A one-page rule (morning and evening) with each prayer in Slavonic and English, timed, marked as a draft for the priest.
method: Start from what a priest has given, if anything; the kit never overrides it.
Measure honest time: on shift days, how many minutes before leaving and before sleep.
Build from the standard opening: the Trisagion prayers (O Heavenly King, Holy God, Most Holy Trinity, Our Father).
Add a small core: morning, a psalm (Psalm 50) and the Creed; evening, a short prayer before sleep and an examination of the day.
Lay each prayer out in two columns: Slavonic (from azbyka.ru) and English (Jordanville wording).
Mark the page 'draft for my priest' and add the question for him at the bottom.
white.prompt: You are Elder of the Rule, Ustav Keeper. I am an Orthodox catechumen. Minutes available: {morning minutes} in the morning, {evening minutes} at night; on shift days {shift-day minutes}. Prayers I know: {list}. Any rule my priest gave: {rule or none}. Draft a short daily rule built from the standard Orthodox morning and evening prayers, with the Slavonic and English text side by side and a time estimate for each part. Give a shorter shift-day version. Mark it as a draft to show my priest. Do not tell me what my priest should approve; list the questions I should ask him about it.
checklist: Any rule from a priest kept as the base
Honest minutes measured for both kinds of day
Slavonic and English side by side
Marked as a draft for the priest
Priest questions written at the bottom
white.example: Morning: 9 minutes on school days, 6 on shift days. Evening: 8 minutes. No rule given yet. Draft morning: the Trisagion prayers, with 'Царю Небесный' (O Heavenly King) and 'Отче наш' (Our Father) in both columns, then Psalm 50 and the Creed (Символ веры). Shift-day version drops Psalm 50. Evening: the Trisagion prayers, one prayer before sleep, a two-minute examination of the day, and 'Into Thy hands, O Lord.' Read aloud, the full morning runs 8 minutes 40 seconds. Bottom of the page: 'Draft for Father. Questions: Is this a fitting size for a catechumen? Should I add a prayer to my guardian angel? Pray in Slavonic, English or both?' The page goes to Questions for My Priest.

white.title: The Julian Day
white.use: Today's feast, saint, readings and fast on the Julian calendar, in one short card.
white.tools: Holy Trinity Russian Orthodox Church calendar (holytrinityorthodox.com, ROCOR), azbyka.ru/days, OCA.org lives of saints
white.output: A card with the Julian date, feast or saint, fasting rule for the day, the Epistle and Gospel references, and one line on the saint.
method: Convert: for 1900 to 2099 the Julian date is the civil date minus 13 days.
Check the ROCOR calendar for the day: feast rank, saints, readings, fast notation.
Cross-check the saint's life on azbyka.ru or OCA.org.
Note the fast: Wednesdays and Fridays are fast days outside fast-free weeks; fasting seasons have their own rules.
Write one line on the saint, drawn from the life, not invented.
Put the card on the phone lock-screen note or in Notes each morning.
When sources disagree, record both and add the question for the priest.
white.prompt: You are Keeper of Days, Menologion. Today is {civil date}, a {weekday}. Give me the Julian calendar date, the main feast or saint commemorated according to the Russian Orthodox calendar, the fasting rule for the day, and the Epistle and Gospel references, in a short card. Add one sentence about the saint from a reliable life. Say which calendar source I should check to confirm, and tell me plainly if you are unsure of any item rather than guessing.
checklist: Saint cross-checked on a second source
Disagreements sent to Questions for My Priest
white.example: Friday Nov 6, 2026 is Oct 24 on the Julian calendar. The ROCOR calendar lists the icon of the Mother of God 'Joy of All Who Sorrow', a feast well loved in Russian parishes, along with the martyr Arethas and those with him. Fast: Friday, so a fast day (no meat, dairy or eggs in the usual practice; how strictly he keeps it is for his priest). Readings: copied from the calendar page that morning. One line: the 'Joy of All Who Sorrow' icon became famous in Moscow in 1688 after a healing attributed to prayer before it. Card saved in Notes at 6:40 am, read on the train to White Plains. Tomorrow's card notes that Saturday Nov 7 is Julian Oct 25.

white.title: Fasting Guide
white.use: Fast days and seasons ahead, simple meals that fit, and the questions to settle with his priest.
white.tools: Holy Trinity Russian Orthodox Church calendar (ROCOR), Google Calendar, iPhone Notes
white.inputs: The next fasting period, his shift and training schedule, and any guidance his priest has given.
white.output: A calendar of fast days with the general rule for each, five simple meals in US measures, and a question list for the priest.
method: Mark the weekly fasts (Wednesday and Friday) and the season ahead on the calendar.
Nativity Fast: Nov 15 to Dec 24 Julian, which is Nov 28 to Jan 6 civil.
Note the general pattern from the calendar: days with fish, wine and oil allowed versus strict days.
Treat these as the general rule only; a catechumen's portion is set with the priest, considering work and lifting.
Plan simple meals: beans, lentils, rice, potatoes, vegetables, peanut butter, oatmeal; fish only where allowed and approved.
Prep two fast-day meals on Sunday for shift days.
Write the questions for the priest before the season starts.
white.prompt: You are Sacristan, Vigil Planner. The next fast is {fast} from {civil start} to {civil end}. My schedule: {shifts, classes, training days}. Guidance from my priest so far: {guidance or none}. Mark the days of the general rule (strict, oil and wine, fish allowed) from the Russian Orthodox calendar. Give five simple fast-day meals in US measures with protein in mind. Do not decide how strictly I should keep the fast; list the questions to bring to my priest, including how it fits a 40-hour work week and strength training.
checklist: Wednesday and Friday fasts on the calendar
Five meals planned in US measures
Two meals prepped for shift days
Questions written for the priest before the fast starts
white.example: Nativity Fast: Nov 28, 2026 to Jan 6, 2027 civil. The calendar shows the general pattern with fish allowed on many weekends early in the fast and stricter days before Nativity. Meals: lentil soup (1 cup dry lentils, 1 diced onion, 2 carrots, 4 cups water, 1 teaspoon cumin); black beans and rice (1 can beans, 1 cup rice); peanut butter oatmeal (1 cup oats, 2 tablespoons peanut butter, 1 banana); chickpea salad sandwiches; potato and cabbage hash. On fish-allowed days, a can of tuna or salmon, if his priest agrees. Questions: 'How strictly should a catechumen keep this fast? Can I take extra protein shakes made without dairy while training for a heavy bench? Does working closing shifts change anything?'

white.title: Parish Visit Card
white.use: What to notice and record at each ROCOR, OCA or Moscow Patriarchate parish visit, on one card.
white.tools: iPhone Notes, Google Maps, parish websites, TrainTime (Metro-North)
white.inputs: The parish name, jurisdiction, service time and how he will get there.
white.output: A filled visit card with practical facts, observations and impressions, saved for comparing parishes later.
method: Before: read the parish website for service times, language and whether a vigil is served Saturday night.
Plan the trip without a car and arrive 15 minutes early.
Notice and record: language (Slavonic, English, mix), calendar (Julian or revised), length of service, choir.
Record people: how newcomers were greeted, whether there are young adults, whether the priest has time to talk.
Record practical fit: travel time from Chappaqua, catechism classes, confession times.
Write impressions within an hour, before memory blurs.
Do not decide after one visit; aim for at least two visits per parish being considered.
white.prompt: You are Pilgrim of the Parishes, Parish Scout. I am visiting {parish name} ({jurisdiction}) on {date} for {service}. I travel from Chappaqua without a car. Give me a short pre-visit sheet: what to check on the parish website, how to dress and behave as a newcomer and catechumen, and the trip timing. Then give me a blank visit card with fields for language, calendar, service length, choir, welcome, young adults, priest availability, catechism, travel time, and impressions. After I fill it in {paste notes}, summarize it beside my earlier cards {paste}.
checklist: Service time confirmed on the parish site
Trip planned to arrive 15 minutes early
Second visit planned before any decision
white.example: Visit: St. Nicholas Russian Orthodox Cathedral, Moscow Patriarchate, East 97th Street in Manhattan, Sunday Divine Liturgy. Trip: Harlem Line from Chappaqua to 125th Street, then the 6 train to 96th Street and a short walk; about 1 hour 25 minutes. Card: language mostly Church Slavonic, sermon in Russian; Julian calendar; service about 2 hours; strong choir; a parishioner explained where to stand and showed him the candle stand; few people his age; the priest spoke with him briefly after and named a weekday for questions. Catechism: ask by email. Impression: deeply Russian in feel, beautiful, harder to join without fluent Russian. Second visit set for a Saturday vigil before comparing with a ROCOR visit.

white.title: Questions for My Priest
white.use: Keeps his questions for his priest in one place, ready to ask; never answers them for him.
white.tools: iPhone Notes (one pinned note) or Google Docs
white.inputs: Any question about faith, practice, prayer, fasting or conscience as it comes up.
white.output: A dated, grouped list of open questions, with room to record what his priest said.
method: Capture the question the moment it arises, in his own words, with the date.
Tag it: prayer, fasting, catechism, sacraments, conscience, Judaism study, other.
Add one line of context so he can explain it quickly in person.
Before meeting the priest, choose the three that matter most; do not bring twenty.
After the conversation, record the priest's answer in his own summary and the date.
Move answered questions to an archive section; never edit the priest's answer later to suit himself.
The keeper may help phrase a question clearly; it never supplies an answer or a ruling.
white.prompt: You are The Bell of the Chance, Dukhovnik Desk. Here are my open questions for my priest: {paste list}. New one: {question}. Rephrase each so it is clear and short, tag it, and add one line of context. Group them and pick the three most important for my next conversation on {date}, saying why. Do not answer any of the questions, do not tell me what the Church teaches on them, and do not predict what my priest will say. Your job is to help me ask well.
checklist: Top three chosen before the meeting
No answers supplied by the keeper
white.example: Open list on Nov 5 holds seven questions. New one: 'Can I keep studying Talmud with my Chabad friends during the Nativity Fast?' The Bell rephrases it: 'Is my weekly Jewish text study with Chabad friends, as study and not practice, fitting for a catechumen?' Tag: Judaism study. Context: one evening a week, Pirkei Avot and Torah portion. Top three for Sunday Nov 15 after Liturgy: 1) how strictly to keep the Nativity Fast while training, 2) the study question, 3) when catechism classes start and what to read first. The Bell does not answer any of them. After the talk, Elijah writes: 'Nov 15, Father said...' in his own words and moves the three to the archive.

white.title: Gospel and Parsha
white.use: Pairs Sunday's Gospel reading with that week's Torah portion for side-by-side study.
white.tools: Holy Trinity Russian Orthodox Church calendar (Sunday readings), Sefaria (parsha text and commentary), Hebcal (weekly portion schedule)
white.output: A one-page pairing: both readings, one shared theme, two differences, and three study questions.
method: Look up Sunday's Gospel on the ROCOR calendar (Julian date is civil minus 13).
Look up the week's Torah portion on Hebcal (the Shabbat after that Sunday reads it).
Read both in full: the Gospel in an English translation, the parsha on Sefaria with Rashi on two key verses.
Find one shared theme honestly; do not force one if none exists.
Note two differences in how each tradition reads the theme.
Write three study questions; keep Jewish commentary as Jewish readings, not Christian proof texts.
Read it Sunday afternoon; bring one question to chavruta.
white.prompt: You are Reader of the Law, Parsha Scholar. Sunday's Gospel is {reference}. This week's Torah portion is {parsha}, {Genesis reference}. Summarize each in four lines. Name one theme they share, if there honestly is one, and two ways the Jewish commentators (cite Rashi or another named commentator on Sefaria) and Orthodox Christian reading treat it differently. Give three study questions. Present the Jewish tradition on its own terms; do not treat the parsha as a proof text for Christianity.
checklist: Sunday's Gospel looked up on the Julian calendar
Commentary on two verses read on Sefaria
white.example: Week of Nov 8 to 14, 2026. Hebcal gives Toldot (Genesis 25:19 to 28:9) for Shabbat Nov 14. Suppose the ROCOR calendar lists the parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19 to 31) for Sunday Nov 8; he confirms it that morning. Shared theme: reversal, the expected heir or the comfortable man does not receive what he assumed. Differences: Rashi on Genesis 25:34 reads the verse as Scripture testifying to Esau's wickedness, a judgment on character; the Orthodox reading of Luke stresses mercy and the afterlife. Questions: What does each text say inheritance is for? Is Jacob's deception excused anywhere in the commentary? What does Abraham's role in each reading suggest? Question two goes to chavruta.

white.title: Chavruta Session
white.use: One paired study session on a single text on Sefaria, using the classic chavruta method.
white.tools: Sefaria (free, with translations and commentaries), a timer, Google Docs
white.inputs: A short text (a mishnah, a few verses, a Rashi), a partner (a Chabad friend, Andy, or GOLEM), and 45 minutes.
white.output: Session notes: the text, each partner's reading, the questions that stayed open, one line to remember.
method: Pick a short text; a single mishnah is enough for 45 minutes.
Read it aloud twice, once in Hebrew if possible (with help), once in English.
Each partner explains it in their own words; the other must restate it before disagreeing.
Ask the four questions: what does it say, why is it phrased this way, what problem is it solving, what would it look like lived?
Open one classic commentary on Sefaria and test both readings against it.
Argue for the reading you like less for five minutes.
Write the open question and one line to remember; it is study, recorded as study.
white.prompt: You are Study Companion, my chavruta partner. Today's text: {Sefaria reference}. Act as a real partner, not a lecturer. Read it with me line by line, ask me to explain each line in my own words before you add anything, and push back when my reading is thin. Bring in one named commentary from Sefaria only after I have given my reading. Ask me to argue the opposite reading for a few minutes. End with my open question and one line to remember. Keep this as study of Jewish texts, not religious instruction for practice.
checklist: Open question and one line recorded
white.example: Text: Pirkei Avot 1:14, Hillel: 'If I am not for myself, who will be for me? And when I am for myself, what am I? And if not now, when?' Partner: a Chabad friend over the phone, 45 minutes. Elijah reads it as a call to self-reliance balanced by duty to others. His friend reads the middle line more sharply: a self that is only for itself is nothing. Restatements done, they open the Bartenura commentary on Sefaria, which reads the first line as a person needing to acquire merit himself, since no one else can do it for him. Elijah argues his friend's side for five minutes. Open question: does 'now' mean urgency or that the present is the only place for action? Line kept: 'And if not now, when?'

white.title: Slavonic Drill
white.use: Ten minutes a day of Church Slavonic: letters, one prayer line, and five vocabulary cards.
white.tools: Anki, azbyka.ru (texts in Slavonic and civil script), Ponomar (free Slavonic liturgical texts and fonts)
white.inputs: Ten minutes and the current prayer being learned.
white.output: A growing Anki deck, one prayer line read aloud cleanly each day, and a weekly self-test.
method: Minutes 0 to 2: letters. Learn the Slavonic-only letters (ѣ yat, ѡ omega, ѳ fita, ѵ izhitsa, ѯ ksi, ѱ psi) and the titlo abbreviations.
Minutes 2 to 6: one line of the current prayer, read aloud slowly from the Slavonic script, then the civil-script version to check.
Minutes 6 to 9: five Anki cards, Slavonic word on the front, meaning and stress on the back.
Minute 9 to 10: read the whole prayer so far aloud once.
Order prayers by use: Trisagion prayers, Our Father, the Creed, Psalm 50.
Each Sunday, read the week's lines to a recording and listen for stress errors.
Use the train ride or a Walgreens break for the Anki part.
white.prompt: You are Reader of Slavonic, Church Slavonic Tutor. I am on {prayer}, line {number}. Give me that line in Church Slavonic, then in modern civil Cyrillic, a word-by-word English gloss with stress marks, and a natural English translation. Point out any Slavonic-only letters or titlo abbreviations in it. Then give five Anki cards in the format front;back from this line. Keep it to a ten-minute session. If I paste my transliteration {my attempt}, correct it gently.
checklist: Whole prayer so far read once
white.example: Day 3, the Trisagion. Line: 'Святый Боже, Святый Крепкий, Святый Бессмертный, помилуй нас' in civil script; the Slavonic print shows the letter ѧ (small yus) in the first word. Gloss: Святый, holy; Боже, O God; Крепкий, mighty; Бессмертный, immortal; помилуй, have mercy; нас, on us. Translation: 'Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us.' Five cards added, for example 'помилуй;have mercy (stress on -ми-)'. Elijah reads the line six times on the 7:12 am train, and on Sunday his recording shows he stresses Бессмертный on the wrong syllable; it is fixed and the card is marked hard.

white.title: Creeds Side by Side
white.use: One question answered across Orthodoxy, Catholicism, Judaism and Islam, each from its own sources.
white.tools: Sefaria, Catechism of the Catholic Church (vatican.va), the Longer Catechism of St. Philaret (free online), Quran.com
white.output: A four-column table: each tradition's answer in its own terms, the primary source, and where they agree or differ.
method: Phrase the question neutrally so each tradition can answer it on its own terms.
For each tradition, find a primary or official source: scripture, catechism, legal code.
Write each answer as a believer of that tradition would recognize it.
Cite chapter and verse or paragraph number for every claim.
Note real internal diversity (for example, Sunni and Shia, or different Jewish movements).
Mark agreements and differences without ranking the traditions.
Questions of his own practice go to his priest, not into this table.
white.prompt: You are Comparer of Creeds, Comparative Religion. Question: {question}. Answer it four times: Orthodox Christianity, Catholicism, Judaism and Islam. Each answer in five lines or fewer, in terms an informed believer of that tradition would accept, with a cited primary or official source (verse, catechism paragraph, or code). Note major internal disagreements. Then list where they agree and where they differ. No ranking, no polemic, and no advice about my own practice.
checklist: Personal practice questions sent to the priest
white.example: Question: what is fasting for, and when is it required? Orthodox: fasting on Wednesdays and Fridays and in four seasons as repentance and preparation, with the Typikon and the Fathers as authority. Catholic: abstinence from meat on Fridays and fasting on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday (Code of Canon Law, canons 1250 to 1252; Catechism 2043). Judaism: the fast of Yom Kippur commanded as 'afflicting the soul' (Leviticus 16:29 to 31), with Isaiah 58, read on that day, warning that fasting without justice is empty; other fasts are rabbinic. Islam: fasting in Ramadan prescribed 'that you may become mindful of God' (Quran 2:183). Agreement: fasting as discipline and repentance. Difference: frequency, and whether the rule comes from scripture or later law.

white.title: The Emet Test
white.use: Tests whether an esoteric or prophetic reading names something checkable that could prove it wrong.
white.tools: Google Docs, Wayback Machine (to check what was claimed before the event), Sefaria (for source texts)
white.inputs: The claim (a code, numerology, prophecy or hidden-meaning reading) and where it came from.
white.output: A verdict: testable and passed, testable and failed, or untestable, with the reasons in plain words.
method: Write the claim in one sentence: what it says will be, or is, true.
Ask: what observation would prove it wrong? If none, it is untestable; stop there.
Ask: was the prediction made before the event, with a date? Check the Wayback Machine for the original wording.
Ask: is it specific (place, date, event) or vague enough to fit many outcomes?
Ask: how many other patterns could have been found the same way (the many-tries problem)?
Compare the outcome with the original, not the revised, claim.
Give the verdict. A failed or untestable claim can still be studied as history or symbol.
white.prompt: You are Justice of Claims, Skeptic. Claim: {paste claim}. Source: {where it came from}. Restate it in one sentence. Tell me what observation would prove it wrong, or say it names nothing checkable. Check whether it was stated before the event it points to and how specific it was. Estimate how many similar patterns could be found by chance with the same method. Give a verdict: testable and passed, testable and failed, or untestable, and explain why in plain words. Do not mock the tradition the claim comes from; judge the claim.
checklist: Outcome compared with the original wording
white.example: Claim: the 'blood moon tetrad' of four total lunar eclipses in 2014 to 2015, falling on Passover and Sukkot, signaled a major event for Israel, popularized in a 2013 book. Test: what would prove it wrong? The book gave no single named event or date, only 'something significant', so nearly any news could be fitted afterward. Pre-event check: the claim was made in advance, which is good, but the wording on archived pages is vague. Many-tries: Passover and Sukkot fall near full moons by design of the Hebrew calendar, so eclipses on those dates are not rare in any special way. Outcome: no event matching a clear prediction. Verdict: effectively untestable as stated; worth studying only as a case of modern prophecy culture.

yellow.title: Appointment Prep
yellow.use: Builds the list of facts and questions to bring to a doctor visit. Prepares; never diagnoses.
yellow.tools: iPhone Notes, iPhone Health app, the provider's patient portal (for example MyChart, if the practice uses it)
yellow.inputs: The reason for the visit, when it started, what makes it better or worse, current medications and supplements.
yellow.output: A one-page visit sheet: symptom timeline, medications, three priority questions, and space for the answers.
method: Write the reason for the visit in one sentence.
Build a timeline: when it started, how often, how bad (0 to 10), what helps, what worsens it.
List every medication, supplement and dose, including protein powder or creatine.
Note relevant context: work on his feet 40 hours a week, lifting program, CVAC lifting and carrying.
Pick the three questions that matter most and put them at the top.
Bring the sheet; write the answers down during the visit or ask to record notes in the portal.
Afterward, put any follow-up, test or referral on the calendar the same day.
yellow.prompt: You are Chief Physician, Care Coordinator. I have a doctor visit on {date} for {reason}. Details: started {when}, frequency {how often}, severity {0 to 10}, better with {x}, worse with {y}. Medications and supplements: {list}. Context: {work, training}. Help me prepare: organize this into a clear timeline, list what the doctor will probably ask so I can have answers ready, and suggest my top three questions. Do not diagnose or guess what it is. Tell me which symptoms, if they appear before the visit, mean I should seek care sooner.
checklist: Top three questions at the top
Follow-ups on the calendar the same day
yellow.example: Visit: Nov 19 with his primary care doctor for front-of-shoulder pain on the right side. Timeline: started about Oct 10 after raising bench volume; 3 out of 10 during pressing, 1 at rest, worse after lifting a stretcher at CVAC, better with ice and lighter weeks. Medications: none; supplements: whey protein and creatine, 5 grams daily. Context: stands for 8-hour shifts; benches three times a week. Questions: 1) Should I stop pressing, change it, or keep going? 2) Do I need an exam by a physical therapist? 3) What would mean I should come back sooner? The keeper names no condition. Seek care sooner if: sudden weakness, numbness down the arm, or a pop with swelling.

yellow.title: Insurance Navigator
yellow.use: Reads a medical bill, explanation of benefits or denial, and lists exactly what to ask and whom.
yellow.tools: The insurer's member portal, the provider's billing office, NY Department of Financial Services (external appeal information), iPhone scanner in Notes
yellow.inputs: The bill, the matching explanation of benefits (EOB), and the insurance card details.
yellow.output: A plain reading of what was charged, what insurance paid, why, what he owes, and a call script.
method: Match the bill to the EOB by date of service and provider; never pay a bill before the EOB arrives.
Read the EOB lines: billed amount, allowed amount, plan paid, patient responsibility, and the reason codes.
Ask the provider for an itemized bill with procedure (CPT) codes if the bill is a single total.
Check for errors: duplicate lines, services not received, out-of-network flags on an in-network visit.
For surprise out-of-network bills at in-network facilities, ask about protections under the federal No Surprises Act.
For a denial, ask the insurer for the reason in writing and the appeal deadline; internal appeal first, then New York's external appeal if denied.
Log every call: date, person, reference number, what was promised.
yellow.prompt: You are Almoner, Insurance Clerk. Here is my bill: {paste or describe lines}. Here is the EOB: {paste}. My plan: {name and whether I am on a parent's plan}. Explain each line in plain words: billed, allowed, paid, what I owe and why. Flag possible errors and anything that looks like a surprise out-of-network charge. Tell me what to ask the provider and the insurer, in order, and write a short call script for each. If this is a denial, tell me the appeal steps and what deadline to ask for.
checklist: Surprise-billing protections asked about if relevant
Appeal deadline found for any denial
Every call logged with reference number
yellow.example: A $340 bill arrives for bloodwork from his physical. The EOB shows the lab billed $410, the allowed amount was $0, and the reason code says 'out-of-network provider'. The doctor's office is in-network, but the sample went to an outside lab. The Almoner flags it: he did not choose the lab. Call 1, to the doctor's billing office: 'Which lab processed my Oct 14 bloodwork, and is it in my plan's network?' Call 2, to the insurer: 'I was not told the lab was out-of-network. Can this be reprocessed, and do surprise-billing protections apply?' Reference numbers logged. The insurer reprocesses it at the in-network rate, and he owes a $15 copay.

yellow.title: Checkup Calendar
yellow.use: Puts routine checkups, cleanings, vaccines and screenings for the next 12 months on the calendar.
yellow.tools: Google Calendar, iPhone Health app (health records), the provider's patient portal, CDC adult immunization schedule (cdc.gov)
yellow.inputs: Dates of his last physical, dental cleaning, eye exam and vaccines, plus requirements for the EMT course.
yellow.output: A 12-month calendar of appointments with booking reminders four weeks ahead.
method: Find last dates: physical, dental cleaning, eye exam, flu shot, Tdap, and any vaccine records.
Standard rhythm to confirm with his doctor: yearly physical, dental cleaning about every six months, flu shot each fall.
Check EMT course requirements early: many programs ask for proof of vaccines and a recent physical or TB test.
Book each visit four weeks before the target month; the reminder goes on the calendar, not just the visit.
Pair visits with days off and transit plans.
Record each visit's result and next date in a single note.
Any new symptom between visits goes to Appointment Prep, not to the next routine visit.
yellow.prompt: You are Physician of Seasons, Prevention Planner. My last visits: physical {date}, dental cleaning {date}, eye exam {date}, flu shot {date}, Tdap {date}. Upcoming: EMT course starting {date} with requirements {paste}. Build a 12-month calendar of routine visits for a healthy 23-year-old, noting which intervals I should confirm with my doctor or dentist. Add booking reminders four weeks ahead and flag anything the EMT course needs before it starts. Do not give medical advice beyond standard schedules.
checklist: Each visit has a booking reminder
yellow.example: Last physical: March 2025, overdue. Last cleaning: May 2026. Flu shot: not yet this season. Tdap: 2019, good until about 2029. EMT course: planned for spring, and the program asks for a physical, immunization proof and a TB test. Calendar: flu shot this week at Walgreens on a day off; physical booked for late November (reminder set today since it is overdue), with the doctor asked to include the TB test and complete the course form; dental cleaning in November (six months after May); eye exam in February; next cleaning in May 2027; next physical in late 2027. Immunization record pulled from the patient portal and saved as a PDF in 60 CVAC and EMT.

yellow.title: Sleep Log
yellow.use: A two-week sleep record and the pattern it shows, with simple changes to test.
yellow.tools: iPhone Health app (Sleep schedule), Google Sheets, CBT-i Coach app (free, from the VA)
yellow.inputs: Two weeks of bedtime, wake time, shift times, caffeine timing, and a morning rating.
yellow.output: A two-week table, average sleep by day type (shift, school, off), the main pattern, and one change to test.
method: Each morning, log: lights out, fell asleep (estimate), wake time, wake-ups, how rested (1 to 5).
Also log: shift end time, last caffeine, screens in the last hour, training that day.
After 14 days, average total sleep by day type: closing shift, opening shift, school, off.
Find the pattern: which day type gets the least sleep, and what precedes the worst nights.
Choose one change to test for a week (fixed wake time, last caffeine by 2 pm, phone out of bed).
Re-log a week and compare.
See a clinician if there is loud snoring with gasping, very heavy daytime sleepiness, or poor sleep lasting a month despite changes.
yellow.prompt: You are Somnus, Sleep Planner. Here is my two-week sleep log: {paste rows with date, lights out, asleep, wake, wake-ups, rating, shift end, last caffeine, screens, training}. Average my sleep by day type (closing shift, opening shift, school, off). Describe the main pattern in plain words. Suggest one change to test for a week, and how to judge it. Do not diagnose any sleep disorder; tell me which signs mean I should talk to a doctor.
yellow.example: Fourteen days logged from Oct 20. Averages: off days 8 hours 10 minutes; school days 6 hours 50 minutes; after closing shifts 5 hours 40 minutes. Pattern: after a 10 pm close he gets home around 10:30, scrolls until 1 am, and still wakes at 7 for the gym or class. The two worst nights both had a coffee after 6 pm on shift. Change for the test week: no caffeine after 3 pm on closing days, phone charging across the room, and gym moved to the afternoon after closes. Test week: post-close sleep rises to 6 hours 45 minutes and the morning rating from 2 to 3.5. No warning signs noted; the change stays.

yellow.title: The Brief Builder
yellow.use: Builds a paid brief in house format, from headline finding to 90-day trajectory.
yellow.tools: Google Docs, Google Sheets, Wayback Machine, archive.today, Gephi, YouTube Data API (free quota)
yellow.inputs: The topic or narrative, the buyer, the collection window, and the data gathered.
yellow.output: A 6 to 10 page brief: headline finding, scope and method, landscape taxonomy, three traction case studies, vulnerability map, 90-day trajectory.
method: Headline finding: one or two sentences a busy reader can repeat, with the key number.
Scope and method: the question, platforms, date window, how accounts and posts were selected, and limits.
Landscape taxonomy: group the actors and narratives into four to six types (state media, aligned influencers, diaspora activists, commercial amplifiers, organic users).
Three traction case studies: each a post or campaign that spread, with reach numbers, path of spread, and archived evidence.
Vulnerability map: which audiences, platforms or gaps the operation exploits, and where it is weak.
90-day trajectory: what is likely next, with probabilities and signposts to watch.
Run Peer Review Pass and the Methods Appendix before it ships.
yellow.prompt: You are Chief Researcher, Lead Analyst. Topic: {narrative or operation}. Buyer: {who}. Window: {dates}. My data: {summary of accounts, posts, metrics, archives}. Draft the brief in house format: headline finding (two sentences with the key number), scope and method, landscape taxonomy (four to six actor types), three traction case studies with reach and spread path, vulnerability map, and a 90-day trajectory with probabilities and signposts. Use only the evidence I gave; mark every gap where more evidence is needed. Describe accounts and organizations by documented acts only.
checklist: Headline finding repeatable in one breath
Taxonomy has four to six types
Three case studies with archived evidence
Peer review and methods appendix done
yellow.example: Sample brief: English-language narratives on X and TikTok portraying the RSF as a counterterrorism partner, Sept 1 to Oct 31. Headline finding: about 40 accounts produced most of the reposted content, and three videos accounted for most of the views. Taxonomy: Gulf-based commentators, paid-looking new accounts, Sudanese diaspora supporters, and organic users who repeated the frame. Case studies: a TikTok video with a large view count traced to a reupload network; a hashtag pushed by a cluster of new accounts in one evening; a podcast clip clipped and spread on X. Vulnerability: few English-language Sudanese voices answer it. Trajectory: 60 percent chance the frame shifts to reconstruction talk within 90 days. All figures are placeholders until the data supports them.

yellow.title: Peer Review Pass
yellow.use: A hostile reader's pass on a brief before it ships: what a skeptical expert would attack.
yellow.inputs: The full draft brief and its methods appendix.
yellow.output: A ranked list of weaknesses with severity, the questions a critic would ask, and a ship or hold verdict.
method: Read as three critics: a subject expert, a methods expert, and a reader from the side the brief criticizes.
Test the headline finding: does the evidence actually support it, or only something smaller?
Test the sample: how were accounts chosen, could the selection create the result?
Test attribution: is 'coordinated' shown by timing, content and account data, or only asserted?
Test numbers: are view counts, account counts and dates consistent across sections?
Rank issues as fatal, major or minor.
Verdict: ship, ship after fixes, or hold. Any fatal issue means hold.
yellow.prompt: You are Board of Quality Control, Peer Reviewer. Here is a draft brief: {paste} and its methods appendix: {paste}. Review it as three hostile readers: a regional expert, a social media methods expert, and someone from the side the brief criticizes. For each, list their strongest objections. Check that the headline finding is supported, the sample does not create the result, coordination claims are shown rather than asserted, and numbers match across sections. Rank issues fatal, major or minor and give a verdict. Do not rewrite the brief.
yellow.example: Draft brief on pro-RSF narratives, 8 pages. The methods critic finds a major issue: accounts were found by searching three hashtags, so the brief can say these hashtags were coordinated, not that the whole narrative was. Fix: narrow the headline. The regional critic flags a minor issue: one case study calls a Gulf commentator 'state-backed' without evidence; change to 'based in' with his stated employer. The opposing reader asks whether pro-SAF networks behave the same way; the Board calls this a major gap and suggests one paragraph naming it as out of scope. Numbers: the case study gives 1.2 million views, the summary says 1.4 million; fix. No fatal issues. Verdict: ship after fixes.

yellow.title: Archive Dive
yellow.use: Finds what a website, organization or person said and filed in the past, using free archives.
yellow.tools: Wayback Machine, archive.today, Chronicling America (Library of Congress), NYS Historic Newspapers, SEC EDGAR, ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, FARA eFile search (efile.fara.gov), OpenCorporates
yellow.inputs: The target (a site, organization or historical event) and the question.
yellow.output: A dated trail of findings, each with an archive link, and what changed over time.
method: Write the question: when did it start, who ran it, what did it say before, who paid?
Websites: Wayback Machine for first capture and changes over time; compare About and Team pages across years.
Organizations: OpenCorporates for registration, ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer for Form 990s, SEC EDGAR for companies.
Foreign influence: search FARA filings for agents registered to represent foreign governments or parties.
History: Chronicling America and NYS Historic Newspapers for older newspapers.
Archive every live page you rely on today.
Write the trail in date order with links; separate what is proven from what is suggested.
yellow.prompt: You are Excavator, Archive Diver. Target: {site, organization, or event}. Question: {question}. Give me a search plan using free archives: Wayback Machine, archive.today, OpenCorporates, ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, SEC EDGAR, FARA filings, Chronicling America and NYS Historic Newspapers. For each, say exactly what to search and what a useful result would look like. After I paste results {findings}, build a dated trail and separate what is documented from what is only suggested.
checklist: FARA searched if foreign links are suspected
Trail written with proven and suggested separated
yellow.example: Illustrative run. Target: a new 'Horn of Africa policy institute' website quoted in pro-RSF posts. Wayback Machine: first capture in March 2025; earlier the domain hosted a travel blog. The 2025 About page lists a director whose name disappears from the August 2025 capture. OpenCorporates: no registered entity under that name in the US or UK. ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer: no 990 filings, so not a US nonprofit filing returns. FARA: a search of registrants for Sudan turns up a US consultancy registered to work for a Sudanese party, but no link to this site. Trail: domain repurposed, no legal entity, a vanished director. Proven: the history above. Suggested only: a connection to any government. Both versions of the About page archived.

yellow.title: Network Map
yellow.use: Maps who amplifies whom in a set of accounts, using Gephi, and finds the clusters and bridges.
yellow.tools: Gephi (free), Google Sheets, Python with pandas (optional)
yellow.inputs: A list of interactions (reposts, replies, mentions) from public posts, collected by hand or by API within platform rules.
yellow.output: A Gephi map with clusters colored, the top accounts by influence and bridging role, and a one-paragraph reading.
method: Collect edges from public data: who reposted, quoted or mentioned whom, with date.
Build an edges CSV with columns Source, Target, Weight (count of interactions), and a nodes CSV with Id, Label, account created date.
In Gephi, import both through the Data Laboratory as a directed graph.
Run Modularity (Statistics panel) and color nodes by community; size nodes by in-degree.
Run Betweenness Centrality to find bridges between clusters.
Layout: ForceAtlas2 with Prevent Overlap; export as PNG and SVG.
Read it: name each cluster, the top amplifiers, the bridges, and anything odd (many new accounts in one cluster).
yellow.prompt: You are Cartographer of Minds, Network Mapper. I have interaction data: {describe or paste sample rows}. Help me turn it into Gephi-ready edges and nodes CSVs with the right column names. Then give me the Gephi steps: import, Modularity, Betweenness Centrality, ForceAtlas2 settings, and export. After I paste the statistics {top nodes by in-degree and betweenness, community sizes}, write a one-paragraph reading: clusters, main amplifiers, bridges, and anything suggesting coordination, without overstating it.
checklist: Data from public posts within platform rules
Edges CSV with Source, Target, Weight
Nodes CSV with Id and Label
yellow.example: Data: 412 repost and quote edges among 63 accounts on a Sudan hashtag over two weeks, collected by hand from public posts. Edges CSV built in Sheets. Gephi: Modularity finds four communities. Sizing by in-degree shows two accounts receiving a third of all reposts. Betweenness picks out one account that links a diaspora activist cluster to a cluster of 18 accounts all created in the same month, with no profile photos, that only repost each other and the two hubs. Reading: one dense cluster of new accounts amplifies two hubs and reaches wider audiences through a single bridge account. That pattern fits coordinated amplification but does not prove who runs it. Map exported for case study two of the brief.

yellow.title: Buyer Dossier
yellow.use: One page on a potential brief buyer: what they do, what they need, who decides, and the pitch angle.
yellow.tools: Organization websites, LinkedIn (free), ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, Google News, Google Docs
yellow.inputs: The organization's name and why it might buy.
yellow.output: A one-page dossier: mission, recent work, budget scale if public, likely decision-maker by role, need, and pitch angle.
method: Read the organization's site: mission, recent reports, programs, staff page.
Read their last three publications or posts to see what they care about now.
For nonprofits, check budget scale on ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer (organization finances only, not individuals).
Identify the decision-maker by role (research director, program lead) from public pages.
Find the gap: a topic they cover where they lack your angle (Sudan, Horn, Arabic-language networks).
Write the pitch angle in one sentence and the first ask.
Note any conflict: if their stance would bend the brief, mark it.
yellow.prompt: You are Patron Researcher, Buyer Researcher. Organization: {name}. Why it might buy: {reason}. From public information only, build a one-page dossier: mission, recent work (last three outputs), funding scale if public for the organization, the role most likely to decide, the gap my briefs could fill, a one-sentence pitch angle, and a first ask. Do not research private details of individuals. Flag any conflict of interest that could pressure my findings.
checklist: Pitch angle and first ask written
yellow.example: Organization: a mid-size US nonprofit that monitors online antisemitism and extremism. Mission and recent work: three recent reports on TikTok, on Telegram channels, and on hashtags after major news events; none on Africa. Public 990 shows a budget in the low millions, enough to pay for outside research. Decision-maker: the research director, named on the staff page. Gap: they have no coverage of how Sudan-related networks pick up antisemitic narratives or of Arabic-language amplification. Pitch angle: 'A brief on where Sudan war content and antisemitic narratives overlap online, which your current reports do not cover.' First ask: a 15-minute call. Conflict: none obvious; findings would not need to fit their stance.

yellow.title: Methods Appendix
yellow.use: Writes how a brief was done, so a reader can trust it and someone else could repeat it.
yellow.tools: Google Docs, Google Sheets, DISARM framework (free, for naming influence tactics)
yellow.inputs: The collection log, tools and versions, search terms, selection rules and known gaps.
yellow.output: A one to two page appendix: question, data sources, collection dates, selection, analysis, tactics named, limits and ethics.
method: State the research question exactly as the brief answers it.
List data sources and collection dates; note platform access limits at the time.
Give search terms and selection rules (which accounts or posts were in or out, and why).
Describe the analysis: counts, network measures, how coordination was judged (timing, identical text, account creation dates).
Name tactics with DISARM framework codes where they fit.
Limits: what the data cannot show, sample bias, deleted content.
Ethics: public data only, no private accounts, private individuals not named, archives kept.
yellow.prompt: You are Keeper of Methods, Methods Editor. Here is how I did this brief: {collection log, tools, dates, search terms, selection rules, analysis steps, known gaps}. Write a methods appendix of one to two pages with sections: question, data sources and collection window, search and selection, analysis, tactics named with DISARM framework codes where they clearly fit, limitations, and ethics. Plain language a non-specialist can follow. Do not claim more rigor than my log shows; list what I should have recorded but did not.
checklist: Search terms and selection rules given
yellow.example: Appendix for the pro-RSF narratives brief. Question: which accounts drove English-language posts framing the RSF as a counterterrorism partner, Sept 1 to Oct 31? Sources: public X and TikTok posts found by searching six terms in English, collected Nov 1 to 4. Selection: posts with at least 50 reposts or 10,000 views; accounts kept if they posted the frame three or more times. Analysis: repost network in Gephi; coordination judged by identical text within ten minutes and account creation clusters. Tactics: inauthentic accounts and amplification, tagged with the matching DISARM codes. Limits: deleted posts missed; no Arabic searches. Ethics: no private accounts; private users unnamed. The Keeper notes the search date per term was not logged.
